section: AA 120B-A - Critical Inquiries in Medical Ethics
subject: AA
title: Critical Inquiries in Medical Ethics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: We will engage with perspectives from feminist bioethics, disability studies, and critical race studies as a basis for analyzing, then developing, ideas and arguments about key topics in the field of medical ethics such as vaccination mandates, racialized health disparities, and biomedical research exploitation. Through frequent exercises and essay assignments, students will cultivate a sophisticated writing process that fosters intellectual growth as well as precision of analysis, persuasive argumentation, coherent organization, selection and incorporation of scholarly sources including scrupulous citation practices, and clarity of style.

section: AA 120L-A - Language, Thought, and Writing: Language + Race + Power
subject: AA
title: Language, Thought, and Writing: Language + Race + Power
Section Details: Miller Library 205 (Active Learning Classroom) | MW | 1:00 PM - 2:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: Thinks with scholars like James Baldwin, Geneva Smitherman, bell hooks, Paulo Freire, Audre Lorde, and April Baker-Bell about 1) the racial and colonial conditions that produced Standard Written English, 2) the social, political, economic, educational, psychological, and ethical stakes of normalizing the language of white enslavers and colonizers, and 3) alternative forms of language arts instruction. Throughout, we'll meditate on how we've been (mis)shaped in the image of the colonizer and work towards reimagining ourselves by reading and writing in a wide variety of genres including op-eds, educational social media threads, academic articles, TedTalks, spoken word, and critical autobiographies.

subject: AA
title: Performance, Politics, and Practice
Description: Introduces students to the study of performance by exploring its power and questioning how it frames our world. We examine how performance helps us make sense of and challenge economic, gendered, sexual, racialized, political, and social structures. Through lectures, critical readings, discussion, field trips, and embodied practice, students will study performance as a creative act, a means of understanding power, a methodology for passing on memory and identity, and a way of comprehending the world. Topics include: theater, dance, performance art, everyday life, protest, and the gendered, sexed, and racialized performance of bodies.

section: AA 125-A - Introduction to African American Cultures
subject: AA
title: Introduction to African American Cultures
Description: Offers a critical introduction to the cultural, political, and social, forces that have shaped the identity of people of African descent in the United States. We will focus on the experiences of African Americans from the Transatlantic Slave trade through contemporary social movements such as Black Lives Matter. Through readings, viewing, listening, and creating, we will examine the major movements, people, and ideas that have shaped African American identity and culture and gain an understanding of how African Americans have informed the broader national and global cultural and political landscapes.

section: AA 162-A - History of the Atlantic World
subject: AA
title: History of the Atlantic World
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Junior Class Standing or Below
Description: Explores the interconnected histories of Europe, North America, Latin America, and Africa through the lens of trade, migration, and the exchange of ideas, including revolutionary ideals. It begins with the reasons why Europeans sought out increasing trading connections with Africa and Asia, and how this drive impacted the so-called "discovery" and subsequent colonization of the Americas. Covered topics include genocide against Native Americans and land dispossession; the importation of African slaves; the growth of the plantation economy, especially in the Caribbean; and slavery. Also covers the Age of Revolutions, including the American, French, Haitian, and Spanish-American revolutions. The course ends with abolitionism and the rise of the mass indenture of South Asians in the 19th century.

subject: AA
title: Histories of the Present
Description: Through a social justice perspective, this discussion-based course asks how social, political, and cultural inequalities in the US have been produced, maintained, and challenged. Examining a wide selection of texts, the course draws on sociological, literary, visual, legal, and geographical methods of analysis to explore US history. We examine the forms and legacies of settler colonialism, enslavement, and the rise of capitalism; formations of race, gender, class, and sexuality; histories of immigration, gentrification, and resistance; and more.

section: AA 218-A - African American Migrations: Exiles, Expats, and Travelers
subject: AA
title: African American Migrations: Exiles, Expats, and Travelers
Description: “There is nothing in the life of America that I miss or yearn for. Barring war or catastrophe, I intend to remain in exile. I shall, of course, keep my American citizenship, my American passport; but I prefer to live out my days among a civilized people,” novelist Richard Wright declared in an unpublished essay, “I Choose Exile” (1951). Wright is part of a long list of African Americans who have expressed their fraught relationship with the nation. We will explore those forms of expression through three figures: the exile, the expat, and the traveler, examining how Black Americans critique the nation and construct alternate sites of home.

section: AA 228-A - Introduction to Race, Ethnicity, and Politics
subject: AA
title: Introduction to Race, Ethnicity, and Politics
Description: Examines broadly the ways in which racial and ethnic minorities influence and are influenced by American politics and public policy.  The course is organized in three parts.  Part I will explore the theoretical and historical contexts of race in American politics.  Part II will focus on race and political behavior, paying close attention to public opinion, participation, and representation.  Part III will examine particular policy-related case studies:  minority education, housing, employment, and criminal justice.

section: AA 247-A - African-American History, from Slavery to Freedom
subject: AA
title: African-American History, from Slavery to Freedom
Description: Explores the experience of blacks in American society from colonial times through the present. Subjects focus on racism, slavery, the role of African Americans in shaping the nation's history, and the ongoing struggle for equality. In exploring these historical developments, the course aims to expose students to a range of primary and scholarly sources; to hone critical thinking and interpretive skills; to help students write clearly, concisely, and precisely; and to foster clear, logical, and informed exchanges of ideas.

subject: AA
title: Anthropology, History, Memory
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY: AY 112, or AY 125, or HI 1XX, and Sophomore class standing or above
Description: Anthropologists have depicted cultural systems as timeless, paying limited attention to how historical experiences produce, and how they are shaped by, everyday beliefs and actions. Examines the significance of history for anthropological understanding and vice versa. Investigates how different cultures construct the past and how the past shapes everyday lives, our own and others. Explores sites such as myths, monuments, bodies, and archives. Questions what is the past? How is it present? How do societies remember? How do they forget? Topics include technology, time, travel, commemoration, war. Formerly offered as Anthropology 298B.

section: AA 267-A - Critical Perspectives on Sports and Societies
subject: AA
title: Critical Perspectives on Sports and Societies
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112
Description: This course explores the connections between sports and a broad range of anthropological concerns, including colonialism, resistance and domination, race, sexuality, and gender. Students consider questions such as: Why do we play the sports we do? Why are sporting performances socially significant, and how have groups and political regimes used this significance? What can teams, players, and brands tell us about how we (and others) see the world? In addressing these questions, students think critically about their own sporting experiences and develop a deeper and subtler understanding of the way that societies make sports and sports make societies.

subject: AA
title: Afrofuturism and Social Justice
Section Details: Miller Library 205 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 1:00 PM - 2:15 PM
Description: What does it mean to imagine a radically different Black future? Or futures—now? Afrofuturism is predicated on a world (or worlds) in which Black people make the future. Through “talking books,” “freedom dreams,” signs and wonderings, speculative visions, or a Midjourney prompt (“/imagine___”), this course invites us to reimagine our world through the lens of Afrofuturism. We will examine existing systems of dominance through various lenses, including literature, music, film, and digital and visual arts. We will engage with the multidimensionality of Afrofuturism (and its tensions with AfricanFuturism), and its implications for community building and social justice work. This is an Across the Walls course open to both students at Colby and students from the Reentry Sisters cohort.

subject: AA
title: Art, Medicine, and Race
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor Permission: ST 112, AA/AM 171, AA/AM 125, AR 101, or AA/AM/AR 157 - Copy
Description: This humanities lab explores the relations among art, medicine, and ideas about race from the eighteenth century to the present. Focusing on the Atlantic world and the African diaspora, we consider how chattel slavery, colonialism, and racial inequality have shaped constructions of medical knowledge, while medicine has informed conceptions of race as it intersects with gender, sexuality, and class. Students conduct independent research, deliver oral presentations, complete several writing assignments, and engage with contemporary artists and scholars.

subject: AA
title: Contemporary Theory
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112, AY 2XX or AY 3XX, a W1 course, and Junior Class Standing or above
Description: An analysis of the contemporary state of cultural anthropology through the investigation of contemporary theoretical approaches of central importance to the discipline. Examination of key theoretical concepts and their relevance for designing research questions, generating ethnographic perspectives, and building anthropological knowledge. Special attention to political economy, symbolic anthropology, poststructuralism, reflexive anthropology, postmodernism, and feminist and postcolonial anthropology. Assignments include both written and oral modes of analysis; strong emphasis on discussion and collaborative debate.

section: AA 334-A - The Great Depression: America in the 1930s
subject: AA
title: The Great Depression: America in the 1930s
Section Details: Miller Library 257 (Seminar Classroom) | T | 7:00 PM - 9:30 PM
Description: The Depression of the 1930s was the most devastating economic collapse of modern times. How did it happen? The 1920s had been the most prosperous time in American history, and many forecast ever-higher living standards. Instead the economy went into a tailspin that affected every group and region and posed a crisis of faith in capitalism. How did Americans cope and how did the experience shape their values and behavior? In what ways did the federal government respond, to what ends, and with what consequences? In exploring these questions, the course will also help students to read critically and to write clearly, concisely, and precisely.

section: AA 341-A - Culture, Mobility, Identity: Encounters in the African Diaspora
subject: AA
title: Culture, Mobility, Identity: Encounters in the African Diaspora
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112 or AA 125, and Sophomore Class Standing or above
Description: Use of text, film, food, and music to examine how African and African-descended people made and remade the modern world. Surveys how past and present cultural practices dialogically shaped the formation, transformation, and flows of the diaspora. Attention to the dynamics of circulation, contact, exchange, and estrangement facilitates travels through the Afro-Atlantic world. Inquiry into archives and other sites of memory enables consideration of the scale, scope, and impact of black action and imagination.

subject: AA
title: Surveillance Culture
Section Details: Miller Library 253 (Seminar Classroom) | TR | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM
Description: Investigates the history and contemporary manifestations of surveillance culture in the United States. Asks about the roles played by surveillance in American culture, and the ways it shape our bodies, behaviors, relationships, communities, and political possibilities. We look at how surveillance unevenly affects marginalized communities, and consider how artists and activists have responded to surveillance culture through tools of resistance. Students will learn to use multiple disciplinary and theoretical frameworks and conduct original research into the techniques and effects of surveillance technologies.

section: AA 393-A - Junior Seminar: Theories of Culture
subject: AA
title: Junior Seminar: Theories of Culture
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: American Studies or African American Studies  Majors/Minors with Junior class standing or above
Description: Introduces students to major currents in cultural theory, including Marxist, structuralist, poststructuralist, and critical race and gender theory. Emphasizes their application to contemporary cultural objects and events. Analytical and interpretive skills will be demonstrated in frequent writing assignments and a final independent research project.

subject: AI
title: Artificial Intelligence Lab
Section Details: Olin 019B (Active Learning Classroom) | R | 7:00 PM - 9:00 PM | 09/09/2026 - 12/21/2026
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Hosted by the Davis Institute for Artificial Intelligence, this collaborative research laboratory invites students from all four academic divisions to engage in development that leads the AI transformation from a liberal arts perspective. Participants will gain hands-on experience with generative AI and large language models (LLMs) to tackle real-world pedagogical and research challenges. Students will engage with faculty to investigate these challenges, develop a project and produce a final presentation that demonstrates both the potential and ethical responsibility of human-centered AI.

section: AM 125-A - Introduction to African American Cultures
subject: AM
title: Introduction to African American Cultures
Description: Offers a critical introduction to the cultural, political, and social, forces that have shaped the identity of people of African descent in the United States. Through readings, viewing, listening, and creating, we will examine the major movements, people, and ideas that have shaped African American identity and culture and gain an understanding of how African Americans have informed the broader national and global cultural and political landscapes.

title: Histories of the Present

subject: AM
title: Sounding the Great Migration: 1900-1945
Cross-Listed Title: AM 255-A/ MU 255-A - Sounding the Great Migration: 1900
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: MU 111 or MU 181 or by permission of the instructor. Interested students who don't have the prerequisites should contact instructor directly.
Description: In the first half of the twentieth century, millions of Black Americans fled the South in search of better lives in the North and West United States. During this time, Black writers, artists, and musicians nurtured vibrant Black expressive cultures in cities like New York and Chicago. In this course, students will encounter the blues, jazz, gospel, and classical music produced during this period and place musical sound in historical context. Combining interdisciplinary readings, musical analysis, and writing assignments, students will ask questions like: How did Black composers approach Euro-centric classical music? Why were female blues musicians beloved by their listeners but rarely featured in major Black newspapers? And, how did jazz come to be celebrated as a uniquely American art form? Students will practice music analysis in listening journals, critically evaluate readings in reading responses, develop research skills in a short research paper, and make trans-historical connections in a creative final project.

subject: AM
title: Art, Medicine, and Race
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor Permission: ST 112, AA/AM 171, AA/AM 125, AR 101, or AA/AM/AR 157 - Copy
Description: This humanities lab explores the relations among art, medicine, and ideas about race from the eighteenth century to the present. section: AR 111-A - Introduction to Western Art: Prehistory through the Middle Ages
subject: AR
title: Introduction to Western Art: Prehistory through the Middle Ages
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: An examination of the history of the Western tradition of visual arts from cave painting through the end of the Middle Ages. Through lectures, class discussion, museum visits, provides an introduction to the descriptive and critical analysis of works of art in both their formal and material makeup as well as their dependency upon and/or interrelationship with cultural, religious, economic, and historical trends. Previously listed as Art 201.

section: AR 125-A - Art and Architecture of the Islamic World, 622-1258
subject: AR
title: Art and Architecture of the Islamic World, 622-1258
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Examines the history, art, architecture, and archaeology of the Islamic world from the time of Muhammad's flight to Medina in 622 A.D. to the Mongol Invasion of 1258. Explores this pivotal period by surveying the history and material remains of the Umayyad and Abbasid empires in the Middle East, South Asia, and Spain. Familiarizes students with the basic development of Islamic art as well as with the cultural and historical circumstances that led to particular styles and movements. Previously listed as Art 321 and 225.

section: AR 215-A - Art and Archaeology of the Ancient Near East and Egypt
subject: AR
title: Art and Archaeology of the Ancient Near East and Egypt
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Surveys the art and archaeology of Ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia from the origins of urbanism through the Persian period by examining both the art and architecture of these ancient civilizations and the general cultural frameworks that led to their development. Through class discussion, readings, and individual and group projects students become conversant in the history and visual culture of Ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, as well as with the archaeological techniques used to collect and analyze much of this material. Previously listed as Art 315.

subject: AR
title: Drawing I
Description: Lays the foundation for visual thinking and perceptual understanding. Through a sequence of projects, students acquire a working understanding of single and two-point perspective, composition, the use of tonal contrast, and the editing process necessary for clear visual communication. Students will experience drawing both as an analytical tool and an expressive language. Media used include graphite, vine and compressed charcoal, and ink. Outside work is essential. Evaluation includes group critiques, midterm, and final portfolio reviews. Previously listed as Art 141.

subject: AR
title: Printmaking I
Description: Introduction to the materials, techniques, and concepts associated with the medium of printmaking in its traditional and 21st-century forms. Students learn basic print shop and digital image manipulation skills, including use of hand and power tools, paper handling and registration, hand and press printing, Photoshop, and digital laser cutting. Printmaking techniques include relief, monotype, and intaglio. Demonstrations, studio work, and critique form the foundation of this project-based course.

subject: AR
title: Vienna 1900 (in English)
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: In-depth exploration of the Viennese Secession (1898-1905), a pivotal moment in European avant-garde art. Considers artworks, creators (artists, architects, designers), collectors, and the historical and cultural context of Belle-Epoque Vienna. The course also addresses issues related to collecting this material in the post-World War II context and crucial issues of provenance research and restitution of Nazi-looted art.

section: AR 240-A - Digital Media I: From Screen to Prints
subject: AR
title: Digital Media I: From Screen to Prints
Description: This class explores the various ways in which two-dimensional still works can be created as files that will live and be exhibited on the web as well as in high quality printed forms. Students will also learn the technical skills of file types and compression, and the essentials of digital file management and protocols.

subject: AR
title: Painting I
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Junior Class Standing or Below
Description: A project-based introduction to oil painting as both a process and medium. Students acquire an understanding of advanced color theory and its perceived behavior in invented compositions and observed still lifes. They gain an understanding of how formal analysis drives the creative process and allows for clear, personal expression. Individual and group critiques provide feedback for growth. Outside work is essential. Evaluation process includes midterm portfolio and final interview and portfolio reviews.

subject: AR
title: Sculpture I: Dynamic Wood
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Submit a prerequisite override request (on Academic Dashboard) to seek approval.
Description: This introductory sculpture studio presents wood as a primary medium with which to fashion sculptural form. Students learn about the dynamic behavior of wood grain as it applies to concept building and 3D design. This course teaches students the fundamentals of wood milling and fabrication, adhering to both safety and etiquette as defined by the culture of a working studio. Two major projects are supported by sketchbook entries and the creation of models and maquettes.

subject: AR
title: Sculpture II: The Artifact
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AR 265 or Permission of the Instructor
Description: This intermediate sculpture studio engages with concepts and research defined by the 'artifact'. Students create original objects that reference existing or past cultural form, building upon specific material choices and design tenets used by others. Two major projects are supported by research, sketchbook entries, and time to model preliminary concepts.

subject: AR
title: 19th-Century European Art
Description: Introduction to European art of the long 19th century, from the French Revolution to the dawn of modernism. Situates objects in their social context, with particular attention paid to the institutions that regulated art production and reception, and the roles played by artworks in forming national, gender, racial, and class identities. Topics include European art's relationship to political conflict, imperialism, urbanization, industrialization, and technological change. Class discussions are supplemented by visits to museums. Students take two essay-based exams and write a paper.

subject: AR
title: Photography I
Description: Introduction to the tools, materials, and techniques for making wet-process, black-and-white photographs. Coverage of camera operation, use of a light meter in determining proper exposure, film processing, and printing. In addition to technique, and at the core of this course, will be a series of assignments, slide lectures, video presentations, and class discussions involving the theories and processes inherent in the comprehension and practice of using photography as a language of personal creative expression.

subject: AR
title: Art, Medicine, and Race
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor Permission: ST 112, AA/AM 171, AA/AM 125, AR 101, or AA/AM/AR 157 - Copy
Description: This humanities lab explores the relations among art, medicine, and ideas about race from the eighteenth century to the present. Focusing on the Atlantic world and the African diaspora, we consider how chattel slavery, colonialism, and racial inequality have shaped constructions of medical knowledge, while medicine has informed conceptions of race as it intersects with gender, sexuality, and class. Students conduct independent research, deliver oral presentations, complete several writing assignments, and engage with contemporary artists and scholars.

subject: AR
title: Printmaking III
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AR 228, AR 248, or AR 297
Description: Continuation of Art 229 that expands students' knowledge of printmaking in its traditional and 21st-century forms. Covers modular printing, collagraph printing, and advanced methods like paper joining and chine colle. Demonstrations, studio work, and critique form the foundation of this project-based course. Students develop a thematic body of work that culminates in a midterm and final portfolio.

section: AR 340-A - Art and Activism in Contemporary Cuba
subject: AR
title: Art and Activism in Contemporary Cuba
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - SP :: SP: Gender and Sex
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SP 2XX or above
Description: This course will examine how Cuban artists resist state control of the state’s cultural enterprise through artistic practice. The artists studied in this course reject the state’s strategies of isolationism and exceptionalism and bring visibility to art in Cuba and its diaspora, especially by underrepresented artists. Themes will include masculinities and sport; ruins and architecture; infrastructure and energy; sexuality and identity; and censorship and colonialism through artistic practice that prioritizes embodiment while considering Cuban art’s precarity. Students will also develop a facility with queer, postcolonial, and critical race theories that enable critiques of aspects of Cuba’s utopian socialist project.

subject: AR
title: Painting III
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AR 242
Description: Serves as a bridge course between the project-based format of Painting I and II and the independent structure of advanced painting. Students undertake invented abstraction, increased scale, the use of limited palettes, and an independent direction in their studio practice. Particular importance is placed on the ability to develop and maintain a work process with the goal of producing a related body of self-directed work. Students are required to express their intent visually in their work, orally in critiques, and in a written statement. Evaluation includes midterm and final portfolio reviews.

subject: AR
title: Painting IV
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AR 341
Description: Based on the discoveries made in Painting III, students continue to define and express their personal goals and begin their fully independent studio practice. Particular importance is placed on the ability to develop and maintain creative momentum with the goal of producing a cohesive body of self-directed work. Students are required to express their intent visually in their work, orally in critiques, and in a written statement. Evaluation includes midterm and final portfolio reviews. Fulfills the minimum requirement for the studio capstone Senior Art Exhibition.

section: AR 360-A - Digital Media III: Sound as Art
subject: AR
title: Digital Media III: Sound as Art
Description: Sound as Art investigates the act of listening as a creative practice. Students will learn to record and edit audio to create sonic artworks which can function as standalone pieces, or as works to complement and be incorporated within other mediums such as drawing, film, painting, print, or sculpture.

section: AR 381-A - Photography III: Color and Digital Photography
subject: AR
title: Photography III: Color and Digital Photography
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AR 282
Description: Allows students to master the basics--creatively and technically--of digital photographic techniques and materials. Provides a primer for Adobe Photoshop, the appropriate hardware (scanners and printers), and digital cameras. Introduces and explores color photography, its history, methods, and materials and a survey of contemporary work in the medium. Although the curriculum introduces many aspects of digital craft, assignments and projects will include the use of traditional techniques as well. Critical to the course is the continued exploration of photography as a language of visual expression within the fine arts. Students will be using digital and traditional cameras.

subject: AR
title: Photography IV
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AR 381
Description: Provides further exploration of the materials, techniques, and ideas covered in Art 381. Students may choose to work using traditional darkroom techniques and/or digital media according to what is most appropriate for their work. Allows students to improve their skills using advanced methods, materials, and equipment including medium- and large-format cameras. Each student will take on a self-conceived and self-directed semester-long project and take part in regular critiques. They will be expected to express their intentions and results verbally and through a final written statement.

subject: AR
title: Studio Art Capstone
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Senior Class Standing as a Studio Art Major
Description: In this culminating studio art experience, students engage in cross-media discussions and critique with all studio faculty while preparing a body of work for the Senior Art Exhibition. The capstone also focuses on professional development, including résumé writing, creation of a portfolio and artist statement, introduction to graduate programs, and research on employment opportunities. Students meet with guest critics, visit galleries and museums, and participate in a trip to a major arts destination to meet with professionals in the field, funded by the Mirken Family Endowment for Fine Art Practicum and Museum Practice at Colby.

subject: AR
title: Printmaking V
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AR 328
Description: Continuation of Art 428 that expands students' knowledge of printmaking in its traditional and 21st-century forms. This advanced course focuses on mastering techniques, developing individual expression, and creating a body of work.

subject: AR
title: Printmaking VII
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AR 428
Description: Expands student's knowledge of printmaking in its traditional and 21st-century forms. Focuses on mastering techniques, developing individual expression, and creating a body of self-directed work. Students will learn to develop an independent art practice in the Colby print studio. Students will also present their work orally and produce written artist statements. Evaluation includes five critiques throughout the semester.

subject: AR
title: Painting V
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AR 342
Description: Further extends students' ability to develop a mature direction in their work. Expands on the goals and expectations as expressed in Painting IV, including the ability to develop and maintain creative momentum with the goal of producing a cohesive body of self-directed work. Provides stronger preparation for the studio capstone Senior Art Exhibition and for application to graduate school. Students are required to express their intent visually in their work, orally in critiques, and in a written statement. Evaluation includes midterm and final portfolio reviews.

subject: AR
title: Painting VI
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AR 441
Description: Allows students the benefit of the full painting program. Students expand the depth and breadth of their independent process, whether working from still life, figure, landscape, or invented abstraction. Offers the strongest preparation for the studio capstone Senior Art Exhibition and for application to graduate school. Students are required to express their intent visually in their work, orally in critiques, and in a written statement. Evaluation includes midterm and final portfolio reviews.

subject: AR
title: Painting VII
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AR 442
Description: Further exploration of materials, techniques, and ideas developed in Painting VI. Out-of-class work is essential.

section: AR 450-A - Digital Media Advanced Studio I
subject: AR
title: Digital Media Advanced Studio I
Description: Expanding upon the skills and techniques learned through the core Digital Media courses, Advanced Studio I is a rigorous and deep dive into defining a personal creative practice in the field. By combining personal research interests with skills in Digital Media, students will spend the semester deeply invested in creating meaningful works of art for a portfolio and will begin the practice of articulating their interests and methods through written artist statements.

section: AR 460-A - Digital Media Advanced Studio II
subject: AR
title: Digital Media Advanced Studio II
Description: Continuing on Digital Media Advanced Studio I, this is a continued exploration and refining of the personal creative practice in the field. Through continued investment in personal research interests combined with skills in Digital Media, students will spend the semester carefully crafting meaningful works of art for a portfolio and will continue to hone their skills in articulating their interests and methods through written artist statements.

subject: AR
title: Sculpture V
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AR 265, 266, 365, and 366, or Permission of Instructor
Description: This advanced studio cultivates individual research skills and creative expression. Students identify a core interest - social, political, ecological, historical, or personal narrative - to which they can respond through a materials-based practice. To cultivate student ownership of their sculptural works, the studio is structured around individual projects.

subject: AR
title: Photography V
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AR 382
Description: Provides further exploration of the materials, techniques, and ideas covered in Art 382. Students may choose to work using traditional darkroom techniques and/or digital media according to what is most appropriate for their work. Students will improve their skills using advanced methods, materials, and equipment including medium- and large-format cameras. Each student will take on a self-conceived and self-directed semester-long project and take part in regular critiques. They will be expected to express their intentions and results verbally and through a final written statement.

section: AR 494-A - Senior Research Seminar in Art History
subject: AR
title: Senior Research Seminar in Art History
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Senior Class Standing as an Art History Major
Description: In this capstone seminar designed for senior art history majors, students learn to conduct advanced research in the discipline. Students design their own research topics and plans, create annotated bibliographies and abstracts for their projects, and produce a final paper of 25 or more pages, the equivalent of an academic journal article. They are expected to work closely with the instructor as well as consult other professors with expertise in their area(s) of interest.

subject: AS
title: Introduction to Astrophysics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: PH: Working knowledge of calculus, or PH 141 (IP) or PH 143 (IP)
Description: A general introduction based on topics needed for astrophysical research, accessible to all who are comfortable with calculus and computer analysis of data. Topics include celestial mechanics, thermal radiation, spectral line creation, radiative transfer, star formation, nucleosynthesis, stellar evolution, galaxy structure, and cosmology. Weekly labs alternate between afternoon and night. Students must be available Monday through Thursday evenings for five required observing labs held on clear nights to be selected by the instructor. Lecture and laboratory.

subject: AY
title: Cultural Anthropology
Description: Introduction to the study of human societies and cultures through the concepts and methods of anthropology. Course material will (a) explore the great diversity of human social and cultural arrangements through the investigation of cultural communities around the world and the distinct ways their members experience and understand their lives and (b) investigate the larger historical, political, economic, and symbolic frameworks that shape contemporary human societies and cross-cultural interactions worldwide. Assignments emphasize clarity, concision, and coherence of written and oral arguments, as well as control over and understanding of course content.

subject: AY
title: Digital Infrastructure and Development
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112
Description: Infrastructures are complex networks involving movement of people, ideas, and technology. This anthropological class will consider topics of digital technology, "development", time, labor, space, and identity in a global context. In doing so, we will unpack how these structures are, at times, concepts and programs which can exclude and ostracize marginalized members of society. Students will follow classic and new debates in anthropology and informatics literature which will broaden their understanding of infrastructure constructions on a global level.

section: AY 212A-A - Feeling, Sensing, Thinking in Catastrophic Times
subject: AY
title: Feeling, Sensing, Thinking in Catastrophic Times
Description: This course examines emotionality and affect as forms of mediation within larger crises in the global order. How should we think about ordinary violence and trauma, for example, in the aftermath of partition in India and the Korean war? What is the affective dimension of necropolitical brutality in postcolonial Sub-Saharan Africa and elsewhere? What are the limits of affect theory for conceptualizing blackness? We will engage works across many disciplines to think about the political, social, historical, philosophical and cultural construction of emotions, affect, sensibility and their translations in language.

section: AY 213A-A - Constructing the Enemy: Race, Religion and Globalization
subject: AY
title: Constructing the Enemy: Race, Religion and Globalization
Description: In this course, we will examine the political-economic and psycho-affective processes of racialization and religionization in colonialism, imperialism, and war. What is the genealogy of race in the construction of the figure of the enemy? What is the relation between the religious invention of the infidel and the racial invention of the Black? How are the natives—represented as “savages”—informing the construction of the “enemy combatant” in the age of terror? We will engage with works in anthropology, postcolonial theory, Black studies, political philosophy, and subaltern studies to think about race, religion and globalization.

subject: AY
title: Introduction to World Music
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Examines a range of classical, traditional, and contemporary musics from areas as diverse as India, West Africa, the Caribbean, Eastern Europe, and the Middle East, among others. Each unit engages a broader sociocultural issue to enable students to think deeply and critically about the music in question, exploring such topics as music and Apartheid, the Arab Spring, and the appropriation of "world" music by Western musicians. Students will have the opportunity to perform some of the music they study, including West African drumming patterns, salsa dance steps, and Bulgarian vocal practices, among others, and there will be guest performances. No prior musical experience necessary.

subject: AY
title: Anthropology, History, Memory
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY: AY 112, or AY 125, or HI 1XX, and Sophomore class standing or above
Description: Anthropologists have depicted cultural systems as timeless, paying limited attention to how historical experiences produce, and how they are shaped by, everyday beliefs and actions. Examines the significance of history for anthropological understanding and vice versa. Investigates how different cultures construct the past and how the past shapes everyday lives, our own and others. Explores sites such as myths, monuments, bodies, and archives. Questions what is the past? How is it present? How do societies remember? How do they forget? Topics include technology, time, travel, commemoration, war. Formerly offered as Anthropology 298B.

section: AY 260-A - Love and Intimacy in the Middle East
subject: AY
title: Love and Intimacy in the Middle East
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112
Description: This course introduces students to the social science of love, intimacy, emotions, gender relations, and family in the Middle East and North Africa through ethnography, theory, cinematic/literary text, and interdisciplinary scholarship. Students examine intimacy as both personal experience and social phenomena shaped by political economies, cultural norms, media, and state power. Through regional cases (including Iran, Egypt, Turkey, and Tunisia) students learn key frameworks such as waithood and emerging adulthood and develop skills in critical analysis, area studies, and anthropological writing.

section: AY 262-A - Music in Life, Music as Culture: Introduction to Ethnomusicology
subject: AY
title: Music in Life, Music as Culture: Introduction to Ethnomusicology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Provides students with a theoretical and methodological introduction to ethnomusicology, a discipline that is rooted in exploring music not merely as an aesthetic object, but as a cultural force that reflects and shapes our everyday lives. Topics include music and medicine, migration, war, ethnicity, and spirituality, among others. Topics will be explored through a close reading of seminal texts and an examination of relevant theory. Students will also learn the fundamentals of conducting ethnographic fieldwork through attending a religious ceremony and a concert, and creating a podcast based on the soundscapes of Colby's campus.

section: AY 266-A - Pixelated Parts: Race, Gender, Video Games
subject: AY
title: Pixelated Parts: Race, Gender, Video Games
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112  and may not have previously completed AY 197- Imagining Video Games, or AY 298- Pixelated Parts
Description: This course considers the politics of video games and their surrounding ecosystems—games and their conditions and processes of production, the representations and spaces of identification that come with the play of games, the communities that players generate among themselves, and the affective and material interactions that result when players look at a screen, hold a controller, type on a keyboard, and move a mouse. This class pays close attention to the politics of race, gender, and sexuality as they emerge in gaming contexts and demonstrates, in doing so, how games shape, are shaped by, and sometimes critique and creatively re-imagine the political worlds that surround them.

section: AY 267-A - Critical Perspectives on Sports and Societies
subject: AY
title: Critical Perspectives on Sports and Societies
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112
Description: This course explores the connections between sports and a broad range of anthropological concerns, including colonialism, resistance and domination, race, sexuality, and gender. Students consider questions such as: Why do we play the sports we do? Why are sporting performances socially significant, and how have groups and political regimes used this significance? What can teams, players, and brands tell us about how we (and others) see the world? In addressing these questions, students think critically about their own sporting experiences and develop a deeper and subtler understanding of the way that societies make sports and sports make societies.

subject: AY
title: Researching Cultural Diversity
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112, AY 2XX or GS251, a W1 course, and Sophomore Class Standing or Above
Description: Focus on ethnography as both the central research strategy of anthropologists and the written text produced by such research. Examines anthropological methods of data collection and ethnographic writing as these encompass not only the discipline's historical focus on localized communities but also contemporary understandings of connections to global processes, the analysis of complex inequalities, and a reflexive and engaged relationship with the human world. Explores practical strategies for conducting ethnographic research, including interviewing, observation, and other modes of qualitative data collection; the ethical issues presented by such research; and the application of analytical and theoretical models.

subject: AY
title: Art, Power, and Politics
Section Details: Lovejoy 102 (Active Learning Classroom) | M | 1:00 PM - 3:30 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112
Description: This course examines how a range of anthropologists and other theorists have considered the relationship between art, power, and politics. What can the artistic works of various societies say about their worlds that other creations cannot? What claims can art make about the workings of power, and what artistic techniques does power itself employ? Why can some artworks persuade and manipulate us when others do not? This course approaches these questions from a number of different directions, including: the politics of perception, the place of art in modern life, the artistry of terror, the art of protest and propaganda, and the dream of building a beautiful regime.

subject: AY
title: Contemporary Theory
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112, AY 2XX or AY 3XX, a W1 course, and Junior Class Standing or above
Description: An analysis of the contemporary state of cultural anthropology through the investigation of contemporary theoretical approaches of central importance to the discipline. Examination of key theoretical concepts and their relevance for designing research questions, generating ethnographic perspectives, and building anthropological knowledge. Special attention to political economy, symbolic anthropology, poststructuralism, reflexive anthropology, postmodernism, and feminist and postcolonial anthropology. Assignments include both written and oral modes of analysis; strong emphasis on discussion and collaborative debate.

section: AY 341-A - Culture, Mobility, Identity: Encounters in the African Diaspora
subject: AY
title: Culture, Mobility, Identity: Encounters in the African Diaspora
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112 or AA 125, and Sophomore Class Standing or above
Description: Use of text, film, food, and music to examine how African and African-descended people made and remade the modern world. Surveys how past and present cultural practices dialogically shaped the formation, transformation, and flows of the diaspora. Attention to the dynamics of circulation, contact, exchange, and estrangement facilitates travels through the Afro-Atlantic world. Inquiry into archives and other sites of memory enables consideration of the scale, scope, and impact of black action and imagination.

subject: AY
title: Liberation Struggles
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112 or GS 101, or permission of instructor
Description: Is revolutionary change possible today? Explores the promises and failures of radical movements from the First International in 1864 to the "global uprisings" of recent years. Considers the historical genealogy of today's transnational movements and their complex relationships to the modern nation-state. To what extent do labor, anarchist, anticolonial, indigenous struggles, as well as the World Social Forum, Arab Spring, and Black Lives Matter, offer ways to understand the world today and to imagine alternative political futures? Strong emphasis on discussion and collaborative debate.

subject: BC
title: Medical Biochemistry
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CH 241 and (BI 163 or 164) and must not have taken BC 367/368
Description: Introduction to the fundamental principles of biochemistry. Course content and format are designed for students intending to proceed to health professional school. Lecture topics include amino acids and proteins; enzyme kinetics, mechanisms, and inhibition; lipid and carbohydrate structure and function; and the organization and functions of the major human metabolic pathways. Discussions include clinical case studies and other applications of biochemistry on human health. Students may not receive credit for both this course and Biochemistry 367 or 368. Lecture only.

section: BC 367-A - Biochemistry of the Cell I
subject: BC
title: Biochemistry of the Cell I
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Biology, Chemistry, CH-BioChem, CH- Cell and Molecular BB, BI- BioChem, or BI- Cell and Molecular BB Majors, or Chemistry Minors (who have taken CH 242, and either BI 163 or 201), and must not have taken BC 362
Description: Introduction to biochemical processes. Topics include the structure and function of the major classes of biological molecules (proteins, carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and lipids). Lectures, homework, and discussion focus on content-related problem-solving, critical-thinking, and communication skills. The optional laboratory introduces the fundamental biochemical techniques such as PCR, enzyme and protein assays, and gel electrophoresis. Students may not receive credit for both Biochemistry 362 and 367.

section: BI 100-A - Navigating the World of STEM Research
subject: BI
title: Navigating the World of STEM Research
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year Class Standing
Description: This course will focus on understanding how STEM researchers use scholarly literature to understand the nature of a field of inquiry, design and conduct their own research and how researchers then communicate their findings and make an argument from their data. Students will go through all of these steps in an abbreviated way throughout the course. Students will also prepare to apply for summer research opportunities by creating a resume and profiles on Handshake and Linked IN, and research the various career fields that align with their personal values and interests.

subject: BI
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
Section Details: Miller 008 (Active Learning Classroom) | MWF | 10:00 AM - 10:50 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Must not have taken SC 306 previously
Description: This course introduces the principles and methods of epidemiology as applied to public health practice. Students examine the historical development of epidemiology; the role of epidemiology in disease prevention; and differences between infectious and chronic disease epidemiology. Topics include sources of epidemiologic data; basic statistical concepts; measures of disease frequency and association; study designs; bias, confounding, and causal inference; and descriptive analysis of morbidity and mortality patterns.

section: BI 118-A - Sustainable Agriculture and Food Systems
subject: BI
title: Sustainable Agriculture and Food Systems
Description: Agriculture is a fundamental way in which humans interact with their environment and is at the nexus of ecological, social, and economic systems. An introduction to the ecological bases, practicalities, and philosophies of food and agricultural systems. Provides a foundation in such concepts as agroecology, sustainable soil management, pest and weed control, and organic farming. Also considers social, economic, and public-policy issues. Field trips to local farms and other agricultural institutions. Cannot be counted toward the biology major.

section: BI 118-B - Sustainable Agriculture and Food Systems
subject: BI

section: BI 124-A - Unraveling the Answers to Beautiful Biological Questions
subject: BI
title: Unraveling the Answers to Beautiful Biological Questions
Section Details: Miller 008 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 2:30 PM - 3:45 PM
Description: Explores the wonders of biology from the lens of current events, addressing some of the great biological questions and theories. Students will dissect complex scientific issues, renew childhood fascinations with the natural world, and bring a more informed perspective of how science generates knowledge to issues that impact their families, communities, and society. Students will experience a collaborative, team-based learning environment that stimulates questions and actively involves students in the process of constructing and analyzing knowledge by answering beautiful biological questions. Cannot be counted toward the biology major.

section: BI 142-A - Cancer: From the Clinic to the Lab and Back
subject: BI
title: Cancer: From the Clinic to the Lab and Back
Section Details: Olin 019B (Active Learning Classroom) | MWF | 9:00 AM - 9:50 AM
Description: Cancer has a nearly universal capacity to impact our lives. This course aims to answer frequent questions (what causes cancer? how many people get cancer? when will we cure cancer?) by providing a biological and clinical perspective on how cancer arises and progresses as a disease. We will additionally focus on the influences of genetic and environmental factors in contributing to specific types of cancer, and provide an overview on traditional and emerging cancer diagnostics and therapeutics.

subject: BI

section: BI 163-A - The Cellular Basis of Life
subject: BI
title: The Cellular Basis of Life
Description: An examination of cells as the fundamental unit of life. Aspects of evolutionary biology, cell biology, molecular biology, and genetics are discussed. A major objective is development of the intellectual tools to be able to ask and answer interesting biological questions. The objectives of the laboratory are to allow each student to design and conduct experiments, to analyze and present data, to write accurate scientific papers, and to critically evaluate the scientific literature. Lecture and laboratory.

subject: BI
title: Biology Accelerator
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Must be a First-Year student or have not completed a First-year Writing course, and must have AP or IB credit for BI 163 and 164
Description: Workshop-style course developing skills in designing, analyzing and presenting results of biological studies, while reviewing fundamental concepts in biology. This course fills the gap between content knowledge mastered in AP or IB courses and the analytical and writing skills required for success at higher levels. Students may not receive credit for both this course and Biology 163 or 164.

subject: BI
title: Taxonomy of Flowering Plants
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: BI 164 or 201
Description: An overview of evolutionary relationships among flowering plants and their nearest living relatives, and the study of evolutionary processes leading to those relationships. Students will prepare a collection of plant specimens from the local flora, learn to recognize important plant families, use technical keys to identify plants, and become familiar with analytical methods for constructing and evaluating phylogenetic hypotheses. Lecture and laboratory.

subject: BI
title: Evolutionary Cell Biology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: BI 164 or 201
Description: The cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of life. This course will explore the evolution of cells through the lens of eukaryotic diversity, which is mostly microbial. Eukaryotic cells first appeared on Earth around 2 billion years ago with features from the two other domains of life. We will study concepts like the origin and evolution of eukaryotic cells, endosymbiotic theory, eukaryotic cell organization, eukaryotic genomes, and the ecology of eukaryotes. In the course we will discuss how we learn about new microeukaryotes using microscopy and molecular methods and will introduce basic bioinformatic concepts and techniques.

subject: BI
title: Immunology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: BI 164 or 201
Description: An introduction to the cellular and molecular components of immune recognition and effector responses against pathogens, with emphasis on the human immune system. Topics will include immune deficiency, allergy, and autoimmunity.

subject: BI
title: Food: Biochemistry to Biopolitics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ST 112, or BI 163, or permission of instructor. Students should enter a Prerequisite Override Request (through the Academics dashboard) for instructor approval.
Description: This course examines the socio-technical systems of food through a specific theme (e.g., pomology, dairy, grains). Moving beyond basic nutrition, students analyze the biochemistry of food production and transformation alongside political, environmental, and ethical frameworks. Through inquiry-based labs and research, the course investigates how scientific knowledge and technology shape—and are shaped by—cultural identity, policy, and climate change. Students who wish to have their prerequisites overridden should enter a Prerequisite Override Request (the link to the request can be found on Student Academic Dashboards in Workday.

section: BI 230 L-A - Lab: Food: Biochemistry to Biopolitics
subject: BI
title: Lab: Food: Biochemistry to Biopolitics
Description: Lab for ST 230/ BI 230- Food: Biochemistry to Biopolitics

subject: BI
title: Entomology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: BI 164 or 201 or Permission of the Instructor
Description: This course will introduce students to the biology of insects, through a broad survey of their ecology and evolution by means of collection and taxonomic identification, examination and illustration, observation and experimentation, and discussion. Students will prepare a curated specimen collection over the course of several field trips, including one required overnight field trip on a weekend. Exams, quizzes, and writing assignments will be used to evaluate a student's ability to synthesize insect biology at different scales.

subject: BI
title: Marine Communities
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (Env Policy, Env Sci, Env Comp Majors, Marine Sci Minors, or Env Studies Minors) and must have taken ES 118 or ES 120
Description: Introduces students to key ecological interactions in marine communities around the world, including kelp forests, coral reefs, sea grasses, and the open ocean. A key learning goal is improved scientific literacy through in-depth reading and synthesis of scientific papers and the development of a research proposal.

subject: BI
title: Microbiology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: BI 164 or 201
Description: Provides an understanding of the nature and diversity of microorganisms and viruses and the roles they play in the biosphere. Emphasis will be on the microbe itself--its functional, ecological, and evolutionary relationships--as well as the activities it carries out that are of interest to humans. The approach will be fundamental, stressing principles, but with considerable emphasis on how these principles are applied to practical problems in medicine, industry, and the environment. Lecture and laboratory. Credit cannot be earned for both this course and Biology 238.

section: BI 254-A - Marine Biology of Coastal Maine
subject: BI
title: Marine Biology of Coastal Maine
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: BI 164 or 201
Description: A broad survey of the taxonomy, biology, and ecology of Maine's coastal organisms, with a focus on invertebrates and macroalgae. Students will engage with local habitats, including on several field trips and a required overnight weekend field trip to the Colby Island Campus. Further, students will learn the fundamentals of experimental design through analysis of the peer reviewed literature. In laboratory, students will master species identification, describing and distinguishing major taxa, and become adept at making observations, through dissections and the keeping of a detailed anatomical notebook. Meets the Biology field course requirement.

subject: BI
title: Ecology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: BI 164 or 201
Description: Ecology is the study of interactions among organisms and their environment. Studying these interactions provides us with the theoretical foundation for understanding many of the most pressing environmental problems. This course will examine ecological interactions at a wide range of scales from individuals, through populations and communities, to ecosystems. We will study how these interactions produce the patterns and processes we observe in biomes around the world. In the field-based laboratory, we will generate hypotheses, develop experimental designs, and apply statistical analyses to ecological data, while gaining first-hand familiarity with local ecological communities. Lecture and laboratory.  Previously listed as Environmental Studies 271.

subject: CE
title: In the News: Understanding the American Political Moment
Section Details: Cotter Union Page Commons | W | 6:00 PM - 7:00 PM
Description: Students will explore the complexities of American politics and policy through a focus on developing news stories and current events. In a dynamic weekly discussion series hosted by the Goldfarb Center for Public Affairs, students will consider how politics intersects with policy, technology, and culture in practical and emergent ways. Speakers will offer diverse perspectives, from senior leaders to emerging voices across politics, policy, and journalism. Students will be responsible for working in a team to prepare briefing materials and develop questions for one of the semester’s speakers. Through this process, students will gain an understanding of the topics at hand and develop skills in preparing and facilitating conversations about challenging policy issues. Non-graded. Description: The Earth is a dynamic chemical reactor that changes on timescales of seconds to millions of years through natural and anthropogenic forcings. This two-semester sequence explores fundamental chemistry principles, including the structure of the atom, chemical bonding and reactivity, chemical equilibria, and thermodynamics through the lens of Earth's 4.56-billion-year history. By constructing quantitative models of Earth systems, students also learn how Earth processes operate over time and space, how they shape the environments in which we live, and the theoretical and practical limits of resource utilization. Students with prior credit for Chemistry 141, 142, or 147 cannot receive credit for this course.

section: CI 210-A - Contemporary Documentary Filmmaking: A Creative Practice
subject: CI
title: Contemporary Documentary Filmmaking: A Creative Practice
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Students will attend a mandatory weekend-long field trip to the Camden International Film Festival, which will be the catalyst for the class. You will take inspiration from the films you watch and the filmmakers you meet to conceive of your own documentary projects. You will then spend the semester developing your ideas into compelling narrative shorts while learning how to write and pitch an idea in progress. Students will also learn how to research, shoot, and edit, while building ethical relationships with their subjects.

subject: CI
title: Japanese Cinema and Culture
Description: An introduction to Japanese cinema, considering local and global contexts. Because of a significant reemergence since the 1980s, the extensive Japanese filmography will be studied with a primary focus on contemporary films. Different themes will be explored such as Samurai, anime, gender and sexuality, and J-horror to display the diversity and richness plus thematic continuity at key junctures. Since film production exchange has become the norm, the validity of the term “Japanese cinema” itself is questioned. Cinematic (de)construction of “Japan-ness” will yield historical, social, political, economic, and cultural observations. All films are subtitled with English. No prior knowledge of Japanese is assumed or required.

section: CI 246-A - Mafia Movies: Mobsters, Martyrs, and Myths
subject: CI
title: Mafia Movies: Mobsters, Martyrs, and Myths
Section Details: Lovejoy 119 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 2:30 PM - 3:45 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Examines representations of the mafia in Italian and American film, tracing the transformation of a rural Sicilian phenomenon into a transnational cultural myth. Through the analysis of cinematic texts (by Francis Ford Coppola, Martin Scorsese, Marco Tullio Giordana, Lina Wertmüller, and others) alongside historical, literary, and critical readings, the course explores how mafia movies construct and circulate narratives of ethnic identity, migration, gender roles, family, power, and social justice. No prerequisite, all students welcome.

section: CI 256-A - Film for Thought: The Art of French Cinema
subject: CI
title: Film for Thought: The Art of French Cinema
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: FR 128 or 131 or equivalent
Description: A survey of directors, genres, movements, and aesthetics in French cinema from early 20th Century to the present day. Emphasis on the analysis of film style and form: mise-en-scene, cinematography, editing, sound, performance, etc. Students will approach film not only as a form of art, but also as a site of memory and/or a tool of socio-political discourse. Film theory will frame our class discussions. Students will develop visual literacy, analytical skills, critical and creative thinking through innovative visual projects, essays and class discussions. Course conducted in French.

section: CI 316-A - Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality
subject: CI
title: Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please submit a Prerequisite Override request on the Academics dashboard for approval to join. Student must have previously completed CI 142 and CI 321.
Description: Poised in the mid-2010s to be the next major piece of technology for widespread adaptation, the shift to virtual reality and augmented reality that everyone anticipated never occurred. This course looks to investigate virtual reality and augmented reality, studying the particularities, its affordances, and especially the frictions. By hands-on usage paired with readings from cinema and media studies and continental philosophy, students will study virtual reality and augmented reality as a way to hone their critical media analysis faculties so that they can better navigate and understand the implications of a constantly-changing media and technology landscape.

section: CI 321-A - Topics in Film Theory: Theories of Film and Media
subject: CI
title: Topics in Film Theory: Theories of Film and Media
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CI 142
Description: A survey of the major developments in classical and contemporary film and media theory. The course will trace the efforts made to understand film and media, from questions of medium specificity, to their role in the history of art, and to their social, cultural, and political impact.

subject: CL
title: Myth and Magic
Description: Popular culture is fixated on magic, from Harry Potter to Game of Thrones, but the roots of this interest can be found in the myths and magical practices of antiquity. Love and hate, hope and fear, ambition and greed - powerful emotions drove Circe, Medea, and Hekate in myth as well as ordinary mortals in the ancient world. The focus will be on the role of magic in the contested realm of antiquity’s social and gender hierarchies. We will examine the function and fascinating allure of witchcraft by analyzing extracts from literary texts (e.g. Homer, Theocritus, Pindar, Vergil, Horace, and Lucan), protective amulets, and ancient spells designed to seduce the beloved, ward off rivals, silence legal foes, rig sports events, reveal the future, and summon demons.

subject: CL
title: Ancient Medicine
Description: We explore the beliefs, practices, and cultural frameworks that shaped ancient Greek, Roman, Egyptian, and Babylonian healing practices. By examining texts, objects, and architecture, we investigate how different healers understood concepts like physical and mental 'health' and 'disease'. We also ask questions like: Who could be healers? What tools and techniques did they use? How was medical knowledge developed and tested? What social and ethical systems informed medical decision-making? How did patients' genders, ethnicities, ages, and abilities affect their medical experiences? And how can reflecting on these questions help us to better understand modern medical systems, practices, and beliefs?

section: CL 158-A - History of Ancient Greece and the Near East
subject: CL
title: History of Ancient Greece and the Near East
Course Tags: Integrated Studies Clusters :: IS: The Ancient World
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year Class Standing
Description: Offers an overview of ancient Greek history and culture from the Mycenaean society of the Bronze Age to the formation of the Hellenistic kingdoms, and situates this historical survey within the broader context of the histories and cultures of the Near East. We will begin with the foundation of the first cities in the fourth millennium BCE and end with the fall of Ptolemaic Egypt to the Roman Empire. Over the course of the semester, we will read texts ranging from the poems of the priestess Enheduanna to the dialogues of the philosopher Plato. Particular attention will be paid to political, social, and cultural history.

section: CL 215-A - Art and Archaeology of the Ancient Near East and Egypt
subject: CL
title: Art and Archaeology of the Ancient Near East and Egypt
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Surveys the art and archaeology of Ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia from the origins of urbanism through the Persian period by examining both the art and architecture of these ancient civilizations and the general cultural frameworks that led to their development. Through class discussion, readings, and individual and group projects students become conversant in the history and visual culture of Ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, as well as with the archaeological techniques used to collect and analyze much of this material. Previously listed as Art 315.

section: CL 231-A - History of Ancient Greek Philosophy
subject: CL
title: History of Ancient Greek Philosophy
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomore Class Standing or Above
Description: A survey of ancient Greek thought through the ideas of the pre-Socratics, the Sophists, Plato, Aristotle, the Epicureans, and the Stoics. Primary, though not exclusive, attention will be to metaphysical and epistemological issues.

There are two course learning goals: developing students' understanding of the Pinyin system and guiding their practices of pronunciation. Students will enhance their awareness of the Pinyin system and learn a variety of strategies to improve their pronunciation.

subject: CN

Description: An introduction to the essential building blocks of the Mandarin Chinese language. Students will learn the pinyin Romanization system, basic strokes and radicals of the writing system, as well as approximately 200 characters. Basic sentence structures will be introduced within the context of social situations encountered in daily student life. By the end of the course students will be able to employ all four language modalities (listening, speaking, reading, and writing) to exchange basic information about themselves and their studies.

subject: CN
title: Intermediate Chinese I

Description: A continuation of CN126, designed for students who have completed two semesters of Chinese language courses at Colby, or its equivalent. Students will continue development of interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational skills in Mandarin with a specific focus on predictable, familiar topics related to daily activities and personal environment. By the end of the semester, students will be able to handle short social interactions and interact at a functional level in some familiar contexts. Students will also develop the ability to reflect on language learning.

subject: CN
title: Chinese Conversation I

Emphasis on oral/aural practice of patterns and phrases related to such daily situations as going to the post office, talking on the telephone, shopping, ordering in a restaurant, etc. Supplemental vocabulary/phrase lists are supplied.

subject: CN
title: Chinese Conversation II
Description: Intermediate level conversation class with a focus on building language fluency and vocabulary for daily life situations. Nongraded.

subject: CN
title: Third-Year Chinese
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CN 128 or equivalent
Description: A continuation of CN128, designed for students who have completed four semesters of Chinese language courses at Colby, or its equivalent. It is a bridge course between Intermediate and Advanced Chinese language courses. Students will begin to explore sociocultural issues in Chinese. By the end of the semester, students will be able to handle complex social interactions with ease and confidence, and communicate about events and experiences in an organized way. Students will also develop a complex understanding of cultural perspectives and acquire the skills to become an autonomous language learner.

section: CN 453-A - Chinese Food Culture and Its Changing Landscape
subject: CN
title: Chinese Food Culture and Its Changing Landscape
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CN 322 or CN 4XX
Description: An advanced Chinese language course that contextualizes learning through authentic materials focusing on the fascinating and constantly evolving topic of Chinese food culture. A multidisciplinary approach to understanding Chinese food culture in an immersion environment will advance language proficiency levels in all four language modalities--listening, speaking, reading, and writing--by promoting effective cross-cultural communication and fostering an in-depth understanding of the historical, ever-changing, complex Chinese culture. Humanities lab course.

subject: CS
title: Computational Thinking: Visual Media
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Permission of the Instructor: CS-Related Majors/Minors/Statistics Majors/Mathematical Science Majors (or First Years/Sophomores) and must not have taken CS 152, CS 154 or CS 166 (with a C- or better) - Copy
Description: An introduction to computational thinking: how we can describe and solve problems using a computer. Using the Python language, students will learn how to write algorithms, manipulate information, and design programs. They will learn about abstraction, how to divide and organize a process into appropriate components, how to describe processes in a computer language, and how to analyze and understand the behavior of their programs. The projects will focus on manipulating images or generating complex and interesting scenes and animations each week through writing well-constructed programs. Students may not receive credit for both this course and Computer Science 152, 154, or 166.

title: Computational Thinking: Science

title: Computational Thinking: Computer Vision
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CS-Related Majors/Minors/Statistics Majors/Mathematical Science Majors (or First Years/Sophomores) and must not have taken CS 151, 152, or CS 154 (with a C- or better)
Description: A course for students who have some experience programming, but who are not ready for CS231. Using the Python language, students will learn how to write algorithms, manipulate information, and design programs. They will learn about abstraction, how to divide and organize a process into appropriate components, how to describe processes in a computer language, and how to analyze and understand the behavior of their programs. The projects will focus on manipulating images and videos using computer vision. This course enables CS- and AI-related student learning outcomes. Students may not receive credit for both this course and Computer Science 151, 152, 153, or 154.

subject: CS
title: Data Structures and Algorithms
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - PP :: Public Policy
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CS 151, 152, 153, 154, or 166, C- or better
Description: Focuses on the common structures used to store data and the standard algorithms for manipulating them. Standard data structures include lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, hash tables, and graphs. Standard algorithms include searching, sorting, and traversals. Along with implementation details, students will learn to analyze the time and space efficiency of algorithms and how to select appropriate data structures and algorithms for a specific application. In homework, labs, and programming projects, students will implement their own data structures and make use of existing libraries to solve a variety of computational problems.
