subject: CS
title: Computer Organization
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CS/CS-AI Majors who have passed CS 231 with a C- or above
Description: Computer organization focuses on how computers work. Students learn the fundamental hardware components, including storage (RAM, hard disks), input/output mechanisms, and the central processing unit (CPU). They learn how components are designed and built on several levels, including the design of electrical components, machine language, and assembly language. They also learn to program in assembly language for one or more simple processors. Students learn primarily through projects where they design digital circuits, design components of a CPU, or write programs in assembly language.

subject: CS
title: Data Analysis and Visualization
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CS 231, C-  or greater
Description: Prepares students to apply computational data analysis and visualization approaches to real information from a variety of disciplines and applications. Data visualization is the interactive visual exploration of 2-D and 3-D graphic information using techniques that highlight patterns and relationships. Data analysis incorporates data management, data transformations, statistical analysis, data mining, and machine learning. Through programming projects, students will gain hands-on experience with the fundamentals of data analysis and visualization using data from active research projects at Colby and other institutions. Students may not receive credit for both this course and Computer Science 252.

section: CS 310-A - Creating Future Worlds: Computing, Ethics, and Society
subject: CS
title: Creating Future Worlds: Computing, Ethics, and Society
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CS 231, C-  or greater
Description: Explores ethical and moral narratives associated with advances in computing/AI technologies. Students will investigate issues in computing ethics highlighting the responsibility of computing professionals to examine the impact of their work on individuals and society. Topics will include: AI bias, digital disparities, autonomous systems, intellectual property law, cybercrime, information privacy and security, tech corporate culture, and professional conduct in a diverse workplace. Students will critically evaluate and apply literature on responsible technology development and professional codes of ethics with evolving technologies.

section: CS 330-A - Real-World Database Design, Development, and Deployment
subject: CS
title: Real-World Database Design, Development, and Deployment
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Students in a CS-related Program of Study who have taken CS 251 or 252, or CS 231 with C- or better
Description: Approaches database systems from the perspective of database designers, developers, and data analysts. The first course will provide a foundation in database design theory,database query languages and reporting methods, accessible information system UX/UI requirements, database management best practices, and new approaches to applying advances in AI to information modeling, storage, and retrieval. It will include both individual and group programming assignments around data modeling and diagrams, current database design modeling (i.e., RDBS, NoSQL, Spatial, Graph, and Hybrid) as well as evolving AI-driven database applications, information retrieval languages (i.e., SQL/NoSQL), data reasoning/extraction approaches, with an emphasis on accessible information systems.

subject: CS
title: Computer Networks
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CS 231 with C- or better or CS 232
Description: An introduction to fundamental concepts of computer networks and widely used networking technologies.  Topics include application protocol design; principles of congestion and error control protocols; network routing; local, wireless, and access networks; network security; and networking programming.  The Internet suite of protocols will be discussed in depth.  Students will learn about conventional and state-of-the-art computer networks through problem sets and programming projects.

subject: CS
title: Programming Languages
Section Details: Diamond 123 (Active Learning Classroom) | MWF | 10:00 AM - 10:50 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CS and CS-AI Majors who have taken and passed CS 231 with a C- or greater
Description: A survey of programming languages and paradigms focusing on the design of programming languages and comparing and contrasting different language families, including imperative, object-oriented, functional, and logic paradigms. Topics include syntax, context-free grammars, parsing, semantics, abstract representations of programming processes and structures, memory management, and exceptions. Students will undertake small programming projects in various languages and more extensive projects in two languages of their choice, presenting the characteristics of their chosen languages to their peers at the end of the term.

subject: CS
title: Neural Networks
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Students in CS or CS-related Programs of Study and have taken CS 251 or 252, and MA 121, 125, 130, 135, 161, 122, 160, or 162
Description: An introduction to neural networks from biological and machine learning perspectives. Focuses on neural networks for classification and regression involving large image and text datasets. Topics include fundamental design principles; supervised and unsupervised learning; fully connected and convolutional networks; transfer learning. Students obtain hands-on experience implementing and analyzing the neural networks covered each week in regular projects that explore different application areas.

subject: CS
title: Analysis of Algorithms
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CS or CS-AI Majors who have taken CS 231 C- or better, and (MA 2XX or SC 2XX)
Description: Focuses on classical algorithms in computer science and the analysis of the space and time efficiency of such algorithms as those that sort arrays and lists and search various data structures, including lists, trees, graphs, and strings. All major categories of algorithms are discussed, including iteration, divide and conquer, brute force, exhaustive search, greedy, dynamic programming, and approximation. Unsolvable and intractable problems are also covered, as is the role of NP-completeness. If time permits, some parallel and distributed algorithms will be discussed. Students will learn through problem sets and short programming projects. Students may not receive credit for both this course and Computer Science 376.

subject: CS
title: Algorithmic Game Theory
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CS or CS-related Majors/Minors who have completed CS 231 with a grade or C- or higher, and (MA 274, (or MA 165 with a grade of A- or higher), or MA 275)

section: EA 144-A - Patterns in East Asian History, to 1600
subject: EA
title: Patterns in East Asian History, to 1600
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Juniors and below (Instructor permission required for Seniors)
Description: This survey of early East Asian history covers China, Korea, and Japan from antiquity to the early seventeenth century, examining their independent trajectories and interrelationships. The course gives students a solid grasp of the significant figures, events, ideas, and social developments that have shaped each civilization. The thematic focus in each chronological unit introduces students to key factors that have set the common ground for an East Asian community, such as Confucianism, Buddhism, commercial networks, and diplomatic exchanges. This course also examines how each civilization "localized" these elements as part of "native" culture with independent dynamics. The focus, therefore, alternates between national (China, Japan, Korea) and regional (East Asia, Asia) perspectives.

subject: EA
title: Second Language Pedagogy
Description: An introduction to current research and theory in the area of second language acquisition (SLA). Students will gain an understanding of theories of SLA; the similarities and differences across first and second language acquisition; and the role of individual differences in language learning (including age, first language, and aptitude, among others). Students will also become familiar with the implications for SLA of sociolinguistic differences for English across time and space in the United States. A humanities lab intended for students who are interested in second language learning and teaching.

section: EA 223-A - Economic Statecraft in U.S.-China Relations
subject: EA
title: Economic Statecraft in U.S.-China Relations
Cross-Listed Title: EA 223-A/ GO 222-A - Economic Statecraft in U.S.
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: GO 131
Description: Examines how the U.S and China use economic statecraft against each other, as well as to coerce other countries, in their competition. With the rising significance of economic tools in crafting national security and foreign policy strategies, this course surveys theories of economic statecraft and empirical cases to explore whether, how, and when economic statecraft can be used to advance geopolitical objectives. The topics, including sanctions regimes, U.S.-China trade war, and various global economic initiatives, will enable students to approach some of the most pressing policy debates with rigor.

subject: EA
title: Japanese Cinema and Culture
Description: An introduction to Japanese cinema, considering local and global contexts. Because of a significant reemergence since the 1980s, the extensive Japanese filmography will be studied with a primary focus on contemporary films. Different themes will be explored such as Samurai, anime, gender and sexuality, and J-horror to display the diversity and richness plus thematic continuity at key junctures. Since film production exchange has become the norm, the validity of the term “Japanese cinema” itself is questioned. Cinematic (de)construction of “Japan-ness” will yield historical, social, political, economic, and cultural observations. All films are subtitled with English. No prior knowledge of Japanese is assumed or required.

section: EA 233-A - Voice, Language, and Meaning: Music in the Sinophone
subject: EA
title: Voice, Language, and Meaning: Music in the Sinophone
Description: How does music complicate and confound the conventions of language? The first part of this course explores music aesthetics, criticism and social encounters in the Sinophone. Students gain insights into Confucianist, Daoist, Buddhist, and literati elites’ perspectives on tuning, cosmic harmony, affects and voice in ritual music, qin music and Kun Qu opera from Classical Chinese literature. The second part examines China-West encounters from the reception of Chinese music in North America and Western music in China, interrogating how Chinese language conformed to Western structures while speaking as othered subjects in the Western imaginary.

section: EA 244-A - Brothers at War: The Two Koreas, 1945-Present
subject: EA
title: Brothers at War: The Two Koreas, 1945-Present
Cross-Listed Title: EA 244-A/ HI 244-A - Brothers at War: The Two Koreas, 1945
Section Details: Lovejoy 119 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM
Description: Nukes in the north and K-Pop idols in the south. The two Koreas could not seem more different today, but their division is barely a generation old. Why was Korea split and how did the two halves come to diverge so drastically? To answer these questions, this survey explores inter-Korean relations and their global contexts from division through experiences of civil war, rapid development, and geopolitical rivalry through a range of readings and media. Throughout, North and South Korea have vied for peninsular primacy and global prestige on the one hand, while upholding a shared narrative of common but sundered Korean identity on the other.

subject: EA
title: Chinese Philosophy
Description: An introduction to major thoughts, texts, and thinkers in the "classical" period of Chinese philosophy, which covers roughly the sixth through the third centuries BCE (known as the Warring States period). We will cover Confucius, Mozi, Mencius, Zhuangzi, Laozi, Sunzi, Xunzi, Han Feizi, the Yijing or Book of Changes, and other important texts. Provides an overview of the philosophical questions that motivated thinkers in early China and aims to provide an appreciation for how various answers to these questions have shaped East Asian civilizations generally.

section: EA 297-A - Kill Your Heroes: A Literary History of the Samurai
subject: EA
title: Kill Your Heroes: A Literary History of the Samurai
Description: Imagined as fearless and fiercely loyal warriors, samurai inspire fascination within Japan and worldwide. What explains the urge to tell stories about samurai, and what can these stories tell us about the invention of national identity and the narrativization of history? What can we learn when we set aside our pop-cultural preconceptions to examine the tales that samurai told about themselves? Readings include the medieval epic “Tale of the Heike” and the kabuki play “Treasury of Loyal Retainers”; we will also explore cinematic representations of samurai, including Kurosawa’s masterpiece “Ran” and the Hollywood blockbuster “The Last Samurai.”

subject: EA
title: From Qi to Chemistry
Description: This course introduces the study of science, technology, and medicine in premodern China. Rather than treating science as a fixed or universal category, the course examines how those in premodern China understood the natural world and produced knowledge about it. Using case studies across time, we will ask: What counted as “science”? How did knowledge practices relate to broader social, cultural, and political contexts? And how can the study of premodern China challenge or expand our assumptions about what science is?

section: EA 333-A - Colby and China: Alumni, Archives, and U.S.–China Encounters, 1850–1950
subject: EA
title: Colby and China: Alumni, Archives, and U.S.–China Encounters, 1850–1950
Description: This course examines U.S.–China encounters from the mid-nineteenth to the mid-twentieth century through the experiences of Colby College alumni who lived and worked in China during the period. Drawing on Colby’s Special Collections, other archives, and supplementary readings, students will explore the lives of missionaries, educators, physicians, journalists, and Chinese students whose careers intersected with major moments in modern Chinese history—from the late Qing and Republican era to revolution and war. Using alumni diaries, correspondence, photographs, campus publications, and institutional records, the course investigates themes such as American missionary influence, women’s education, nationalism and anti-imperialism, and U.S. involvement in the Sino-Japanese War and Chinese Civil War. Students will develop foundational archival research skills and gain hands-on experience with primary sources and digital humanities tools while critically assessing how a liberal arts education shaped global engagement.

section: EA 493-A - Seminar: Advanced Research in East Asia
subject: EA
title: Seminar: Advanced Research in East Asia
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Senior Class Standing and (EALC Majors/Minor, HI Majors, or GS Majors in the following concentrations: Asia, Development Studies, Human Rights/Social Justice, Int'l Econ Policy, Int'l Relations/Foreign Policy)
Description: An examination of methods for researching East Asia. Introduces students to the major debates that have come to define the field of East Asian studies, from John Fairbank's response to the West to Edward Said's orientalism, and prepares them with the skills necessary to engage Asian sources for independent research. Students will develop an independent research project on East Asia in any area of the humanities or social sciences, which, with approval from the student's major department, may be developed into a senior honors thesis.

subject: EC
title: Principles of Microeconomics
Description: Introduces the fundamental problem in economics: limited resources to satisfy unlimited needs and wants. Concentration on how markets allocate these scarce resources and when they fail to operate efficiently. After analyzing costs, students look at how firms in market structures ranging from perfectly competitive to monopolistic make decisions. Key principles are illustrated by applying them to current economic issues. Students will use standard economic models to describe market structures and the effects of policy interventions, solve problems using graphical or algebraic models of these markets, and choose an appropriate model to analyze economic events described in news articles.

Students will develop their analytical problem-solving skills, hone their ability to think critically, gain experience in building and understanding theoretical models, and sharpen their capacity to understand and critique macroeconomic policy.

Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (ECFM Majors or ECON- Track 1 Minors) who have completed EC 133 and have Sophomore Class Standing or above
Description: Introduction to financial accounting and financial statement analysis from the stakeholders' perspective. The statement preparation process is reviewed and analyzed. Accounting concepts, measurement conventions, limitations of financial statements, and the substantive and ethical issues that influence statement preparation and presentation are reviewed. Relates accounting and analysis to microeconomics, finance, and macroeconomic events and public policy, with reference to overlapping concepts and topics. subject: EC
title: Environmental and Natural Resource Economics
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - PP :: Public Policy
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ECON Majors, ES Majors, or ECON Minors who have completed EC 133 and Sophomore Class Standing or above
Description: The objective is to develop and apply economic tools to current environmental and resource-management issues. Causes of and remedies to environmental and resource-management problems are analyzed through economic modeling. These models in turn serve as the theoretical foundation for designing and evaluating policy instruments and practices. Students will learn to analyze current environmental problems and assess the effectiveness of environmental and resource-management policies using economic tools.

title: Corporate Finance II
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (ECON, ECFM, or ECON- Track 1 Minors) who have taken EC 211
Description: An examination of (1) the issues firms face in obtaining long-term financing and establishing a dividend policy, (2) the effects of capital structure on the cost of capital and the value of the firm, (3) international corporate finance, and (4) the use of financial derivatives, including options, to manage financial risk

subject: EC
title: Behavioral Economics
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - PP :: Public Policy
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (ECON Majors, ECFM Majors, or ECON- Track 2 Minors) who have taken EC 223 (C- or above)
Description: Study of the economic models that combine standard economic rationality assumptions with psychologically plausible assumptions. We examine whether these new models improve our ability to understand and predict behavioral phenomena, including altruism, procrastination, self-control, errors in statistical reasoning, and stereotypes.

subject: EC
title: Econometrics
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - PP :: Public Policy
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ECON or ECFM Majors who have completed EC 223, C- or better and (EC 293 (with a C- or better) or PS 214/215 or SC 212/321)
Description: An introduction to quantitative methods used for the analysis of economic phenomenon, covering the theoretical development of the ordinary least squares regression framework, tools for model specification and estimation, hypothesis testing, methods for correcting errors in parameter estimation, and the analysis of econometric results in the context of a wide range of empirical applications. Through lab exercises and a final empirical project, develops model-building skills, builds confidence in applying econometric methods to real-world data, deepens the understanding of statistical inference, and improves the capacity for communicating econometric results.

subject: EC
title: Computational Macroeconomics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ECON major or ECFM major or Economics track 2 minor and has completed EC 223
Description: Modern macroeconomic analysis is performed on computers. Economists use computers to analyze large amounts of data, solve models with no analytic solution, and conduct experiments on simulated economies. This course does not require any prior coding knowledge and provides an introduction to (i) the mathematical theory of dynamic programming to analyze dynamic economic decision-making and (ii) practical general programming basics and numerical methods to solve and simulate economies and conduct policy experiments. We will use Matlab in this course.

subject: EC
title: Poverty and Food Insecurity
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ECON or ECFM Majors or ECON Track 2 Minors and EC 225 or ((SC 321 or PS 215), (EC 133 and 134), and (MA 120, 125, 130, 135, or 160))
Description: Household food insecurity has many determinants including, socioeconomic status, time, the food environment, education, and culture. This course will explore the economic determinants of food insecurity and why it still persists today. Using a multidisciplinary approach, we will conduct a detailed investigation of the four main contributors to food insecurity: inadequate income, time, food environment, and nutrition education. Within each unit we will discuss the societal occurrence, characterize formal econometric models, and use publicly available data to address simple research questions. In addition to gaining a greater appreciation for how economics is applied, we will gain a better understanding of econometric and data management tools.

subject: EC
title: Gender in the Macroeconomy
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ECON major or ECFM major or Economics track 2 minor and has completed EC 223
Description: Studies gender differences and their effect on macroeconomic outcomes (labor markets, wealth, income). We will cover theoretical models and concepts which allow us to analyze economic behavior of men and women, households, and families. We will learn about recent developments and current topics in gender economics and discuss their consequences for the macro-economy. Examples of topics are: the decline in men's labor force participation, assortative mating, and the differential impact of recessions on men and women. We will combine data with the theory to enhance our understanding of how gender differences impact the aggregate.

subject: EC
title: International Trade
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (ECON Majors, ECFM Majors, or ECON- Track 2 Minors) who have taken EC 223 (C- or above)
Description: An introduction to international trade theory and policy. Topics include the determinants of international trade patterns, the gains from trade, distributional effects, increasing returns and scale economies, outsourcing, commercial policy, factor movements, trade agreements, and labor and environmental standards. Students will understand and be able to manipulate the major international trade models and analyze current trade policy issues in the context of these models both orally and in writing.

subject: EC
title: International Finance
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ECON major or ECFM major or Economics track 2 minor and has completed EC 224
Description: This course examines exchange rates and their role in the global economy. Topics include currency determination, real exchange rates and purchasing power parity, interest rate parity conditions, exchange rate regimes, foreign exchange markets and intervention, and the role of the U.S. dollar. The course introduces core open-economy models and theories of currency crises and sudden stops, including major historical and contemporary episodes. Students will learn to interpret exchange rate movements, evaluate policy tradeoffs, and apply economic theory and data to analyze international financial developments.

subject: EC
title: Senior Thesis Seminar
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ECON or ECFM Majors with Senior Class Standing
Description: An intensive collaborative research experience for honors or senior thesis projects. Required for all honors and senior thesis students.

section: EC 468-A - Seminar: Challenges of the Anthropocene: Views from the Global South
subject: EC
title: Seminar: Challenges of the Anthropocene: Views from the Global South
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission and EC 393 (IP) and Senior Class Standing as an Economics Major or Economics: Financial Markets Concentration
Description: Developing countries face a range of environmental issues, including poor air quality, mismanaged water resources, and unsustainable land use. Even countries with progressive economic indicators often struggle to improve environmental outcomes. Why does environmental quality continue to stagnate in developing countries? What policies can we implement to address environmental challenges? How can we leverage data to inform policymaking? We explore these questions by surveying the empirical economic research on the environment in the Global South. We will identify methodological trends, types and sources of data, and areas for policy intervention.

section: EC 470-A - Seminar: The City in Economic History
subject: EC
title: Seminar: The City in Economic History
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission and EC 393 (IP) and Senior Class Standing as an Economics Major or Economics: Financial Markets Concentration
Description: Since its founding, the United States has steadily become urbanized. What economic forces have caused people to move to cities? Can history explain today's urban locations and spatial patterns? Focusing primarily on U.S. urban growth since 1800, students will read, present, and discuss academic articles on topics such as suburbanization, zoning, local infrastructure investment, urban quality of life, housing, and racial and economic inequality. Students will build the economic models and tools necessary to complete an original empirical research paper in urban economic history.

subject: EC
title: Seminar: Global Production
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission and EC 393 (IP) and Senior Class Standing as an Economics Major or Economics: Financial Markets Concentration
Description: Many goods and services include components that are produced in multiple countries. Global production chains are organized within multinational enterprises or may take place through contractual arrangements. Studies the determinants of cross-border investment and production and their implications for the welfare of people in all countries. Readings are drawn largely from recent original research papers. An original empirical research project provides a deeper understanding of how economic research is conducted and evolves. Oral communication skills are developed through class discussion, presentations, and debates.

subject: EC
title: Seminar: Stereotypes and Discrimination
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission and EC 393 (IP) and Senior Class Standing as an Economics Major or Economics: Financial Markets Concentration
Description: Stereotypes shape perceptions and actions. We will examine the causes of stereotypes and their consequences on economic decisions, outcomes, and policy. Using insights from behavioral economics, we will study how economists theoretically model stereotypes and why we cannot rely on markets to eliminate incorrect beliefs. We will draw on recent experimental economic research to study how stereotypes affect economic decision-making and how stereotypes lead to discrimination. Topics to be covered include: social norms, implicit bias, self-stereotyping, and inaccurate statistical discrimination. This course relies heavily on applying concepts covered in intermediate microeconomics, statistics, and econometrics to reading and discussing economic articles and conducting research.

subject: ED
title: Education and Social Justice
Section Details: Diamond 123 (Active Learning Classroom) | MW | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM

subject: ED
title: Schools and Society
Section Details: Diamond 123 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: The complex relationships between schools and society will be examined by reviewing a variety of theoretical perspectives and empirical studies. Topics include social mobility and stratification; social reproduction; the dynamics of race, class, and gender in education; various forms of capital; teaching as a profession; and school choice. Particular attention will be given to the ways that small interactions within educational settings have much larger implications within society.

section: ED 215-A - Child and Adolescent Development in Education
subject: ED
title: Child and Adolescent Development in Education
Section Details: Diamond 123 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 9:30 AM - 10:45 AM
Description: Explores the lives of contemporary children and adolescents. Goals include 1) understanding how differences in gender, race, ethnicity, social class, and sexual orientation shape the experience of young people; 2) understanding selected theoretical and empirical work in the field of child and youth studies; 3) developing relationships with local young people; and 4) honing key academic and intellectual skills. In addition, students are required to spend 10-15 hours in a local educational setting.

subject: ED
title: Second Language Pedagogy
Description: An introduction to current research and theory in the area of second language acquisition (SLA). Students will gain an understanding of theories of SLA; the similarities and differences across first and second language acquisition; and the role of individual differences in language learning (including age, first language, and aptitude, among others). Students will also become familiar with the implications for SLA of sociolinguistic differences for English across time and space in the United States. A humanities lab intended for students who are interested in second language learning and teaching.

section: ED 243-A - Schooling Around the World: Comparative Perspectives
subject: ED
title: Schooling Around the World: Comparative Perspectives
Section Details: Diamond 123 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 2:30 PM - 3:45 PM
Description: Introduces students to interdisciplinary approaches that aim for comparing the emergence, function, and purposes of schooling in diverse national as well as sub-national contexts around the world. Students critically examine global phenomena such as colonialism, modernization, and globalization and their impacts on educational systems and practices. Students also examine contemporary issues such as role of nation state and civil society in education, global education reform movements, dialectic relationship between development and education, and alternative methods of teaching and learning. Previously offered as Education 297 (Fall 2019).

subject: ED
title: Curriculum and Methods
Section Details: Diamond 123 (Active Learning Classroom) | MW | 2:30 PM - 3:45 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (ED Majors/minors, or ED Studies Minors with Professional Certification, or ED Major in Educational Studies with a Concentration in Professional Certification) who have taken ED 101 and have Senior Class Standing
Description: A consideration of various teaching and assessment methods as well as curriculum design for secondary classrooms. Students develop knowledge and skills to meet Maine Standards for Initial Teacher Certification. Students write and present lesson plans, create assessment protocols, develop a coherent unit of study using a backward design model, and complete a minimum of 30 hours working with a cooperating teacher in a secondary classroom. Previously listed as Education 431.

subject: ED
title: Motivation and Learning
Section Details: Diamond 123 (Active Learning Classroom) | MW | 1:00 PM - 2:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Any Education course

section: ED 342-A - Community-Focused Project-Based Learning Experience in Schools
subject: ED
title: Community-Focused Project-Based Learning Experience in Schools
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission and students must have taken ED 101, ED 213, ED 215, or ED 217
Description: In this course, students will learn innovative education strategies critical to 21st century learning, gain experience working with K-12 students, and have the opportunity to affect meaningful change in the local community. Students will partner with a local K-12 partner to identify a community problem, and then using the frameworks of design thinking, place-based learning, and project-based learning – create and test possible solutions for the problem. Projects will culminate with a public presentation to interested stakeholders led by the Colby student, and their K-12 mentor teacher and students. Project must be approved by instructor prior to registering for course.

section: ED 493C-A - Senior Seminar: Bridging the Research-Practice Gap
subject: ED
title: Senior Seminar: Bridging the Research-Practice Gap
Section Details: Miller Library 034 (Seminar Classroom) | T | 1:00 PM - 3:30 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Senior Class Standing as an Education Major or Minor
Description: Starting with the concept of the “research-practice gap,” this course asks how educators from teachers to state-level policymakers make decisions about what to do, and what research is for. This course draws on frameworks of research use and organizational learning as well as insights from varied research paradigms such as impact evaluations and practitioner research. We will study and interrogate concepts such as validity, rigor, and relevance while learning about educational policy issues from multiple perspectives. Using these foundations, we will work to support local educators, advocates, and decision-makers in generating, communicating, and learning from usable research.

section: EN 116B-A - The Country and the City
subject: EN
title: The Country and the City
Section Details: Miller Library 253 (Seminar Classroom) | TR | 9:30 AM - 10:45 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: This course examines representations of country and city life in literature, from antiquity to the present. Through in-class discussion and written work, students will practice techniques of literary analysis, employ critical thinking in analyzing and discussing literature, and will gain a foundation in all aspects of college-level writing. Topics for class discussion include: economic, racial, and historical factors that contribute to literary imaginings of country and city life; how and why country or city life is romanticized or demonized in literature; how aesthetic representations of country and city have changed over time.

section: EN 120D-A - Language, Thought, and Writing: Writing as a Fan
subject: EN
title: Language, Thought, and Writing: Writing as a Fan
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: In this writing-intensive seminar, we devote particular attention to the ways that form, voice, and style shape meaning, both in literary texts and in college-level academic writing. How do writers adapt, reclaim, repurpose, and critique the work of other writers? We will read poetry and prose from a variety of historical periods with particular attention to themes of race and gender. Throughout, we explore how writing about literature or engaging as "fans" can make us better, more attentive, and even more critical readers, and how reading with enthusiasm can make us more effective and thoughtful writers.

section: EN 120G-A - Language, Thought, and Writing: Community Literacy and Migration
subject: EN
title: Language, Thought, and Writing: Community Literacy and Migration
Section Details: Miller Library 319 (Seminar Classroom) | MWF | 10:00 AM - 10:50 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: Where are we? Why are we here and how did we arrive? How do we know what we know? Who needs our stories? We'll use these questions to explore essays, literary texts, images, and more as we gain literacy-reading and writing ability as well as cultural knowledge-about Colby, our communities, and migration. We'll reflect on, analyze, narrate, and research our journeys and compare them to stories by Margaret Cavendish, bell hooks, and Mohsin Hamid. Students will develop a college-level writing practice while asking why we migrate, what we carry with us, and how we become creators of new knowledge.

section: EN 120J-A - Language, Thought, and Writing: True Crime
subject: EN
title: Language, Thought, and Writing: True Crime
Section Details: Lovejoy 103 (Active Learning Classroom) | MW | 2:30 PM - 3:45 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: Why are we so fascinated by stories of violence? How do we reconcile our own subject position as media consumers with the very real personal and societal fallout of interpersonal violence?  This course teaches the basics of composition, information literacy, rhetorical analysis, and effective argumentation through immersion in the multimedia world of contemporary true crime. We will examine the conventions of true crime writing as it manifests both globally and locally, interrogating the psychology, science, and biases that inhere in the ways crimes are investigated, publicized, and adjudicated.

section: EN 120L-A - Language, Thought, and Writing: Language + Race + Power
subject: EN
title: Language, Thought, and Writing: Language + Race + Power
Section Details: Miller Library 205 (Active Learning Classroom) | MW | 1:00 PM - 2:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: Thinks with scholars like James Baldwin, Geneva Smitherman, bell hooks, Paulo Freire, Audre Lorde, and April Baker-Bell about 1) the racial and colonial conditions that produced Standard Written English, 2) the social, political, economic, educational, psychological, and ethical stakes of normalizing the language of white enslavers and colonizers, and 3) alternative forms of language arts instruction. Throughout, we'll meditate on how we've been (mis)shaped in the image of the colonizer and work towards reimagining ourselves by reading and writing in a wide variety of genres including op-eds, educational social media threads, academic articles, TedTalks, spoken word, and critical autobiographies.

section: EN 125-A - Island Humanities: Exploring the Humanities theme
subject: EN
title: Island Humanities: Exploring the Humanities theme
Description: Offered by the Center for the Arts and Humanities, this one-credit seminar series engages with experts from a variety of fields who explore the humanities theme of “Islands” in all its forms. In this course, you will participate in discussions with scholars, writers, and artists from a wide array of areas, giving you a comprehensive understanding of the theme. Through conversation, debate, and hands-on workshops, you will develop your own ideas and opinions on the theme while participating in humanities-centered modes of inquiry. Nongraded.

subject: EN
title: Introduction to Cinema Studies
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Junior Class Standing or Below
Description: An introduction to the discipline of cinema studies, its history, and dominant approaches. Functions as a gateway to the minor and serves as a prerequisite for the required film theory course.

subject: EN
title: Introduction to Cinema Studies
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Junior Class Standing or Below
Description: An introduction to the discipline of cinema studies, its history, and dominant approaches. Functions as a gateway to the minor and serves as a prerequisite for the required film theory course.

section: EN 178-A - Language, Thought, and Writing: Introduction to Creative Writing
subject: EN
title: Language, Thought, and Writing: Introduction to Creative Writing
Section Details: Lovejoy 103 (Active Learning Classroom) | MW | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: Process-centered exploration of the fundamentals of writing fiction, poetry, nonfiction, drama, and hybrid forms. Students bring questions about self to a rigorous writing practice. Through reading and writing -- in both creative and critical modes -- we interrogate the many ways self is understood and expressed in the literary arts. Students write in a variety of forms, with peer review and revision guiding their choices. Readings reflect a wide range of backgrounds, traditions, and voices.

section: EN 178-B - Language, Thought, and Writing: Introduction to Creative Writing
subject: EN
title: Language, Thought, and Writing: Introduction to Creative Writing
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: Process-centered exploration of the fundamentals of writing fiction, poetry, nonfiction, drama, and hybrid forms. Students bring questions about self to a rigorous writing practice. Through reading and writing -- in both creative and critical modes -- we interrogate the many ways self is understood and expressed in the literary arts. Students write in a variety of forms, with peer review and revision guiding their choices. Readings reflect a wide range of backgrounds, traditions, and voices.

subject: EN
title: Foundations of Literary Studies
Section Details: Lovejoy 119 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 9:30 AM - 10:45 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course (IP)
Description: How and why do we read? How do we decide what counts as literature? What counts as knowledge for readers of imaginative texts? We begin to answer these questions in this broad ranging course. Required for the English major, the introduction to college-level literary studies incorporates poetry, drama, and fiction, explores canon formation with a historical range of literary works, and emphasizes close reading, interpretive vocabulary, and critical writing skills. Also introduces students to critical perspectives and scholarly research.

subject: EN
title: Foundations of Literary Studies
Section Details: Lovejoy 103 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course (IP)
Description: How and why do we read? How do we decide what counts as literature? What counts as knowledge for readers of imaginative texts? We begin to answer these questions in this broad ranging course. Required for the English major, the introduction to college-level literary studies incorporates poetry, drama, and fiction, explores canon formation with a historical range of literary works, and emphasizes close reading, interpretive vocabulary, and critical writing skills. Also introduces students to critical perspectives and scholarly research.

section: EN 229-A - Restaging the Real: 20th Century Theater and Performance
subject: EN
title: Restaging the Real: 20th Century Theater and Performance
Description: Throughout the 20th century, theatre and performance engage with crises of representation, by turns rejecting and reworking the concept of the “real” toward new forms and purposes. Through readings (plays, manifestos, performance history texts, performance theory), screenings (recorded performance, films), lecture, and discussion, this course will explore ways in which these experimental evolutions respond to surrounding sociopolitical contexts and craft interconnected histories. Students will trace major developments across key movements (e.g. symbolism, theatre of the absurd, postdramatic theatre, etc), and investigate how each rethinks/disrupts “the real” amid the echoes of early realism.

subject: EN
title: Critical Theory
Section Details: Miller Library 205 (Active Learning Classroom) | MW | 2:30 PM - 3:45 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course (IP)
Description: Introduction to major ideas in critical theory that influence the study of language, literature, and culture. Students gain mastery over an array of theoretical discourses and develop awareness of how underlying assumptions about representation shape reading practices. Possible approaches include classical theory, cultural materialism, structuralism, poststructuralism, psychoanalysis, Marxism, feminist theory, or postcolonial theory. Students learn to read complex arguments, recognize assumptions about interpretation and language, and use theoretical approaches and tools for interpreting the systems of representation that constitute culture.

subject: EN
title: Critical Theory
Section Details: Miller Library 205 (Active Learning Classroom) | MW | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course (IP)
Description: Introduction to major ideas in critical theory that influence the study of language, literature, and culture. Students gain mastery over an array of theoretical discourses and develop awareness of how underlying assumptions about representation shape reading practices. Possible approaches include classical theory, cultural materialism, structuralism, poststructuralism, psychoanalysis, Marxism, feminist theory, or postcolonial theory. Students learn to read complex arguments, recognize assumptions about interpretation and language, and use theoretical approaches and tools for interpreting the systems of representation that constitute culture.

subject: EN
title: Fiction Writing I
Section Details: Miller Library 241 (Seminar Classroom) | MW | 2:30 PM - 3:45 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course
Description: Writing short literary fiction. No prior experience with fiction writing presumed, only interest. Class sessions will be devoted to talking about fiction basics, analyzing short stories, and critiquing fellow students' fiction in workshops. Outside of class, students will be writing fiction exercises and complete stories, as well as reading professional stories. By the end of the semester, students should have insight into the creative process. They should have learned the basics of the craft of writing, and they should have practiced what they have learned through writing and rewriting.

subject: EN
title: Poetry Writing I: Ecopoetics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course
Description: How does poetry capture our relationship to the natural world in an era of climate change? Can art confront ecological crisis? In this ecopoetry workshop, students investigate poetic process and craft by reading and critically analyzing contemporary poetry about nature, writing their own environmental works, and offering feedback on the work of their peers. By semester’s end, students will produce a portfolio of revised poems and a statement of what they have learned about their creative process, aesthetic preferences, and their growing mastery of craft through an ecological lens. No prior experience with poetry or environmental studies presumed. Prerequisite: W1. Fulfills English P and LE requirement.

subject: EN
title: Poetry Writing I
Section Details: Miller Library 253 (Seminar Classroom) | TR | 1:00 PM - 2:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course
Description: What distinguishes a poem from a story from an advertisement from a phone call home? How do poems get written? And does it need to rhyme? In this workshop, students investigate these and many other questions about poetic process and craft by reading and critically analyzing contemporary poetry, writing their own poems, and offering feedback on the work of their peers. By semester's end, students will produce a portfolio of revised poems and a statement of what they have learned about their creative process, aesthetic preferences, and their growing mastery of craft. No prior experience with poetry presumed. Fulfills English P requirement.

subject: EN
title: Creative Nonfiction Writing I
Section Details: Lovejoy 103 (Active Learning Classroom) | MW | 1:00 PM - 2:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course
Description: A creative writing workshop that introduces students to the forms and possibilities of creative nonfiction, including essays of time and place, memoirs, profiles, and literary journalism. Progresses through a review of models, writing exercises, drafts, and finished pieces, with an emphasis on the workshop process, in which students share work and comment on each others' efforts.

section: EN 283-A - Environmental Humanities: Stories of Crisis and Resilience
subject: EN
title: Environmental Humanities: Stories of Crisis and Resilience
Section Details: Olin 019B (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 1:00 PM - 2:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course (IP)
Description: What can literature teach us about nature and environmental justice? Do the humanities and environmental studies share a vision of a sustainable future? Is it possible to understand climate change without telling stories about its uneven global impacts? To address these and other questions, we will examine how the environmental humanities implicitly respond to the "two cultures" debate. We will then investigate the relationship between environmental justice and western societies' extractive logics, economies, and management of nature. From within this theoretical framework we will analyze novels, poetry, and environmental films. Fulfills English C and D requirements.

section: EN 283-B - Environmental Humanities: Stories of Crisis and Resilience
subject: EN
title: Environmental Humanities: Stories of Crisis and Resilience
Section Details: Olin 019B (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 2:30 PM - 3:45 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course (IP)
Description: What can literature teach us about nature and environmental justice? Do the humanities and environmental studies share a vision of a sustainable future? Is it possible to understand climate change without telling stories about its uneven global impacts? To address these and other questions, we will examine how the environmental humanities implicitly respond to the "two cultures" debate. We will then investigate the relationship between environmental justice and western societies' extractive logics, economies, and management of nature. From within this theoretical framework we will analyze novels, poetry, and environmental films. Fulfills English C and D requirements.

subject: EN
title: Global Middle Ages
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course
Description: What did it mean to imagine a global world in the Middle Ages? We will answer this question by reading accounts of travelers from Christian, Muslim, and Jewish traditions; meeting the fictional English knight John Mandeville, who claimed to have ventured as far from home as China and Indonesia, and the very real 10th-century Muslim traveler Ibn Fadlan, who trekked through what is now Russia and Scandinavia. We will study the history of map-making, compare fictional and historical accounts of crusade, and consider how a multi-cultural medieval world is represented in medieval fantasy like Game of Thrones. The only prerequisite is curiosity about the Middle Ages. Fulfills English C, D, and E requirements.

section: EN 312-A - Death and Dying in the Middle Ages
subject: EN
title: Death and Dying in the Middle Ages
Section Details: Miller Library 319 (Seminar Classroom) | MW | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course
Description: Medieval writers approached death in a variety of ways: as heroic sacrifice, tragic loss, and inevitable transition. We will trace themes of death and dying through late medieval literature and explore topics including heaven, hell, and the Last Judgment; grief and mourning; death by violence and accident; the Black Plague; and the idea of a good death. Genres we will read include elegy, dream vision, and lyric, and study; authors include Chaucer and the Pearl Poet, as well as anonymous works. Some readings will be in Middle English; no previous experience with medieval literature is required. Fulfills English E and P requirements.

section: EN 326-A - Strange Natures: Queer Landscapes of Early American Literature
subject: EN
title: Strange Natures: Queer Landscapes of Early American Literature
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course
Description: How did early American representations of the natural world serve to challenge conventional assumptions about hierarchy and identity, about the proper organization of society and sexual relations? Although nature has often been invoked to enforce categories of status among people, we will pay attention to moments where nature explicitly or implicitly poses "a challenge to an assumed order of things" (Jack Halberstam). Writers include Wheatley Peters, Poe, Emerson, Thoreau, Douglass, Dickinson, and Whitman. Fulfills English C, D and LE requirements.

subject: EN
title: Shakespeare and Injustice
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course
Description: "Mercy seasons justice," Portia famously says to Shylock in The Merchant of Venice, but what does she really mean by that? Taking this question as a starting point, students in this course will examine justice and injustice in Shakespeare's plays as well as in/justice in the many adaptations of them. We will research, adapt, and write about a set of plays that students select, asking what we ought to do with Shakespeare and his fraught legacies, and whether it is possible or desirable to use Shakespeare's work to seek justice or to describe and uncover injustice in our own communities. Fulfills English E requirement.

subject: EN
title: Climate Fiction
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course
Description: Investigates contemporary literature, film, and media in the developing genre known as "climate fiction." We will situate these texts within the environmental humanities, an interdisciplinary field that combines scientific-cultural discourses about the environment with humanistic concerns for justice. We will ask how cli-fi narrates disaster on a global scale, but also strives to imagine more just futures that combine environmentalism and social equality. These texts will be paired with philosophical and eco-critical writings that will aid our development of the humanistic methodologies needed to analyze this new genre. Fulfills English C and LE requirement.

subject: EN
title: African-American Literature: An Introduction
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course
Description: This course offers an introduction to African American literature from 1865 to the present, engaging a range of genres including poetry, fiction, essays, art, music, and film. We will study major writers and intellectual traditions, including Du Bois, Hurston, Baldwin, and Morrison, alongside key cultural movements. The course examines how literature articulates questions of power, freedom, identity, and culture, and how these works shape and respond to American history and experience. Fulfills English D requirement. Prerequisite: Any W1 course. Four credit hours. L, U.

subject: EN
title: Fiction Writing II
Section Details: Miller Library 220 (Seminar Classroom) | MW | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: EN 278
Description: An intermediate workshop in writing fiction. Focuses on the writing and revision of the literary short story, with particular attention to the structure of dramatic action, character, texture and tone, inspiration, and the process of revision. Prerequisite: English 278.

subject: EN
title: Poetry Writing II
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: EN 279
Description: Presupposes basic familiarity with the poetic uses of metaphors, images, lines, and fresh and rhythmic diction. Requires students to read more extensively and analytically in contemporary poetry and continue their practice working with the kind of divergent thinking that makes poetry possible. Students will also undertake a more sophisticated investigation of the interplay of syntax with lineation, the nuances of pacing and structure, the resources of associative thinking, the gambits of rhetoric, and the complexities of tone. Final portfolio, emphasis on revision. Fulfills English P requirement. Prerequisite: English 279

section: EN 413W-A - Author course: Phillis Wheatley and her Literary Afterlives
subject: EN
title: Author course: Phillis Wheatley and her Literary Afterlives
Section Details: Miller Library 220 (Seminar Classroom) | R | 1:00 PM - 3:30 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course
Description: Phillis Wheatley (Peters) was twenty and enslaved in 1773 when she published a book of poetry that challenged the racialized assumptions of her era. She has since become a literary foremother who's influenced Black theologians, activists, creative writers, artists, and scholars. This course brings Wheatley's poetry into conversation with the 230+ years of creative and scholarly work she inspired, including the contemporary poetry of drea brown, Honorée Fanonne Jeffers, and Tiana Clark. Students will read Wheatley's oeuvre, including her elegies, war poetry, and letters, as well as scholarship that meditates on our methods of reading her. Fulfills English C, D, and P requirements.

subject: EN
title: Honors Proseminar
Section Details: Miller Library 205 (Active Learning Classroom) | R | 8:00 AM - 9:15 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Co-enrolled in EN 483
Description: Practicum for students undertaking senior honors theses in English.

section: EN 493K-A - Seminar: World Literature: Globalization and Its Discontents
subject: EN
title: Seminar: World Literature: Globalization and Its Discontents
Section Details: Miller Library 220 (Seminar Classroom) | W | 1:00 PM - 3:30 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: A W1 course, and either EN 271 or any upper level Humanities course
Description: This seminar focuses on 'world literature' from a variety of angles including poetry, short stories, the novel, essays, film and music. We will consider the political and cultural dimensions of these works and analyze how fiction takes up issues such as identity and language, the concept of the nation state, colonialism and postcolonialism, and the afterlife of war. The objective will be to explore how writers and creative works from different parts of the world reflect the aesthetic and political sensibilities of the places from which they emerge. The class will examine some of the ways individual and collective struggles for liberation are imagined across transnational contexts in an era of globalization. Fulfills English C and D requirements.

subject: ER
title: Earth Systems Chemistry I
Section Details: Olin 019B (Active Learning Classroom) | MWF | 10:00 AM - 10:50 AM
Description: The Earth is a dynamic chemical reactor that changes on timescales of seconds to millions of years through natural and anthropogenic forcings. This two-semester sequence explores fundamental chemistry principles, including the structure of the atom, chemical bonding and reactivity, chemical equilibria, and thermodynamics through the lens of Earth's 4.56-billion-year history. By constructing quantitative models of Earth systems, students also learn how Earth processes operate over time and space, how they shape the environments in which we live, and the theoretical and practical limits of resource utilization. Students with prior credit for Chemistry 141, 142, or 147 cannot receive credit for this course.

section: ER 121 L-A - Lab:Earth Systems Chem I
subject: ER
title: Lab:Earth Systems Chem I

section: ER 121 L-B - Lab:Earth Systems Chem I
subject: ER
title: Lab:Earth Systems Chem I

subject: ER
title: From Stardust to Planets
Section Details: Miller 008 (Active Learning Classroom) | MWF | 9:00 AM - 9:50 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Students may not earn credit for GE 125 and any from GE 122, 123, 127, 128, 129, or 141
Description: Explores the physical and chemical evolution of the Earth in the context of solar system formation. By studying the development of the terrestrial (rocky) planets, students will be introduced to fundamental concepts in geology. As students investigate geologic processes on other planetary bodies, they will develop a deeper understanding of our own planet's evolution and geology. We will focus on important questions, such as "How did Earth become a habitable planet?" and "How has humanity impacted the Earth's evolution?" High-school-level chemistry is recommended but not required to succeed in the course.

section: ER 125 L-A - Lab: From Stardust to Planets
subject: ER
title: Lab: From Stardust to Planets

section: ER 125 L-B - Lab: From Stardust to Planets

subject: ER
title: The Water Planet
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ:  Students may not earn credit for GE 129 and any from: GE 122, 123, 125, 127,  128, or 141
Description: Examines processes controlling the flow of energy and mass between the atmosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, and anthrosphere through the framework of our planet's oceans. Geologic processes both rapid (earthquakes) and slow (sea-floor spreading) are linked with sustaining the planet. Lab and field work develop the skills needed to observe and model processes shaping our environment. Problem solving fosters critical thinking and classroom debates focus on research and communications skills via current issues like coastal development. Credit cannot be earned for both this course and Geology 122, 123, 125, 127 or 141.

section: ER 129 L-A - Lab: The Water Planet
subject: ER
title: Lab: The Water Planet

section: ER 129 L-B - Lab: The Water Planet
subject: ER
title: Lab: The Water Planet

subject: ER
title: Earth Structure and Tectonics
Description: Applies fundamental concepts of stress and strain to understand the different styles of deformation at convergent, divergent, and transform plate boundaries; the physical and chemical mechanisms that control the strength of plate-bounding fault zones; how these deformation mechanisms change with increasing depth in Earth; and how to read the rock record of plate-tectonic deformation. Students also will develop fundamental field-observation skills, and practice written and graphical communication skills as they are applied in the Earth sciences. Three required field trips extend into the athletic zone.

section: ER 254-A - Earth Surface Processes: Introduction to Geomorphology
subject: ER
title: Earth Surface Processes: Introduction to Geomorphology
Description: An examination of the processes driving landscape change over time with field-based study in Maine. Students will measure sediment-transport processes, analyze and interpret satellite imagery using python, synthesize field measurements of stream flow and sediment size, and communicate their data and interpretations in writing, orally, and graphically. A mix of lectures, discussions, student presentations, lab exercises, and field study. Three required field trips will extend outside of normal class time.

subject: ER
title: Paleoceanography
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ER 262 (formerly GE 262)
Description: This primary literature synthesis course examines past global change through the lens of the marine sedimentary record. Students explore the major physical and geochemical proxies used in paleoceanographic research and focus on understanding the major scientific questions addressed, methods and instrumentation used, and advantages and limitations of each proxy tool. Students also develop critical thinking skills through the interpretation of primary datasets and literature, and improve their written and oral presentation skills through communicating scientific findings.

subject: ES
title: Environment and Society
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year Class Standing
Description: An interdisciplinary course introducing students to environmental challenges by exploring Maine’s environment and its important role in the history of the modern environmental movement. Students will read influential writings from authors who were shaped by Maine and influenced the world. The course will include immersive field visits exploring Maine’s oceans, forests, freshwater systems, biodiversity, agriculture, and engaging with local practitioners to learn how Maine has been a national leader in addressing environmental challenges. Students will also learn about Colby’s innovative sustainability efforts and work on a project related to sustainability at Colby or in Waterville. Intended for students interested in becoming Environmental Studies majors or minors.

subject: ES
title: Environment and Society
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year Class Standing
Description: An interdisciplinary introduction to major environmental challenges, including climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution. Students will explore the science behind these issues, examine potential policy responses, and analyze the historical, social, and economic structures that shape environmental outcomes. Through critical reading, lively discussion, academic research, and experiential learning in Maine’s natural environments, students will develop a deeper, multifaceted understanding of environmental problems and the possibilities for change.

subject: ES
title: Taxonomy of Flowering Plants
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: BI 164 or 201
Description: An overview of evolutionary relationships among flowering plants and their nearest living relatives, and the study of evolutionary processes leading to those relationships. Students will prepare a collection of plant specimens from the local flora, learn to recognize important plant families, use technical keys to identify plants, and become familiar with analytical methods for constructing and evaluating phylogenetic hypotheses. Lecture and laboratory.

section: ES 214-A - Introduction to GIS and Spatial Analysis
subject: ES
title: Introduction to GIS and Spatial Analysis
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomores and above who have not earned credit for ES 212 or ES 214J
Description: An introduction to geographic information systems' (GIS) data management and visualization capabilities as well as the theory and application of spatial analysis techniques. Topics covered include spatial data representation in a GIS, effective map making, coordinate systems and projections, exploratory spatial data analysis (ESDA), and spatial statistical analysis.

subject: ES
title: Ecological Restoration and Management
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ES 118, ES 120*, or ST 112
Description: Conservation in the twenty-first century often means intervening to restore degraded lands, manage species, and adapt to climate change. Human societies have shaped landscapes for millennia, using diverse systems of knowledge and management. Industrial development profoundly altered many of those relationships. This course explores the modern science of ecological restoration alongside the complex history of human relationships with the environment and practices of stewardship and land transformation. Through lecture, discussion, and a hands-on restoration lab in the Colby Woods, students learn the practice of ecological restoration while engaging ethical and practical questions about managing ecosystems in a changing world.

section: ES 231-A - Environmental and Natural Resource Economics
subject: ES
title: Environmental and Natural Resource Economics
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - PP :: Public Policy
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ECON Majors, ES Majors, or ECON Minors who have completed EC 133 and Sophomore Class Standing or above
Description: The objective is to develop and apply economic tools to current environmental and resource-management issues. Causes of and remedies to environmental and resource-management problems are analyzed through economic modeling. These models in turn serve as the theoretical foundation for designing and evaluating policy instruments and practices. Students will learn to analyze current environmental problems and assess the effectiveness of environmental and resource-management policies using economic tools.

subject: ES
title: International Environmental Policy
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (Env Policy, Env Sci, Env Comp Majors, or Env Studies Minors) and must have taken ES 118 or ES 120
Description: The principles and rules relating to environmental protection are one of the fastest growing areas of international law. Introducing students to key foundational principles, governance structures, and regulatory techniques, this course will explore each of the major areas of international environmental regulation through case studies and analyses of international environmental treaties relating to, for example, atmospheric protection, climate change, and freshwater and marine resources. The ever-increasing overlap with other areas of international law such as human rights and trade will also be explored. Special attention will be paid to the perspectives of countries in the Global South, and to the justice implications of international environmental law and policy.

subject: ES
title: Marine Communities
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (Env Policy, Env Sci, Env Comp Majors, Marine Sci Minors, or Env Studies Minors) and must have taken ES 118 or ES 120
Description: Introduces students to key ecological interactions in marine communities around the world, including kelp forests, coral reefs, sea grasses, and the open ocean. A key learning goal is improved scientific literacy through in-depth reading and synthesis of scientific papers and the development of a research proposal.

section: ES 254-A - Earth Surface Processes: Introduction to Geomorphology
subject: ES
title: Earth Surface Processes: Introduction to Geomorphology
Description: An examination of the processes driving landscape change over time with field-based study in Maine. Students will measure sediment-transport processes, analyze and interpret satellite imagery using python, synthesize field measurements of stream flow and sediment size, and communicate their data and interpretations in writing, orally, and graphically. A mix of lectures, discussions, student presentations, lab exercises, and field study. Three required field trips will extend outside of normal class time.

section: ES 255-A - Marine Biology of Coastal Maine
subject: ES
title: Marine Biology of Coastal Maine
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: BI 164 or 201
Description: A broad survey of the taxonomy, biology, and ecology of Maine's coastal organisms, with a focus on invertebrates and macroalgae. Students will engage with local habitats, including on several field trips and a required overnight weekend field trip to the Colby Island Campus. Further, students will learn the fundamentals of experimental design through analysis of the peer reviewed literature. In laboratory, students will master species identification, describing and distinguishing major taxa, and become adept at making observations, through dissections and the keeping of a detailed anatomical notebook. Meets the Biology field course requirement.

subject: ES
title: Atmospheric Chemistry
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CH 122, 142, or 147
Description: An investigation of Earth's atmosphere and the chemical and physical principles that shape it. Fundamental processes that determine atmospheric composition and climate, including multistep reaction mechanisms, chemical kinetics, molecular spectroscopy, photolysis, and heterogeneous chemistry, are introduced. Specific topics treated will include atmospheric composition, structure, and motion; element cycling; the transfer of solar and longwave radiation; stratospheric composition and chemistry; tropospheric oxidation processes; air pollution; and the role of human activity in global change.

subject: ES
title: Global Health
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ES 118 or 120*, or a NatSci course (Sophomore Class Standing or above)
Description: An introduction to the principles and measures of global health, disease burdens, and environmental determinants of health, including poverty, climate change, pollution, population, violence, and lack of safe food, clean water, and fuels. We will also study international health institutions, key actors, and environmental regimes for the regulation of environmental health hazards. Through small-group presentations and discussion we will explore global case studies that highlight the complex relationship between human health and the environment.

subject: ES
title: Ecology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: BI 164 or 201
Description: Ecology is the study of interactions among organisms and their environment. Studying these interactions provides us with the theoretical foundation for understanding many of the most pressing environmental problems. This course will examine ecological interactions at a wide range of scales from individuals, through populations and communities, to ecosystems. We will study how these interactions produce the patterns and processes we observe in biomes around the world. In the field-based laboratory, we will generate hypotheses, develop experimental designs, and apply statistical analyses to ecological data, while gaining first-hand familiarity with local ecological communities. Lecture and laboratory.  Previously listed as Environmental Studies 271.

section: ES 283-A - Environmental Humanities: Stories of Crisis and Resilience
subject: ES
title: Environmental Humanities: Stories of Crisis and Resilience
Section Details: Olin 019B (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 1:00 PM - 2:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: W1 course (IP)
Description: What can literature teach us about nature and environmental justice? Do the humanities and environmental studies share a vision of a sustainable future? Is it possible to understand climate change without telling stories about its uneven global impacts? To address these and other questions, we will examine how the environmental humanities implicitly respond to the "two cultures" debate. We will then investigate the relationship between environmental justice and western societies' extractive logics, economies, and management of nature. From within this theoretical framework we will analyze novels, poetry, and environmental films. Fulfills English C and D requirements.

section: ES 283-B - Environmental Humanities: Stories of Crisis and Resilience

title: Environmental Humanities: Stories of Crisis and Resilience

subject: ES
title: Conservation Biology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ES Majors/Minors who have taken ES 118 or 120, or a NatSci course (Sophomore Class Standing or above)
Description: Concepts of conservation biology are examined in detail. Topics include patterns of diversity and rarity, sensitive habitats, extinction, captive propagation, preserve design, and reclamation of degraded or destroyed ecosystems. Interdisciplinary solutions to the challenges of protecting, maintaining, and restoring biological diversity are discussed. Offered in alternate years.
