We will ask how cli-fi narrates disaster on a global scale, but also strives to imagine more just futures that combine environmentalism and social equality. These texts will be paired with philosophical and eco-critical writings that will aid our development of the humanistic methodologies needed to analyze this new genre. Fulfills English C and LE requirement.

section: ES 345-A - Offshore Energy: Environmental Permits and Community Planning
subject: ES
title: Offshore Energy: Environmental Permits and Community Planning
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (Env Policy, Env Sci, Env Comp Majors, or Env Studies Minors) and must have taken ES 118 or ES 120
Description: Building an offshore wind farm requires environmental assessment of ecological and human impacts, obtaining permits, and community approval. This process is expensive, lengthy, and vital to the success of an offshore wind farm, and the clean energy transition. Using a case study approach, this course takes a hands-on approach to guide students through the process of renewable energy development from start to finish, open ocean to operational wind farm. The course has an emphasis on protection of marine species, consideration of ocean users such as fishing communities, and ways to work with local communities to improve equity and justice in decision-making. Students will develop the necessary, and applied skills to enter the energy workforce.

subject: ES
title: Paleoceanography
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ER 262 (formerly GE 262)
Description: This primary literature synthesis course examines past global change through the lens of the marine sedimentary record. Students explore the major physical and geochemical proxies used in paleoceanographic research and focus on understanding the major scientific questions addressed, methods and instrumentation used, and advantages and limitations of each proxy tool. Students also develop critical thinking skills through the interpretation of primary datasets and literature, and improve their written and oral presentation skills through communicating scientific findings.

subject: ES
title: Climate Justice and Health
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ES 118 or 120* (Sophomore Class Standing or above)
Description: Examines the impacts of changing climate dynamics on human livelihoods, rights, health, and well-being. Through interdisciplinary readings, class discussions, research projects, and innovative communications, students will engage deeply with data from the natural and social sciences about human impacts, adaptations, and vulnerabilities, as well as explore climate justice activism. Key learning goals include improved information literacy and written and oral communication skills and increased understanding of the ways climate change is impacting the world in which we live.

subject: ES
title: Global Climate Policy
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ES 234 or GO 131
Description: Climate change impacts are widespread; in many spaces doom and gloom is the dominant narrative. What are the successes of global climate policy? What role do non-state actors, like civil society organizations play? This course focuses on challenges and possible solutions in global climate policy and international climate negotiations. We will engage with scholarship from across academic disciplines alongside work by practitioners and activists. Students will virtually observe United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) negotiations on a key issue, evaluate the outcome, and craft a policy brief with concrete recommendations.

subject: ES
title: Global Climate Policy
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ES 234 or GO 131
Description: Climate change is a global problem. How and whether a world of sovereign states can cooperate to reduce climate change risks to manageable levels are critical questions, but there is no political or expert consensus around the best way forward. This course will study global climate politics and policy in the context of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. Students will work individually and in groups to critically assess and propose international governance responses relating to climate mitigation, adaptation, loss and damage, and finance provision. Special attention will be paid to the vulnerabilities of small island developing states, and to climate justice.

subject: ES
title: Environmental Studies Colloquium
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ES: Senior Class Standing in Environmental Studies
Description: Attendance at selected program colloquia during the fall and spring semesters; written reflections to be submitted. Required of all senior environmental studies majors. Typically taken in addition to a normal four-course semester. One credit hour for the year.

subject: ES
title: Environmental Policy Practicum
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ES 233 or 234 and Senior Class Standing as an Environmental Policy Major
Description: An in-depth analysis of current issues and policies affecting the environment. Students work individually and collaboratively on a project with a common theme and are assigned unique roles as researchers, editors, and technical coordinators. Reading and discussion of primary literature is augmented with invited speakers, field trips, and student presentations.

subject: ES
title: Environmental Science Research Experience
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ES 271 or BI 271, and Senior Class Standing as an Env Science,  Env Comp, or Env Policy Major
Description: Causes of and solutions to selected environmental problems are investigated through lectures, laboratory and field work, discussions, and guest presentations. Focuses on completion of a group research project to investigate freshwater, forest or marine ecosystems. Research results are presented in a public forum at the end of the semester. The civic engagement component provides useful information to the community and the state and gives students experience interacting with interested stakeholders. Skill development includes research, communication (both oral and written), and collaborative work skills.

subject: ES
title: Environmental Science Research Experience
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ES 271 or BI 271, and Senior Class Standing as an Env Science,  Env Comp, or Env Policy Major
Description: Causes of and solutions to selected environmental problems are investigated through lectures, laboratory and field work, discussions, and guest presentations. Focuses on completion of a group research project to investigate freshwater, forest or marine ecosystems. Research results are presented in a public forum at the end of the semester. The civic engagement component provides useful information to the community and the state and gives students experience interacting with interested stakeholders. Skill development includes research, communication (both oral and written), and collaborative work skills.

subject: FR
title: French I
Description: First in a sequence that develops communication skills in a careful progression over three semesters. In addition to working on the four traditional skills of language acquisition--speaking, comprehension, reading, and writing--students will be introduced to the cultural contexts of France and the Francophone world. Use of audio and videotaped material is an integral and required part of class work. Students are placed in the appropriate level by their score on the College Board French SAT Subject test, a placement test during fall orientation, or through consultation with a member of the faculty in French.

subject: FR
title: French II
Section Details: Lovejoy 102 (Active Learning Classroom) | MTWR | 9:00 AM - 9:50 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: FR 125 or equivalent
Description: Strengthens and expands the skills introduced and practiced in French 125 by offering a learning environment conducive to the practice and development of writing, reading, listening, and oral performance. Because language practice is closely tied to cultural understanding, we use authentic texts and contexts that foster linguistic competence while highlighting the diversified cultural contribution of the French and Francophone world.

Description: Builds reading skills in French and broadens cultural knowledge of the Francophone world through a wide variety of texts and media. Emphasis is on the texts and contexts of culture, whether in France and/or in the Francophone world. Engages students in critical thinking and develops writing and oral expression.

section: FR 224-A - French Studies Lab Project: Maine, Ecology, and Gender
subject: FR
title: French Studies Lab Project: Maine, Ecology, and Gender
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: FR 128 or 131 or equivalent
Description: Students hone their skills in oral and written French through "hands-on" learning. Projects focused on a specific issue or topic may include: arts initiative involving the community and Colby museum, creative performance or exhibit, design project, Digital Humanities platforms, educational materials for local schools, environmental initiatives, field work, non-profit work and engagement with local organizations, public podcast, social media, and translation. This experiential course fosters intellectual curiosity, collaboration, learning by doing, problem solving, critical and creative thinking along with skills in research and project management.

subject: FR
title: Advanced Grammar and Composition
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: FR 128 or 131 or equivalent
Description: Provides a comprehensive overview of French grammar through presentations of the overall structure and frequent practice in writing. Required of majors and open to others wishing to improve their written expression in French.

subject: FR
title: Intensive Spoken French
Description: Exclusively for French majors or students preparing for study in a French-speaking country. Weekly practice in oral French conducted by the French language assistant under the direction of a faculty member. May be repeated once for credit. Nongraded.

section: FR 256-A - Film for Thought: The Art of French Cinema
subject: FR
title: Film for Thought: The Art of French Cinema
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: FR 128 or 131 or equivalent
Description: A survey of directors, genres, movements, and aesthetics in French cinema from early 20th Century to the present day. Emphasis on the analysis of film style and form: mise-en-scene, cinematography, editing, sound, performance, etc. Students will approach film not only as a form of art, but also as a site of memory and/or a tool of socio-political discourse. Film theory will frame our class discussions. Students will develop visual literacy, analytical skills, critical and creative thinking through innovative visual projects, essays and class discussions. Course conducted in French.

section: FR 340-A - Trauma and Resilience in the Francophone World
subject: FR
title: Trauma and Resilience in the Francophone World
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: FR 231, and FR 2XX, 3XX, or 4XX
Description: The concept of resilience is essential to navigating the diverse challenges of the 21st century, which range from post-colonial trauma to ecological crisis and social pressure. This course invites students to explore how the Francophone world approaches mental health and wellbeing in the face of such challenges. By examining past and present remedies, they will learn how psychiatry addresses trauma and evaluate its relevance in contemporary contexts. Through studying the concept of resilience from a Francophone perspective, students will explore how to navigate traumas, including ecological, digital, post-colonial, sociological, and migratory. This course offers a unique opportunity to reflect on the art of navigating traumas while preparing to face challenges of tomorrow.

section: FR 493T-A - Seminar: Trauma and Resilience in the Francophone World
subject: FR
title: Seminar: Trauma and Resilience in the Francophone World
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Senior Class Standing as a French Studies Major
Description: The concept of resilience is essential to navigating the diverse challenges of the 21st century, which range from post-colonial trauma to ecological crisis and social pressure. This course invites students to explore how the Francophone world approaches mental health and wellbeing in the face of such challenges. subject: GK
title: Intermediate Ancient Greek
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: GK 111 or GK 111j
Description: The second of a two-semester sequence in which students learn to read the ancient Greek of classical Athens. Careful attention to grammar, syntax, and vocabulary forms the foundation of the course.

section: GK 248-A - Topics in Ancient Greek Literature: Homer
subject: GK
title: Topics in Ancient Greek Literature: Homer
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: GK 131 or GK 200 level or above
Description: Reading and discussion of original ancient Greek texts. Drawn from the long history of ancient Greek, texts vary from year to year. Attention will be paid to the literary histories and historical contexts of the selected readings. May be repeated for credit.

subject: GM
title: Elementary German I
Description: Introductory course for students with little or no previous knowledge of German. Development of all four skills: listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Communicative and interactive acquisition of grammar and vocabulary via study of contemporary life in the German-speaking countries. Audiovisual materials and integrated multimedia accompany textbook instruction.

subject: GM
title: Elementary German I
Description: Introductory course for students with little or no previous knowledge of German. Development of all four skills: listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Communicative and interactive acquisition of grammar and vocabulary via study of contemporary life in the German-speaking countries. Audiovisual materials and integrated multimedia accompany textbook instruction.

section: GM 127-A - Intermediate German I: Exploring German Studies
subject: GM
title: Intermediate German I: Exploring German Studies
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: GM 126 or equivalent
Description: An investigative and experiential course focused on content/disciplinary practices in the field of German Studies and different forms of (non-)digital storytelling, GM127 is an introduction to extended readings and writings in German via cultural contexts. Leads students toward understanding the intersections of the German-speaking world and their studies at Colby via modular exploration of the field of German Studies (that is, by equipping students with the tools for analysis of aesthetic and intellectual accomplishments representative of major periods in German, Austrian, and Swiss history, the course will enable students to address the question What constitutes German Studies?) and through different forms of storytelling. Humanities lab course.

subject: GM
title: Conversation Group
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: GM 125 or GM 126
Description: Review and practice for students at the intermediate level. A selection of written, visual, and audio German language and culture sources will provide the basis for discussion and conversation. Does not count toward the language requirement or the German major and minor. Conducted in German. May be repeated for credit. Nongraded.

subject: GM
title: Vienna 1900 (in English)
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: In-depth exploration of the Viennese Secession (1898-1905), a pivotal moment in European avant-garde art. Considers artworks, creators (artists, architects, designers), collectors, and the historical and cultural context of Belle-Epoque Vienna. The course also addresses issues related to collecting this material in the post-World War II context and crucial issues of provenance research and restitution of Nazi-looted art.

subject: GM
title: The German Songbook
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: GM 128 or equivalent
Description: This course focuses on the cultural history of German songs and music from the Romantic era through contemporary hip hop and Schlager. It is an exploration of the musical and lyrical engagement with topics ranging from nature and being human to gender and power as well as artistic representations of changing notions of Germanness. Analysis and discussion of different forms of musical expressions, secondary and critical literature, and the ways in which music interconnects to the world. Weekly reflective writings, short critical essays, student presentations, participation in writing workshop, final research project. Prereqs: GM 128 or equiv.

subject: GM
title: Current Topics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: GM 127 or GM 128 or equivalent
Description: An informal weekly meeting for students at the advanced level for conversation practice. Source materials include newspaper and magazine articles, contemporary German film, television broadcasts, and podcasts, along with other media. Does not count toward the language requirement or the German major and minor. Conducted in German. May be repeated for credit. Nongraded.

section: GM 342-A - Contested Subjects in German Culture
subject: GM
title: Contested Subjects in German Culture
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Has taken one GM 2XX course taught in German
Description: Introduction to critical analysis of contested subjects in German and German-speaking cultures. While topics vary, this course will refine close reading skills of written and visual texts, including poetry, works of art, drama, short stories, prose, and film that focus on culturally contested topics. Focus on critical, written and interpretive analysis, student presentations, and exposure to relevant cultural, theoretical, and historical sources. Conducted in German.

section: GO 111-A - Introduction to American Government and Politics
subject: GO
title: Introduction to American Government and Politics
Description: How does the American government work? An examination of the relationships among American values, politics, government institutions, and public policy. Focus on the methodologies of political science as tools for expanding understanding of political phenomena and behavior. Credit toward the major cannot be earned for both Government 111 and 115.

section: GO 111-B - Introduction to American Government and Politics
subject: GO
title: Introduction to American Government and Politics
Description: How does the American government work? An examination of the relationships among American values, politics, government institutions, and public policy. Focus on the methodologies of political science as tools for expanding understanding of political phenomena and behavior. Credit toward the major cannot be earned for both Government 111 and 115.

subject: GO
title: Introduction to International Relations
Description: An introduction to the basic concepts and theories of international relations, focusing primarily on the core issues of war and peace as they have evolved in the international system, as well as the prospects for cooperation through international institutions to address issues such as human rights, nuclear proliferation, the world economy, and the global environment.

subject: GO
title: Introduction to International Relations
Description: An introduction to the basic concepts and theories of international relations, focusing primarily on the core issues of war and peace as they have evolved in the international system, as well as the prospects for cooperation through international institutions to address issues such as human rights, nuclear proliferation, the world economy, and the global environment.

subject: GO
title: Introduction to International Relations
Description: An introduction to the basic concepts and theories of international relations, focusing primarily on the core issues of war and peace as they have evolved in the international system, as well as the prospects for cooperation through international institutions to address issues such as human rights, nuclear proliferation, the world economy, and the global environment.

section: GO 145A-A - Leadership in the Ancient World
subject: GO
title: Leadership in the Ancient World
Course Tags: Integrated Studies Clusters :: IS: The Ancient World
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: To understand leadership in both ancient and contemporary times, the course will be informed by theoretical approaches to leadership (e.g. trait theory, situational theories, behavioral theories), as well as theories related to issues such as power, authority, and influence. Additionally, the course will utilize case studies, historical and textual analysis, and cross-cultural comparisons. By exploring the roots of leadership, the course seeks to provide students a deeper understanding of the evolution of leadership practices, and how these practices have shaped contemporary leadership theories and practices.

subject: GO
title: Introduction to Political Theory
Description: What are the nature and purpose of the modern state or of any political community? What is freedom? What is justice? How do such ideals relate to the design and functioning of political institutions? Political theory is the subfield within political science that addresses these and related normative and methodologically foundational questions. Introduction to classic works of political theory by Aristotle, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Marx, and Mill. Students will demonstrate their understanding of the primary texts and their ability to formulate original arguments in political theory by means of papers and exams; class sessions are conducted as a mixture of lecture and discussion.

section: GO 197-A - The Politics of A.I. in Literature and Theory
subject: GO
title: The Politics of A.I. in Literature and Theory
Section Details: Miller Library 319 (Seminar Classroom) | TR | 9:30 AM - 10:45 AM
Course Tags: Integrated Studies Clusters :: IS: 360 Degrees of A.I.
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: Since long before artificial intelligence became technologically feasible, writers and philosophers have engaged in speculation over its political implications and the changes it may impose on society and our very definition of humanity. In this class, we will read canonical contributions to the fictional representation of A.I., explore their themes alongside innovations in social theory, and discuss the complex interaction between technology, literature, and debates over citizenship, political freedom, and human flourishing.

section: GO 222-A - Economic Statecraft in U.S.-China Relations
subject: GO
title: Economic Statecraft in U.S.-China Relations
Cross-Listed Title: EA 223-A/ GO 222-A - Economic Statecraft in U.S.
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: GO 131
Description: Examines how the U.S and China use economic statecraft against each other, as well as to coerce other countries, in their competition. With the rising significance of economic tools in crafting national security and foreign policy strategies, this course surveys theories of economic statecraft and empirical cases to explore whether, how, and when economic statecraft can be used to advance geopolitical objectives. The topics, including sanctions regimes, U.S.-China trade war, and various global economic initiatives, will enable students to approach some of the most pressing policy debates with rigor.

subject: GO
title: Media and Politics
Description: An assessment of the role of the media in American politics. Examines the media as an institution and how it is both influenced by and reflects our system of government. What functions, for example, do contemporary news outlets afford the democratic process? Is there a connection between the way news is transmitted and the way citizens interact with government? Throughout much of American history the press has been considered a watchdog and the "fourth branch" of government. The challenge in this course is to explore the nexus of the theoretical role assigned to the mass media and its present character.

section: GO 228-A - Introduction to Race, Ethnicity, and Politics
subject: GO
title: Introduction to Race, Ethnicity, and Politics
Description: Examines broadly the ways in which racial and ethnic minorities influence and are influenced by American politics and public policy.  The course is organized in three parts.  Part I will explore the theoretical and historical contexts of race in American politics.  Part II will focus on race and political behavior, paying close attention to public opinion, participation, and representation.  Part III will examine particular policy-related case studies:  minority education, housing, employment, and criminal justice.

subject: GO
title: International Environmental Policy
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (Env Policy, Env Sci, Env Comp Majors, or Env Studies Minors) and must have taken ES 118 or ES 120
Description: The principles and rules relating to environmental protection are one of the fastest growing areas of international law. Introducing students to key foundational principles, governance structures, and regulatory techniques, this course will explore each of the major areas of international environmental regulation through case studies and analyses of international environmental treaties relating to, for example, atmospheric protection, climate change, and freshwater and marine resources. The ever-increasing overlap with other areas of international law such as human rights and trade will also be explored. Special attention will be paid to the perspectives of countries in the Global South, and to the justice implications of international environmental law and policy.

section: GO 252-A - Introduction to Politics of the Middle East
subject: GO
title: Introduction to Politics of the Middle East
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Provides the analytical and historical background for making sense of politics in the Arab world today. Highlights the main drivers of politics in the region, with particular emphasis paid to the intersection of political and economic forces, domestic and regional or international factors, and Islam and politics. Explores the roots of authoritarianism in the region, the dynamics that sustain it, and key impediments to substantive (as opposed to cosmetic) democratization. Examines the combination of forces that produced both the Arab Spring of 2011 and the turmoil that followed it. Open to first-years. Fulfills the introductory comparative politics requirement.

section: GO 253-A - Introduction to Latin American Politics
subject: GO
title: Introduction to Latin American Politics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: An overview of important political and economic phenomena in Latin America over the past century. How can Latin America escape its persistent problems with underdevelopment, poverty, and inequality, and what is the role of a democratic government in tackling these problems? Topics covered include state-directed development models, populism, democratic breakdown and democratization, free market economic models, and contemporary leftist alternatives. Open to first-years. Fulfills the introductory comparative politics requirement.

subject: GO
title: Introduction to Policy Analysis
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: EC 293, GO 281, PS 214, SC 212, or SO 271
Description: This course offers an introduction to major theories and approaches in the analysis of public policy, with a particular focus on policy effects. Topics to be covered include case selection, the logic of causal inference, randomized experiments, quasi-experimental designs, comparing quantitative and qualitative approaches, causal mechanisms, and costs and unintended consequences.

subject: GO
title: Introduction to Policy Analysis
Section Details: Lovejoy 102 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 2:30 PM - 3:45 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: EC 293, GO 281, PS 214, SC 212, or SO 271
Description: This course offers an introduction to major theories and approaches in the analysis of public policy, with a particular focus on policy effects. Topics to be covered include case selection, the logic of causal inference, randomized experiments, quasi-experimental designs, comparing quantitative and qualitative approaches, causal mechanisms, and costs and unintended consequences.

subject: GO
title: Modern Political Theory
Description: An introduction to major works of modern political theory. Readings include Machiavelli, Montesquieu, Rousseau, Hegel, Nietzsche, and others. Students will learn to analyze these foundational texts, reading them to understand what they are asserting and the justifying reasons they offer to support those assertions. Additionally, students will construct their own theories of politics and/or apply insights from the foundational texts to contemporary issues. This course satisfies the new [pending approval] Government Department political theory requirement. Students will prepare two presentations and sit for two exams.

section: GO 281-A - Concepts and Methods of Political Science Research
subject: GO
title: Concepts and Methods of Political Science Research
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomore Class Standing or above with a Government major
Description: An introduction to a variety of approaches to the study of political phenomena, intended to prepare students to craft and complete more sophisticated research projects in political science. After discussion of the nature and aims of scientific inquiry and the general features of effective research design, focus is on two broad methodological perspectives: explanation and interpretation. Topics include hypothesis testing and statistical analysis, the problem of historical truth, symbolic representation, and discourse analysis. Students will complete a number of different types of assignments and will apply course ideas to develop their own original research design.

section: GO 281-B - Concepts and Methods of Political Science Research
subject: GO
title: Concepts and Methods of Political Science Research
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomore Class Standing or above with a Government major
Description: An introduction to a variety of approaches to the study of political phenomena, intended to prepare students to craft and complete more sophisticated research projects in political science. After discussion of the nature and aims of scientific inquiry and the general features of effective research design, focus is on two broad methodological perspectives: explanation and interpretation. Topics include hypothesis testing and statistical analysis, the problem of historical truth, symbolic representation, and discourse analysis. Students will complete a number of different types of assignments and will apply course ideas to develop their own original research design.

section: GO 314-A - Civil Liberties in American Constitutional Law
subject: GO
title: Civil Liberties in American Constitutional Law
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Junior Class Standing or Above

subject: GO
title: Elements of the Law
Section Details: Diamond 123 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 1:00 PM - 2:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomore Class Standing or Above
Description: This course is about the law as an institution. It examines the building blocks and core concepts that constitute our legal system. During the semester, we will examine recurring themes across different areas of the law and connect them to their roots in fields like moral and political philosophy, economics, psychology, sociology, and history. Topics covered include the origins of the common law; the nature of (and challenges with) reasoning from precedent; the limits of the freedom to contract; the tradeoffs between rules versus discretion when regulating systems; and interpretation of statutes. Readings will consist primarily of appellate judicial opinions.

subject: GO
title: The European Union
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: GO 131 or GO 259
Description: How should we understand the European Union? Is it a regional trade bloc, an international organization, or even a state--and, if so, what kind? Is it, as some have suggested, a superpower on par with the United States? If it is as significant as many attest, what are the implications for the primacy of nation-states and national sovereignty? A detailed and critical understanding of what the EU is and how it works. Through a variety of assignments, students analyze the design, construction, and operation of the new institutions of governance in Europe.

section: GO 420A-A - Seminar: Controversies in Contemporary Electoral Politics
subject: GO
title: Seminar: Controversies in Contemporary Electoral Politics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: GO 111 and Senior Class Standing as a Government Major
Description: For nearly 200 years, Americans have pinned the democratic character of their system on elections. In many ways, we have become an election-crazed nation, ever-hoping that the next grand contest or the next great candidate will save the day. But tectonic shifts abound – changes that are distorting the very nature of the process. From the rise of fear-centered partisanship, new limits on voter access to the polls, the omnipotence of social media, declining standards of objectivity, foreign interference, the reemergence of the partisan press, the growing weight of elites and more, elections – our grand democratic feasts – are transforming before our eyes. This seminar will explore these and a host of critically important topics. Prerequisite: Government 111 or 115 and senior standing as a government major.

subject: GO
title: Seminar: Memory and Politics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.

subject: GO
title: Seminar: Political Violence
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Senior Class Standing as a Government Major
Description: Explores a variety of theoretical perspectives on, and case studies of, political violence, with particular emphasis on terrorism (both secular and religious) and ethnic conflict. Examines drivers of radicalization and violent extremism, the factors that lead to the rise, decline, and/or demise of terrorist organizations, and the nexus between transnational organized crime and international terrorism. Introduces key concepts and analytical frameworks and provides students with an opportunity to apply them to a case study of their choice. Students present the preliminary results of their research projects to the class.

section: GO 456-A - Seminar: Civil Society and Social Change in Latin America
subject: GO
title: Seminar: Civil Society and Social Change in Latin America
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: What are civil society organizations and what is their place in politics? This research seminar examines the evolution of civil society in contemporary Latin American democracies and their roles in effecting social and political change. Over the past 30 years, civil society organizations in Latin America have become vehicles for poor and otherwise marginalized communities to access the political system. Topics include the collective action problem, the role of civil society organizations in interest representation and service provision, relationships with political parties and international donors, and participatory governance.

subject: GO
title: Policy Lab Practicum
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission and must have taken EC 293, GO 281, PS 214, SC 212, or SO 271
Description: For this practicum, students carry out an in-depth, real-world policy analysis or evaluation project in an area of their interest for a partner organization in the community. Students meet as a group once a week, as well as individually with the instructor, who provides close mentoring and support. The bulk of the work is done outside the classroom visiting field sites, consulting with stakeholders, gathering and analyzing data, and producing a professional final report. The practicum serves as a bridge between academic policy knowledge and practical application. This course may be repeated for additional credit.

subject: GS
title: Introduction to Global Studies
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: The course introduces students to a transdisciplinary framework to grasp how the seemingly separate fields of politics, history, culture, the economy, and the environment are all interconnected and integral to analyzing major global issues. We use different genres of materials to examine these issues from diverse locations in the world and attend to global inequalities. We also consider how they affect our everyday lives. By discussing multiple perspectives and connecting contemporary issues to historical processes, this course invites you to reflect critically on how the world is constituted and how global concerns are framed.

section: GS 212-A - Feeling, Sensing, Thinking in Catastrophic Times
subject: GS
title: Feeling, Sensing, Thinking in Catastrophic Times
Description: This course examines emotionality and affect as forms of mediation within larger crises in the global order. How should we think about ordinary violence and trauma, for example, in the aftermath of partition in India and the Korean war? What is the affective dimension of necropolitical brutality in postcolonial Sub-Saharan Africa and elsewhere? What are the limits of affect theory for conceptualizing blackness? We will engage works across many disciplines to think about the political, social, historical, philosophical and cultural construction of emotions, affect, sensibility and their translations in language.

section: GS 213-A - Constructing the Enemy: Race, Religion and Globalization
subject: GS
title: Constructing the Enemy: Race, Religion and Globalization
Description: In this course, we will examine the political-economic and psycho-affective processes of racialization and religionization in colonialism, imperialism, and war. What is the genealogy of race in the construction of the figure of the enemy? What is the relation between the religious invention of the infidel and the racial invention of the Black? How are the natives—represented as “savages”—informing the construction of the “enemy combatant” in the age of terror? We will engage with works in anthropology, postcolonial theory, Black studies, political philosophy, and subaltern studies to think about race, religion and globalization.

subject: GS
title: Global History
Description: An introduction to patterns and processes in world history. Themes include the evolution of trade and empire, global balances in military and political power, impacts of disease, the evolution of capitalism, slavery and its abolition, global migrations, industrialization, imperialism, and decolonization. Students read essays and study maps of historical patterns and processes and write essays to hone their critical-thinking and writing skills. Critical Race - Indigeneity, race, and identity course.

subject: GS
title: Global History
Description: An introduction to patterns and processes in world history. Themes include the evolution of trade and empire, global balances in military and political power, impacts of disease, the evolution of capitalism, slavery and its abolition, global migrations, industrialization, imperialism, and decolonization. Students read essays and study maps of historical patterns and processes and write essays to hone their critical-thinking and writing skills. Critical Race - Indigeneity, race, and identity course.

subject: GS
title: Researching Cultural Diversity
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112, AY 2XX or GS251, a W1 course, and Sophomore Class Standing or Above
Description: Focus on ethnography as both the central research strategy of anthropologists and the written text produced by such research. Examines anthropological methods of data collection and ethnographic writing as these encompass not only the discipline's historical focus on localized communities but also contemporary understandings of connections to global processes, the analysis of complex inequalities, and a reflexive and engaged relationship with the human world. Explores practical strategies for conducting ethnographic research, including interviewing, observation, and other modes of qualitative data collection; the ethical issues presented by such research; and the application of analytical and theoretical models.

subject: GS
title: Liberation Struggles
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112 or GS 101, or permission of instructor
Description: Is revolutionary change possible today? Explores the promises and failures of radical movements from the First International in 1864 to the "global uprisings" of recent years. Considers the historical genealogy of today's transnational movements and their complex relationships to the modern nation-state. To what extent do labor, anarchist, anticolonial, indigenous struggles, as well as the World Social Forum, Arab Spring, and Black Lives Matter, offer ways to understand the world today and to imagine alternative political futures? Strong emphasis on discussion and collaborative debate.

subject: GS
title: Global Climate Policy
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ES 234 or GO 131
Description: Climate change impacts are widespread; in many spaces doom and gloom is the dominant narrative. What are the successes of global climate policy? What role do non-state actors, like civil society organizations play? This course focuses on challenges and possible solutions in global climate policy and international climate negotiations. We will engage with scholarship from across academic disciplines alongside work by practitioners and activists. Students will virtually observe United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) negotiations on a key issue, evaluate the outcome, and craft a policy brief with concrete recommendations.

section: HI 111-A - The Not So Distant Past: Europe 1000-1600
subject: HI
title: The Not So Distant Past: Europe 1000-1600
Section Details: Miller 008 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Juniors and below (Instructor permission required for Seniors)
Description: An interdisciplinary survey of medieval, Renaissance and Reformation Europe from 1000 to 1600 focusing on analysis of primary sources.Throughout the course, emphasis will be placed on critical understanding of major events and issues based on the whys and hows of history. Classes will be primarily discussion-based. H

section: HI 120I-A - United States and the Cold War
subject: HI
title: United States and the Cold War
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: This writing-intensive course examines the United States during the Cold War. It will consider events at home and abroad, covering topics such as McCarthyism, the atomic bomb, the Vietnam War, civil rights, popular culture, and the legacies of the Cold War. Students will develop their writing skills through a variety of writing assignments and workshops.

section: HI 120K-A - From King Cotton to Civil Rights: Transformations in the American South Since 1865
subject: HI
title: From King Cotton to Civil Rights: Transformations in the American South Since 1865
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously

section: HI 120K-B - From King Cotton to Civil Rights: Transformations in the American South Since 1865
subject: HI
title: From King Cotton to Civil Rights: Transformations in the American South Since 1865
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously

section: HI 131-A - Survey of U.S. History, to 1865
subject: HI
title: Survey of U.S. History, to 1865
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Junior Class Standing or Below
Description: This course surveys U.S. history through Reconstruction. We give special consideration to the central paradox of slavery and freedom in the U.S., as well as to conflicts between Indigenous and European peoples. It is impossible to “cover” all of U.S. history in this period. Instead, we follow a chronological trajectory and explore a theme each week. Themes include colonization, slavery, religion, labor, gender, and war. Throughout, we listen empathetically to voices from the past, and center marginalized voices who have not been the writers of historical narratives.

section: HI 141-A - Genocide and Globalization: 20th-Century World History
subject: HI
title: Genocide and Globalization: 20th-Century World History
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Junior Class Standing or Below

section: HI 144-A - Patterns in East Asian History, to 1600
subject: HI
title: Patterns in East Asian History, to 1600
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Juniors and below (Instructor permission required for Seniors)
Description: This survey of early East Asian history covers China, Korea, and Japan from antiquity to the early seventeenth century, examining their independent trajectories and interrelationships. The course gives students a solid grasp of the significant figures, events, ideas, and social developments that have shaped each civilization. The thematic focus in each chronological unit introduces students to key factors that have set the common ground for an East Asian community, such as Confucianism, Buddhism, commercial networks, and diplomatic exchanges. This course also examines how each civilization "localized" these elements as part of "native" culture with independent dynamics. The focus, therefore, alternates between national (China, Japan, Korea) and regional (East Asia, Asia) perspectives.

section: HI 162-A - History of the Atlantic World
subject: HI
title: History of the Atlantic World
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Junior Class Standing or Below
Description: Explores the interconnected histories of Europe, North America, Latin America, and Africa through the lens of trade, migration, and the exchange of ideas, including revolutionary ideals. It begins with the reasons why Europeans sought out increasing trading connections with Africa and Asia, and how this drive impacted the so-called "discovery" and subsequent colonization of the Americas. Covered topics include genocide against Native Americans and land dispossession; the importation of African slaves; the growth of the plantation economy, especially in the Caribbean; and slavery. Also covers the Age of Revolutions, including the American, French, Haitian, and Spanish-American revolutions. The course ends with abolitionism and the rise of the mass indenture of South Asians in the 19th century.

section: HI 173-A - History of Latin America, 1491 to 1900
subject: HI
title: History of Latin America, 1491 to 1900
Description: To understand the historical roots of Latin America's enduring tensions and conflicts, students analyze and discuss sources (especially primary ones), and write short historical essays. Themes include the first American civilizations, the Conquest and construction of colonial hierarchies, independence, liberalism and conservatism, neocolonialism and nationalism.

section: HI 173 D-A - Disc: Hist Latin America

subject: HI
title: Germany and Europe, 1871-1945
Description: What went wrong with Germany from the first unification to the catastrophe of Nazism? Examining the question of German peculiarities within the European context and the debate on continuities in recent German history. Focus on critical reading and writing skills and on understanding historical processes including patterns of exclusion and intolerance.

section: HI 244-A - Brothers at War: The Two Koreas, 1945-Present
subject: HI
title: Brothers at War: The Two Koreas, 1945-Present
Cross-Listed Title: EA 244-A/ HI 244-A - Brothers at War: The Two Koreas, 1945
Section Details: Lovejoy 119 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM
Description: Nukes in the north and K-Pop idols in the south. The two Koreas could not seem more different today, but their division is barely a generation old. Why was Korea split and how did the two halves come to diverge so drastically? To answer these questions, this survey explores inter-Korean relations and their global contexts from division through experiences of civil war, rapid development, and geopolitical rivalry through a range of readings and media. Throughout, North and South Korea have vied for peninsular primacy and global prestige on the one hand, while upholding a shared narrative of common but sundered Korean identity on the other.

section: HI 247-A - African-American History, from Slavery to Freedom
subject: HI
title: African-American History, from Slavery to Freedom
Description: Explores the experience of blacks in American society from colonial times through the present. Subjects focus on racism, slavery, the role of African Americans in shaping the nation's history, and the ongoing struggle for equality. In exploring these historical developments, the course aims to expose students to a range of primary and scholarly sources; to hone critical thinking and interpretive skills; to help students write clearly, concisely, and precisely; and to foster clear, logical, and informed exchanges of ideas.

subject: HI
title: Caribbean History
Section Details: Miller Library 205 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 9:30 AM - 10:45 AM
Description: This course is an introductory survey of Caribbean history from the pre-Columbian era to the twenty-first century. It explores how Indigenous peoples, Africans, Creoles, and Europeans shaped and defined the region. Students examine how people in the region understood and experienced the region’s geography, cultures, and political systems, considering colonialism, slavery, and imperialism alongside abolitionist movements, political revolutions, and Indigenous resistance that reshaped the modern Caribbean.

section: HI 266-A - The Making of Modern Africa
subject: HI
title: The Making of Modern Africa
Section Details: Miller 008 (Active Learning Classroom) | MW | 1:00 PM - 2:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.

subject: HI
title: Astrology: A Global History
Description: Astrology flourished among polytheists, Jews, Christians and Muslims for thousands of years. What does the case study of astrology show us about intellectual life in the premodern world? Where does astrology fit in to the broader history of religion and science? And what should today’s historians do, methodologically, with “not real” ideas that prove to be so powerful? Working through antiquity and the Middle Ages, we explore astrology’s intersection with politics, science, medicine, and astral magic.

subject: HI
title: Global History
Description: An introduction to patterns and processes in world history. Themes include the evolution of trade and empire, global balances in military and political power, impacts of disease, the evolution of capitalism, slavery and its abolition, global migrations, industrialization, imperialism, and decolonization. Students read essays and study maps of historical patterns and processes and write essays to hone their critical-thinking and writing skills. Critical Race - Indigeneity, race, and identity course.

subject: HI
title: Global History
Description: An introduction to patterns and processes in world history. Themes include the evolution of trade and empire, global balances in military and political power, impacts of disease, the evolution of capitalism, slavery and its abolition, global migrations, industrialization, imperialism, and decolonization. Students read essays and study maps of historical patterns and processes and write essays to hone their critical-thinking and writing skills. Critical Race - Indigeneity, race, and identity course.

subject: HI
title: From Qi to Chemistry
Description: This course introduces the study of science, technology, and medicine in premodern China. Rather than treating science as a fixed or universal category, the course examines how those in premodern China understood the natural world and produced knowledge about it. Using case studies across time, we will ask: What counted as “science”? How did knowledge practices relate to broader social, cultural, and political contexts? And how can the study of premodern China challenge or expand our assumptions about what science is?

section: HI 333-A - Colby and China: Alumni, Archives, and U.S.–China Encounters, 1850–1950
subject: HI
title: Colby and China: Alumni, Archives, and U.S.–China Encounters, 1850–1950
Description: This course examines U.S.–China encounters from the mid-nineteenth to the mid-twentieth century through the experiences of Colby College alumni who lived and worked in China during the period. Drawing on Colby’s Special Collections, other archives, and supplementary readings, students will explore the lives of missionaries, educators, physicians, journalists, and Chinese students whose careers intersected with major moments in modern Chinese history—from the late Qing and Republican era to revolution and war. Using alumni diaries, correspondence, photographs, campus publications, and institutional records, the course investigates themes such as American missionary influence, women’s education, nationalism and anti-imperialism, and U.S. involvement in the Sino-Japanese War and Chinese Civil War. Students will develop foundational archival research skills and gain hands-on experience with primary sources and digital humanities tools while critically assessing how a liberal arts education shaped global engagement.

section: HI 334-A - The Great Depression: America in the 1930s
subject: HI
title: The Great Depression: America in the 1930s
Section Details: Miller Library 257 (Seminar Classroom) | T | 7:00 PM - 9:30 PM
Description: The Depression of the 1930s was the most devastating economic collapse of modern times. How did it happen? The 1920s had been the most prosperous time in American history, and many forecast ever-higher living standards. Instead the economy went into a tailspin that affected every group and region and posed a crisis of faith in capitalism. How did Americans cope and how did the experience shape their values and behavior? In what ways did the federal government respond, to what ends, and with what consequences? In exploring these questions, the course will also help students to read critically and to write clearly, concisely, and precisely.

section: HI 342-A - The Decade of Maximum Danger: American Society and Politics during the 1960s
subject: HI
title: The Decade of Maximum Danger: American Society and Politics during the 1960s
Section Details: Miller Library 319 (Seminar Classroom) | M | 7:00 PM - 9:30 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomore Class Standing or Above
Description: The utopian hopes for government during the Kennedy and Johnson years, both in solving social problems and in containing communism around the world. Readings focus on the shaping of federal policies, their domestic and global impact, and the cultural and political legacy of this era.

section: HI 356-A - Cultures and Identities of the British Empire
subject: HI
title: Cultures and Identities of the British Empire
Section Details: Miller 008 (Active Learning Classroom) | MW | 2:30 PM - 3:45 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Asks students to examine the construction, maintenance, and blurring of the boundaries of culture and identity within the British Empire over the course of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Explores how empire not only produced new, allegedly stable ethnic and racial identities, but also how these were constantly undermined and challenged, and were subject to change over both time and space. The course will do this by reading and discussing a series of novels written over the course of the nineteenth, twentieth, and twenty-first centuries--both during empire, in other words, and in its wake. Boundaries and Margins humanities theme course.

subject: HI
title: Doing History: Greater Reconstruction
Section Details: Miller Library 257 (Seminar Classroom) | TR | 1:00 PM - 2:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: History Majors who have completed HI 276 (or IP)
Description: In this course we will do three things. First, we will learn about a range of frameworks, theories, and methodologies common to history as a discipline. In essence we will learn about the history of history, what kinds of questions and methods historians use in their work, and why history matters as a distinct discipline. Second, this iteration of the course is rooted in the 1840s-1870s U.S., what some scholars have called "greater reconstruction." In the historical content portion of the course we will learn about reconstruction in the north/south after the Civil War and also what was going on in the U.S. West in terms of Indigenous nations and the government at this time. In the latter part of the class we will also think about the memories of this time period (afterlives of slavery/civil war/reconstruction and conquest) and how these histories continue to be contested and matter today. Third, throughout the class, you will create a scaffolded research proposal based on a topic of your choice (inclusive of lit review and annotated bibliography). This aspect of the class ensures that you have the skills of “doing history” necessary to move forward in your coursework, with a particular emphasis on the research and writing process.

section: HI 414-A - Research Seminar: History of Fear in Europe, 1300-1900
subject: HI
title: Research Seminar: History of Fear in Europe, 1300-1900
Section Details: Miller Library 319 (Seminar Classroom) | R | 1:00 PM - 3:30 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Junior Class Standing or Above
Description: Fear of death, disease, religious war, witches, vampires/ghosts, sexual difference, the Terror of the French Revolution, and serial murder are only a few of the “situations" that have kindled fear that included stereotyping, marginalization, and pogroms. We will explore how the psychology of collective fear, combined with different forms of communication, rumor, and media influenced and changed the course of European history from 1300-1900 . H

section: HI 429-A - History of How to Change the World
subject: HI
title: History of How to Change the World
Section Details: Miller Library 257 (Seminar Classroom) | W | 1:00 PM - 3:30 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Junior Class Standing or Above
Description: Course will cover historical social movements against perceived economic, political, social, racial, and gender-based forms of oppression. We will employ a “bottom up” methodology, studying the strategies used by ordinary people to organize resistance networks to fight for their notion of a more just society. Weekly case studies will be global in scope. This is a reading intensive discussion course; students will read one book per week and come to class prepared to discuss. Students drive class discussions. Students will select one social movement to study in detail and produce a twenty-page paper by the end of term.

section: HL 199-A - Discover and Define: Problems to Venture Concepts in 11 Weeks
subject: HL
title: Discover and Define: Problems to Venture Concepts in 11 Weeks
Section Details: Olin 019B (Active Learning Classroom) | M | 7:00 PM - 9:00 PM | 09/09/2026 - 12/21/2026
Description: Every venture, nonprofit, or creative initiative begins with a problem worth exploring. This course focuses on identifying meaningful problems, generating ideas, and shaping them into well-defined concepts. Youll work through ideation exercises and proven frameworks while hearing from founders on how their work began. Whether exploring entrepreneurship for the first time or returning with a new idea, build a foundation for a startup, nonprofit, creative project, or something without a name yet. It prepares students for Halloran Lab Ideate and Explore grants and further venture coursework. No business background required. All majors welcome!

section: IS 120F-A - Writing the Future: Technoscience and Power
subject: IS
title: Writing the Future: Technoscience and Power
Course Tags: Integrated Studies Clusters :: IS: 360 Degrees of A.I.
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year Class Standing
Description: This course introduces first-year students to critical reading and writing about contemporary science and technology. Students learn to analyze, interpret, debate, conduct library research, and write about the power structures that shape technoscientific landscapes. They tackle big questions concerning artificial intelligence, surveillance, reproductive justice, global pandemics, and more, with the aim of using writing to create a more just and equitable world.

section: IS 134-A - Science of Consciousness, Biological and Artificial
subject: IS
title: Science of Consciousness, Biological and Artificial
Course Tags: Integrated Studies Clusters :: IS: 360 Degrees of A.I.
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year Class Standing
Description: Introduces consciousness studies grounded in a scientific approach, beginning with the "hard problem" of consciousness, how phenomenal experience arises from biological systems. Discussions of potential biomolecular and quantum mechanical underpinnings of conscious experience will lead to the debate around what constitutes artificial sentience (AS) with inherent ethical implications. What does identity or consent mean in relationship to an AS? What rights does an AS have? Can humans terminate an AS? In addition to lectures and weekly readings, students will create an AI driven avatar to create a multimedia artifact exploring these questions.

section: IS 145-A - Leadership in the Ancient World
subject: IS
title: Leadership in the Ancient World
Course Tags: Integrated Studies Clusters :: IS: The Ancient World
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: To understand leadership in both ancient and contemporary times, the course will be informed by theoretical approaches to leadership (e.g. trait theory, situational theories, behavioral theories), as well as theories related to issues such as power, authority, and influence. Additionally, the course will utilize case studies, historical and textual analysis, and cross-cultural comparisons. By exploring the roots of leadership, the course seeks to provide students a deeper understanding of the evolution of leadership practices, and how these practices have shaped contemporary leadership theories and practices.

section: IS 145A-A - Myth and Reason: Literature and Philosophy of Ancient Greece
subject: IS
title: Myth and Reason: Literature and Philosophy of Ancient Greece
Course Tags: Integrated Studies Clusters :: IS: The Ancient World
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year Class Standing
Description: An introductory survey that encourages a holistic understanding of the ancient Greek world by examining key works of literature and core theories of knowledge and reality. Themes include the idea of philosophy as a way of life and the relations between myth and reason, nature and civilization, the feminine and the masculine, mortals and the divine/gods, appearance and reality, and religion and philosophy. Texts are selected from the works of Homer, Hesiod, Sappho, Euripides, Aeschylus, Sophocles, Aristophanes, Plutarch, the PreSocratic philosophers (especially Heraclitus and Parmenides), Plato, and Aristotle.

section: IS 158-A - History of Ancient Greece and the Near East
subject: IS
title: History of Ancient Greece and the Near East
Course Tags: Integrated Studies Clusters :: IS: The Ancient World
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year Class Standing
Description: Offers an overview of ancient Greek history and culture from the Mycenaean society of the Bronze Age to the formation of the Hellenistic kingdoms, and situates this historical survey within the broader context of the histories and cultures of the Near East. We will begin with the foundation of the first cities in the fourth millennium BCE and end with the fall of Ptolemaic Egypt to the Roman Empire. Over the course of the semester, we will read texts ranging from the poems of the priestess Enheduanna to the dialogues of the philosopher Plato. Particular attention will be paid to political, social, and cultural history.

section: IS 197-A - The Politics of A.I. in Literature and Theory
subject: IS
title: The Politics of A.I. in Literature and Theory
Section Details: Miller Library 319 (Seminar Classroom) | TR | 9:30 AM - 10:45 AM
Course Tags: Integrated Studies Clusters :: IS: 360 Degrees of A.I.
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: Since long before artificial intelligence became technologically feasible, writers and philosophers have engaged in speculation over its political implications and the changes it may impose on society and our very definition of humanity. In this class, we will read canonical contributions to the fictional representation of A.I., explore their themes alongside innovations in social theory, and discuss the complex interaction between technology, literature, and debates over citizenship, political freedom, and human flourishing.

subject: IT
title: Italian I
Description: Basic comprehensive course for students with little or no previous knowledge of Italian. Focus is on developing the reading, writing, speaking, and listening skills needed to gain fluency in Italian and on familiarizing students with basic aspects of Italian culture and geography. Learning in the classroom takes place entirely in Italian and is task based, involving group activities, interviews with fellow students, and role-playing exercises.

section: IT 141-A - Introduction to Italian Literary Studies: Poets, Lovers, Revolutionaries
subject: IT
title: Introduction to Italian Literary Studies: Poets, Lovers, Revolutionaries
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: IT 128 or equivalent
Description: In this discussion-intensive course, we will explore the most enduring topics of Italian culture: the nature of love, the role of the artist in society, and the experience of time and death. Students will learn about different artistic genres (lyric poetry, short story, novel, film, contemporary song) and hone analytic skills and writing (rhetorical figures, form-content, stylistics). Students will become familiar with key periods of Italian culture and famous authors (Dante, Boccaccio, Petrarch, Leopardi, Montale, Moravia, Maraini, Deledda, Calvino). In Italian.

subject: IT
title: Italian Conversation
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: IT 125 or equivalent
Description: An informal, weekly, small-group meeting for conversation practice, led by the Italian language assistant. Topics will vary, to include everyday life experience, contemporary culture and media, and literature. Conducted in Italian. May be repeated for credit.

section: IT 247-A - Mafia Movies: Mobsters, Martyrs, and Myths
subject: IT
title: Mafia Movies: Mobsters, Martyrs, and Myths
Section Details: Lovejoy 119 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 2:30 PM - 3:45 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Examines representations of the mafia in Italian and American film, tracing the transformation of a rural Sicilian phenomenon into a transnational cultural myth. Through the analysis of cinematic texts (by Francis Ford Coppola, Martin Scorsese, Marco Tullio Giordana, Lina Wertmüller, and others) alongside historical, literary, and critical readings, the course explores how mafia movies construct and circulate narratives of ethnic identity, migration, gender roles, family, power, and social justice. No prerequisite, all students welcome.

subject: JA
title: Elementary Japanese I
Description: This course introduces the fundamentals of the Japanese language, with an equal emphasis on all four domains of language usage: speaking, listening, reading, and writing. Students will master basic sentence patterns and core vocabulary necessary for everyday conversation. They will also gain command of the two phonetic writing systems used in Japanese, hiragana and katakana, and learn 60 of the most commonly used ideographic characters, or kanji.

subject: JA
title: Intermediate Japanese I
Section Details: Lovejoy 103 (Active Learning Classroom) | MTWR | 10:00 AM - 10:50 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: JA 126 or equivalent
Description: Designed for students who have taken two semesters of Japanese, provides the intermediate level of competency in speaking, writing, reading, and listening. The four skills are simultaneously introduced and practiced in every class with emphasis on balancing accuracy, fluency, and complexity. Also helps students understand how linguistic practice is strongly connected to culture.

Description: This course offers an entry point to advanced Japanese. Students will master complex grammatical constructions and acquire vocabulary necessary to express their thoughts on a variety of social issues. Emphasis is placed on developing natural communication strategies appropriate in a range of situations, from casual to formal. Readings and audiovisual materials will incorporate authentic Japanese aimed at native speakers.

section: JS 123-A - Beit Midrash - Jewish Ideas Lab
subject: JS
title: Beit Midrash - Jewish Ideas Lab
Section Details: Olin 019B (Active Learning Classroom) | T | 7:00 PM - 9:00 PM
Description: The Hebrew term "beit midrash" refers to a communal setting in which learners discover and co-construct meaning through conversation with one another about texts that address significant ideas and raise essential questions. At Colby, these texts include classic and contemporary sources from the Jewish tradition and beyond. Participants of all backgrounds and perspectives learn to assess competing ideas critically, to read closely, and to present their ideas effectively within the context of a supportive community. They become sophisticated thinkers and empowered partners in the collaborative creation of knowledge. Nongraded.

subject: JS
title: Hebrew I
Description: The first of three consecutive courses designed to develop fluency and accuracy in Modern Hebrew. Through an interactive approach to language learning, students gain communicative proficiency and a greater understanding of Israeli society. Videos, audio, and web materials introduce students to the nuanced and rich connections between Hebrew and Jewish culture in Israel and around the world.

subject: JS
title: Hebrew III
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: JS 126
Description: The third of three consecutive courses designed to develop fluency and accuracy in Modern Hebrew. Students will deepen their knowledge of Hebrew grammar and further develop the facilities for written and oral communication in Hebrew. Delves more deeply into Israeli culture through media and literature.

section: JS 143-A - Introduction to the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament

section: JS 148-A - Inclusion and Exclusion: Dilemmas in Israeli Society
subject: JS
title: Inclusion and Exclusion: Dilemmas in Israeli Society
Section Details: Lovejoy 102 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 1:00 PM - 2:15 PM
Description: Explores structures and experiences of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary Israeli society by engaging with three major tensions: (1) Zionism and the role of Palestinian citizens in a Jewish State; (2) attempts to balance secular and religious influences in the public sphere; and (3) creating a national identity for an ethnically and culturally diverse populace. Students will explore how competing worldviews underpin conflict more broadly. This is an Across the Walls course open to both students at Colby and students from the Reentry Sisters cohort.

section: JS 181-A - Conceptions of Jews and Judaism
subject: JS
title: Conceptions of Jews and Judaism
Description: A survey of the history of the Jewish people and the religion called Judaism from the biblical era through the Middle Ages, tracing the development of ideas, texts, beliefs, and practices that continue to influence Jewish life and thought today. Examines Christian and Islamic ideas about Jews and Judaism and the historical impact of inequality, prejudice, and persecution on Jewish society and culture. Students will develop broadly applicable critical reading skills as well as those that relate specifically to the analysis of religious texts.

subject: JS
title: Vienna 1900 (in English)
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: In-depth exploration of the Viennese Secession (1898-1905), a pivotal moment in European avant-garde art. Considers artworks, creators (artists, architects, designers), collectors, and the historical and cultural context of Belle-Epoque Vienna. The course also addresses issues related to collecting this material in the post-World War II context and crucial issues of provenance research and restitution of Nazi-looted art.

section: JS 252-A - Introduction to Politics of the Middle East
subject: JS
title: Introduction to Politics of the Middle East
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Provides the analytical and historical background for making sense of politics in the Arab world today. Highlights the main drivers of politics in the region, with particular emphasis paid to the intersection of political and economic forces, domestic and regional or international factors, and Islam and politics. Explores the roots of authoritarianism in the region, the dynamics that sustain it, and key impediments to substantive (as opposed to cosmetic) democratization. Examines the combination of forces that produced both the Arab Spring of 2011 and the turmoil that followed it. Open to first-years. Fulfills the introductory comparative politics requirement.

section: JS 423-A - Jewish Studies Capstone: Designing the Jewish Studies Lab
subject: JS
title: Jewish Studies Capstone: Designing the Jewish Studies Lab
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Seniors who have completed JS 123 previously. Students may not take JS 123 while currently enrolled in JS 423.
Description: Design and implement the Beit Midrash--Jewish Ideas Lab, a communal setting in which learners of all backgrounds and perspectives discover and co-construct meaning through conversation with one another about texts that address significant ideas and raise essential questions. Capstone participants develop leadership and pedagogical skills while deepening their ability to critically assess competing ideas. Required for senior Jewish Studies majors; open by permission of instructor to all seniors who have attended at least one previous Beit Midrash session. Nongraded.

section: LA 173-A - History of Latin America, 1491 to 1900
subject: LA
title: History of Latin America, 1491 to 1900
Description: To understand the historical roots of Latin America's enduring tensions and conflicts, students analyze and discuss sources (especially primary ones), and write short historical essays. Themes include the first American civilizations, the Conquest and construction of colonial hierarchies, independence, liberalism and conservatism, neocolonialism and nationalism.
