section: LA 239-A - Latin America at the Movies
subject: LA
title: Latin America at the Movies
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SP 135*
Description: An introduction to the cinematography of Latin America covering a broad set of topics, countries and time periods. Students will explore how diverse themes-revolution, modernity, gender, race, labor, and neoliberalism-inform national history, particularly in Mexico, Argentina, Brazil and Cuba, nations that developed an energetic cinematography at various points in the 20th century. Students will gain experience in film analysis and how to articulate the relationship between content and artistic form. Fulfills Spanish G/S requirement.

subject: LA
title: Sociology of Immigration
Description: This course offers an introduction to the sociology of immigration, using the United States as its central case study. We will examine sociological theories explaining why people migrate, the history of U.S. efforts to control population movements, and patterns of immigrant incorporation. Special attention will be paid to the convergence of the immigration and criminal justice systems (often called crimmigration), the complexities of citizenship and legal status, and American public opinion on immigration.

section: LA 253-A - Introduction to Latin American Politics
subject: LA
title: Introduction to Latin American Politics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: An overview of important political and economic phenomena in Latin America over the past century. How can Latin America escape its persistent problems with underdevelopment, poverty, and inequality, and what is the role of a democratic government in tackling these problems? Topics covered include state-directed development models, populism, democratic breakdown and democratization, free market economic models, and contemporary leftist alternatives. Open to first-years. Fulfills the introductory comparative politics requirement.

subject: LA
title: Caribbean History
Section Details: Miller Library 205 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 9:30 AM - 10:45 AM
Description: This course is an introductory survey of Caribbean history from the pre-Columbian era to the twenty-first century. It explores how Indigenous peoples, Africans, Creoles, and Europeans shaped and defined the region. Students examine how people in the region understood and experienced the region’s geography, cultures, and political systems, considering colonialism, slavery, and imperialism alongside abolitionist movements, political revolutions, and Indigenous resistance that reshaped the modern Caribbean.

section: LA 340-A - Art and Activism in Contemporary Cuba
subject: LA
title: Art and Activism in Contemporary Cuba
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - SP :: SP: Gender and Sex
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SP 2XX or above
Description: This course will examine how Cuban artists resist state control of the state’s cultural enterprise through artistic practice. The artists studied in this course reject the state’s strategies of isolationism and exceptionalism and bring visibility to art in Cuba and its diaspora, especially by underrepresented artists. Themes will include masculinities and sport; ruins and architecture; infrastructure and energy; sexuality and identity; and censorship and colonialism through artistic practice that prioritizes embodiment while considering Cuban art’s precarity. Students will also develop a facility with queer, postcolonial, and critical race theories that enable critiques of aspects of Cuba’s utopian socialist project.

section: LA 456-A - Seminar: Civil Society and Social Change in Latin America
subject: LA
title: Seminar: Civil Society and Social Change in Latin America
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: What are civil society organizations and what is their place in politics? This research seminar examines the evolution of civil society in contemporary Latin American democracies and their roles in effecting social and political change. Over the past 30 years, civil society organizations in Latin America have become vehicles for poor and otherwise marginalized communities to access the political system. Topics include the collective action problem, the role of civil society organizations in interest representation and service provision, relationships with political parties and international donors, and participatory governance.

subject: LT
title: Introductory Latin
Description: Latin was the language of Virgil, Ovid, Cicero, and Tacitus, giants in the Western literary tradition, and, for centuries Latin remained the lingua franca of the educated. It also gave rise to the Romance languages and to a vast proportion of English vocabulary. Combines lucid explanations of grammar with cultural information and readings in simplified Latin of major classical texts.

subject: LT
title: Introduction to Latin Literature
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: LT 112, equivalent, or has received a SAT II Subject Test result Latin score greater than or equal to 540
Description: Having mastered Latin grammar and syntax, students now take on the challenges and rewards of reading an unsimplified Latin text. They will learn to translate most Latin texts with the aid of a dictionary; to accomplish a literary, historical, and cultural analysis of any complex text; and to satisfy the rigorous requirements of a demanding work schedule.

section: LT 248-A - Topics in Latin Literature: Conspiracy of Catiline
subject: LT
title: Topics in Latin Literature: Conspiracy of Catiline
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: LT 131, a 2XX or 3XX-level Latin course, 5 on AP Latin, or equivalent
Description: Reading and discussion of original ancient Latin texts. Drawn from the long history of ancient Rome, texts vary from year to year. Attention will be paid to the literary histories and historical contexts of the selected readings. May be repeated for credit. L. Prerequisite: LT131 or equivalent.

subject: MA
title: Calculus with Pre-calculus I
Section Details: Lovejoy 119 (Active Learning Classroom) | MTWF | 8:00 AM - 8:50 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Colby Math Placement, 019 or 025
Description: Designed for students who enter Colby with insufficient algebra and trigonometry background for Mathematics 130. It is expected that all students who complete Mathematics 119 will enroll in Mathematics 120 in the following January. The combination of 119 and 120 covers the same calculus material as Mathematics 125. Completion of 119 alone does not constitute completion of a College calculus course for any purpose; in particular, it does not qualify a student to take Mathematics 130 or 160 nor does it satisfy the quantitative reasoning requirement.

subject: MA
title: Single-Variable Calculus
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Colby Math Placement, 025
Description: Calculus is the result of centuries of intellectual effort to understand and quantify change, such as the position of a moving object or the shape of a curve. Competent users of calculus understand its intellectual structure sufficiently to apply its ideas to a variety of intellectual pursuits. Topics include differential and integral calculus of one variable, including the calculus of exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions. The course covers limits and continuity; differentiation and its applications, antiderivatives, the definite integral and its applications. This course is sufficient preparation for Mathematics 160.

subject: MA
title: Single-Variable Calculus Revisited
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Colby Math Placement MA 030
Description: Calculus studies rates of change and accumulation and is fundamental to quantitative work in the natural sciences, social sciences, and data science. This course assumes prior experience with calculus of a single variable and goes into more depth than Mathematics 125 but is less theoretical than Mathematics 135. Topics covered include limits, continuity, derivatives, and definite integrals of functions of one variable, including the major theorems governing their relationships and their applications. The emphasis is on developing conceptual understanding, rather than mere computation. A computer algebra system such as Sage, Mathematica, or MatLab is used.

subject: MA
title: Honors Calculus I
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Colby Math Placement, 030
Description: The first in a two-course sequence that treats the material of Mathematics 125 and 160 with a focus on the intellectual structure behind the methods. Students will acquire a deep understanding of the theory and foundational facts of calculus, will be able to use the techniques in an intelligent manner, will understand and be able to explain the arguments that undergird those techniques, and will be able to construct original arguments of their own. Topics are presented as a deductive mathematical theory, with emphasis on concepts, theorems, and their proofs. May not be taken for credit if the student has earned credit for Mathematics 160.

subject: MA
title: Series and Multi-variable Calculus
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Colby Math Placement MA 030, or MA 120, 125, 130, or 135
Description: A continuation of Mathematics 120, 125, or 130. Students will learn how to use infinite series, both to represent and to approximate functions, and will extend all of their skills from single-variable calculus to the multivariable setting. Topics: infinite series; vectors and analytic geometry in two and three dimensions; partial derivatives, differentials and the gradient; integration in two and three variables.

subject: MA
title: Linear Algebra
Section Details: Lovejoy 119 (Active Learning Classroom) | MWF | 9:00 AM - 9:50 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: MA 160 or MA 165
Description: Linear algebra is a crossroads where many important areas of mathematics meet, and it is the tool used to analyze the first approximation of complex systems. Students will learn to understand and use the language and theorems in both abstract and applied situations, gain insight into the nature of mathematical inquiry, and learn how to reason carefully and precisely about formally described situations. Topics include vectors and subspaces in R, linear transformations, and matrices; systems of linear equations; abstract vector spaces and the theory of single linear transformation: change of basis, determinants, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and diagonalization.

subject: MA
title: Vector Calculus
Section Details: Lovejoy 119 (Active Learning Classroom) | MWF | 10:00 AM - 10:50 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: MA 160 or MA 165
Description: Develops ideas first seen in Mathematics 122 (and 160) by applying the notions of derivative and integral to multi-variable vector-valued functions. The goal is to understand the high-dimensional versions of the fundamental theorem of calculus and to use these theorems in specific scientific applications. Topics include parameterized curves and surfaces; gradient, divergence, and curl; change of variables and the Jacobian; line and surface integrals; conservative vector fields; Green's, Stokes's, and Gauss's theorems; applications.

subject: MA
title: Mathematical Reasoning
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Proofs are the main method used by mathematicians to develop and communicate their ideas; this course prepares students to read, create, write, and communicate mathematical arguments. Topics include logic and standard methods of direct and indirect proof; the set-theoretic approach to functions and relations; the theory of infinite sets; elementary algebraic structures; and techniques from discrete mathematics.

subject: MA
title: Ordinary Differential Equations
Section Details: Lovejoy 119 (Active Learning Classroom) | MWF | 2:30 PM - 3:20 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomores and above who have taken MA 160 or 165, and MA 253
Description: Differential equations allow us to deduce the long-term behavior of quantities from information about their short-term rates of change; for that reason they are the language of classical science. Students will learn to analyze concrete situations modeled by differential equations and to draw conclusions using equations, graphical techniques, and numerical methods. Topics include theory and solution methods of ordinary differential equations, linear differential equations, first-order linear systems, qualitative behavior of solutions, nonlinear dynamics, existence and uniqueness of solutions, and applications.

subject: MA
title: Numerical Analysis
Section Details: Lovejoy 119 (Active Learning Classroom) | MWF | 11:00 AM - 11:50 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: MA 160 or 165, and MA 253. MA 274 is recommended.
Description: In practice, a solution to a problem might be impossible to obtain by classical methods of manipulating equations. Nonetheless, solutions can often be obtained by numerical methods, usually with the aid of a computer. Numerical analysis is the study of those numerical algorithms. Students will acquire the ability to use standard methods and mathematical software for solving the most common types of numerical problems and to analyze the speed and accuracy of the solutions. Topics include solution by numerical methods of linear and nonlinear equations, systems of equations, and differential equations; numerical integration; polynomial approximation; matrix inversion; error analysis.

subject: MA
title: Abstract Algebra
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomores or above who have taken MA 253 and MA 274
Description: Simply called "algebra" by mathematicians, it is the study of abstract sets with operations and is fundamental in expressing and working in theoretical mathematics. An introduction to that language, to the motivating examples, and to some of the fundamental theorems. Students will develop their ability to discover and write formal arguments, explore the relationship between general theory and specific examples, and learn to recognize algebraic structures where they occur. Topics include groups, rings, and fields: definition, basic theorems, and important examples.

subject: MA
title: Probability
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomores and above who have taken MA 160 or 165
Description: A mathematical introduction to probability theory, the foundation for commonly used inferential statistical techniques (covered in Statistics 482). Students will learn the basic theorems of probability and computational techniques for finding probabilities associated with stochastic processes. Topics include axiomatic foundations, combinatorics, random variables, discrete and continuous probability distributions, special probability distributions, independence, conditional and marginal probability distributions, properties of expectations, moment generating functions, sampling distributions, weak and strong laws of large numbers, and the central limit theorem.

subject: MA
title: Topics in Real Analysis
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomores or above who have taken MA 338. Students who have taken MA 439 previously, and who wish to take it again, may reach out to the instructor for permission to join.
Description: A sequel to Mathematics 338. Students will deepen their understanding of analysis through the exploration of more-advanced topics and will sharpen their ability to read, analyze, construct, and present proofs. Improving one's written and oral communication of mathematics is an integral part of the course. Topics will vary from year to year. May be repeated for credit with permission of instructor.

section: ML 121-A - Elementary Modern Standard Arabic I-A
subject: ML
title: Elementary Modern Standard Arabic I-A
Description: An introduction to Modern Standard Arabic for students with no previous knowledge of the language. Designed to develop all four skills--listening, speaking, reading, and writing--through a proficiency-based, student-centered approach. Students will develop accuracy and fluency in pronouncing and writing Arabic script, gain basic knowledge of vocabulary and grammar, and explore the ethnic, linguistic, and religious diversity of Arabic culture. Nongraded.

section: ML 123-A - Elementary Modern Standard Arabic II-A
subject: ML
title: Elementary Modern Standard Arabic II-A
Description: An introduction to Modern Standard Arabic for students with previous exposure to the language. Designed to expand all four skills--listening, speaking, reading, and writing--through a proficiency-based, student-centered approach. Students will hone accuracy and fluency in pronouncing and writing Arabic script, expand knowledge of vocabulary and grammar, and explore the ethnic, linguistic, and religious diversity of Arabic culture. Nongraded.

subject: MU
title: Bad Music
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: In this course, students will develop writing skills while listening closely to bad music and the people who love it. Students will learn specific musical vocabulary and aural analysis skills as they explore a range of answers to the question: what makes music “bad,” and who gets to decide? Readings will be drawn from journalism, scholarship, and digital discourse, and varied writing assignments will develop specific skills like writing a “bad” first draft, evaluating sources, writing for specific audiences, writing to persuade, and creative writing. The course will culminate in an original research paper.

subject: MU
title: Music Theory I
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Music test placement score (0 - 74) for section A
Description: The first in a sequence exploring the language and composition of Western tonal music. Just as learning a foreign language involves mastering a variety of skills, becoming musically conversant requires the ability to hear, notate, analyze, compose, and perform. Assures that students are fluent in the elements and structure of music, including intervals, scales, triads, seventh chords, basic counterpoint, harmony, and keyboard-style writing. Students compose in a variety of styles and study ear training and sight singing. Concludes with a public recital of student works. Primarily for students with some prior musical training (see also Music 153). Placement tests to determine section enrollment (A or B) will be available Monday, April 27th. More information on the Music Theory Placement Exam is available here. For information on testing out of MU 181, please go here: MU 181 Test Out Exam.

section: MU 191F-A2 - Flute Lessons: Credit, Full Hour
subject: MU
title: Flute Lessons: Credit, Full Hour
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: MU 111, 153, 181, 182, 252, 225, or 4 or 5 on the AP Music Theory exam. Otherwise, request registration for Non-credit section
Description:
For credit lessons: Students electing applied music for credit (MU 191 or MU 193) must play a jury or recital and have completed (or be enrolled in) one of the following: MU111 (Intro to Music), MU153 (Intro to Music Theory through DAW), MU181 (Music Theory I), MU 182 ( Music Theory II), MU252 (Intro to World Music) or MU225 (Intro to Afro-Latin Drumming - formerly MU 298). Students who submit either a 4 or 5 on the AP Music Theory Exam may also take lessons for credit.

IMPORTANT: Applied music instructors are not authorized to waive credit requirements for lessons. If you register for credit lessons but do not meet the prerequisites, you will be automatically moved to the non-credit version of your selected instrument and lesson length.

section: MU 233-A - Voice, Language, and Meaning: Music in the Sinophone
subject: MU
title: Voice, Language, and Meaning: Music in the Sinophone
Description: How does music complicate and confound the conventions of language? The first part of this course explores music aesthetics, criticism and social encounters in the Sinophone. Students gain insights into Confucianist, Daoist, Buddhist, and literati elites’ perspectives on tuning, cosmic harmony, affects and voice in ritual music, qin music and Kun Qu opera from Classical Chinese literature. The second part examines China-West encounters from the reception of Chinese music in North America and Western music in China, interrogating how Chinese language conformed to Western structures while speaking as othered subjects in the Western imaginary.

section: MU 234-A - From Rockabilly to Grunge: A History of Rock 'n' Roll
subject: MU
title: From Rockabilly to Grunge: A History of Rock 'n' Roll
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: A survey of rock music, from its roots in country and blues to the alternative rock scene of the 1990s. Rock music will be considered in relation to race, sex, gender, drugs, technology, marketing, and politics to better understand its powerful position in constructing, challenging, and reinforcing various positions of identity. Students will learn to discuss the musical characteristics of a work, identify its genre and era of composition, and contextualize it within a broader framework of American culture and politics.

subject: MU
title: Introduction to World Music
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Examines a range of classical, traditional, and contemporary musics from areas as diverse as India, West Africa, the Caribbean, Eastern Europe, and the Middle East, among others. Each unit engages a broader sociocultural issue to enable students to think deeply and critically about the music in question, exploring such topics as music and Apartheid, the Arab Spring, and the appropriation of "world" music by Western musicians. Students will have the opportunity to perform some of the music they study, including West African drumming patterns, salsa dance steps, and Bulgarian vocal practices, among others, and there will be guest performances. No prior musical experience necessary.

subject: MU
title: Sounding the Great Migration: 1900-1945
Cross-Listed Title: AM 255-A/ MU 255-A - Sounding the Great Migration: 1900
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: MU 111 or MU 181 or by permission of the instructor. Interested students who don't have the prerequisites should contact instructor directly.
Description: In the first half of the twentieth century, millions of Black Americans fled the South in search of better lives in the North and West United States. During this time, Black writers, artists, and musicians nurtured vibrant Black expressive cultures in cities like New York and Chicago. In this course, students will encounter the blues, jazz, gospel, and classical music produced during this period and place musical sound in historical context. Combining interdisciplinary readings, musical analysis, and writing assignments, students will ask questions like: How did Black composers approach Euro-centric classical music? Why were female blues musicians beloved by their listeners but rarely featured in major Black newspapers? And, how did jazz come to be celebrated as a uniquely American art form? Students will practice music analysis in listening journals, critically evaluate readings in reading responses, develop research skills in a short research paper, and make trans-historical connections in a creative final project.

section: MU 262-A - Music in Life, Music as Culture: Introduction to Ethnomusicology
subject: MU
title: Music in Life, Music as Culture: Introduction to Ethnomusicology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Provides students with a theoretical and methodological introduction to ethnomusicology, a discipline that is rooted in exploring music not merely as an aesthetic object, but as a cultural force that reflects and shapes our everyday lives. Topics include music and medicine, migration, war, ethnicity, and spirituality, among others. Topics will be explored through a close reading of seminal texts and an examination of relevant theory. Students will also learn the fundamentals of conducting ethnographic fieldwork through attending a religious ceremony and a concert, and creating a podcast based on the soundscapes of Colby's campus.

subject: MU
title: Composition Seminar
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: MU 111 (Has completed or in-progress) and has completed MU 181
Description: A combination of lectures, seminars, and workshops addressing the practice and art of music composition. Lectures will expose students to multiple musical genres and techniques utilized by creators in the last century; seminars will address their analytical and philosophical relationship with music by approaching works by composers from multiple traditions and thought-provoking readings; workshops will promote discussion of the students' musical compositions, opening their creative process to feedback from their peers and the instructor.

These topics are developed further in discussions, labs, and problem-solving assignments. May not be taken for credit if the student has earned credit for Physics 143.

subject: PH
title: Honors Physics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year or Sophomore Class Standing
Description: An accelerated, calculus-based, introductory course on Newtonian mechanics supplemented with some coverage of additional special topics. Intended for students who have had substantial courses in physics and calculus in high school. Topics in Newtonian mechanics include kinematics, dynamics, conservation laws, oscillations, and waves. Additional topics include special relativity and nuclear physics. Students acquire knowledge in these areas and skills for solving mathematical problems and doing laboratory work. May not be taken for credit if the student has earned credit for Physics 141.

subject: PH
title: Modern Physics I
Section Details: Miller 008 (Active Learning Classroom) | T | 1:00 PM - 1:50 PM | 09/09/2026 - 12/21/2026
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: PH 145, and MA 160 or MA 165
Description: An introduction to the two central paradigms of non-Newtonian physics: Einstein's special theory of relativity and the quantum behavior of light and matter. The postulates of Einstein are presented and the consequences explored theoretically along with experimental evidence for relativity. The experimental evidence for quantum mechanics is considered from a historical perspective, beginning with Planck's quantum hypothesis for blackbody radiation through to the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom and the experimental evidence for the Schrdinger equation. Students will acquire skills in solving physics problems and learning to communicate the solutions effectively in writing. Lecture and discussion.

section: PH 245-A - Introduction to Quantum Information Science
subject: PH
title: Introduction to Quantum Information Science
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: PH:  MA 120, MA 125, MA 130, MA 135, MA 160, or MA 161 (Has completed or In-progress)
Description: The course provides an introduction to the foundational principles of quantum information science, an emerging combination of physics, mathematics, and computer science. Students will learn the fundamental properties of quantum mechanical systems and how rules governing information processing change when quantum rules replace classical rules. Students will understand the difference between information storage in quantum states versus classical states (quantum bits and classical bits) including the inability to copy quantum bits (the no-cloning theorem) and entanglement, an understanding of quantum computing operations on quantum bits (quantum gates), and be introduced to quantum algorithms.

subject: PH
title: Experiments in Modern Physics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: PH 241 (IP)
Description: Explores physics laboratory practice in connection with the core principles of modern physics. Introduces concepts of experiment design, the use of electronic instrumentation and data acquisition, techniques of data analysis and presentation, and skills in scientific communication through written and/or oral presentations. Lecture and laboratory.

subject: PH
title: Classical Mechanics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: PH: MA 122, MA 160, MA 162, or MA 165
Description: Newton's laws, oscillatory motion, noninertial reference systems, classical gravitation, motion of rigid bodies, and Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics. Lecture and discussion.

subject: PH
title: Electricity and Magnetism
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: PH 145 and MA 262
Description: A theoretical treatment of electrostatics and magnetostatics in vacuum and material media through Maxwell's equations. Lecture and discussion.

section: PH 401-A - Senior Physics and Astronomy Seminar
subject: PH
title: Senior Physics and Astronomy Seminar
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Physics Major and Senior Class Standing
Description: Seminars will focus on student-led discussions of readings from the primary literature and will also include playing host to outside speakers. Required of all senior physics majors.

section: PL 114-A - Central Philosophical Issues: Nature and God
subject: PL
title: Central Philosophical Issues: Nature and God
Description: An introduction to philosophy approached through issues in the philosophy of religion. Stress will be on epistemological questions (regarding how we can have knowledge) in connection with metaphysical questions (regarding the basic features of the universe). Designed to introduce students to the history of Western philosophy; to improve skills of critical reading, writing, and thinking; and to promote thinking on some big-picture issues, such as education, happiness, wisdom, God, spirituality, and knowledge. Readings include Plato, Aquinas, Bacon, Descartes, Hume, and Dewey.

section: PL 117-A - Central Philosophical Issues: Constructions of Difference
subject: PL
title: Central Philosophical Issues: Constructions of Difference
Section Details: Miller 008 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 9:30 AM - 10:45 AM
Description: What makes human beings different from nonhuman animals? How should we understand racial, cultural, gender, class, and other significant human differences? How have all of these kinds of difference been understood historically, and how have colonialism, patriarchy, environmental destruction, white supremacy, and capitalism benefited from these constructions of difference? An introduction to philosophy through prominent questions and themes in critical social theory that provide resources for clear reasoning about creating just communities and for exploring the relationships between academic work and social responsibility.

section: PL 145-A - Myth and Reason: Literature and Philosophy of Ancient Greece
subject: PL
title: Myth and Reason: Literature and Philosophy of Ancient Greece
Course Tags: Integrated Studies Clusters :: IS: The Ancient World
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year Class Standing
Description: An introductory survey that encourages a holistic understanding of the ancient Greek world by examining key works of literature and core theories of knowledge and reality. Themes include the idea of philosophy as a way of life and the relations between myth and reason, nature and civilization, the feminine and the masculine, mortals and the divine/gods, appearance and reality, and religion and philosophy. Texts are selected from the works of Homer, Hesiod, Sappho, Euripides, Aeschylus, Sophocles, Aristophanes, Plutarch, the PreSocratic philosophers (especially Heraclitus and Parmenides), Plato, and Aristotle.

subject: PL
title: Logic and Argumentation
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Argumentation is a subject that covers the processes of reasoning, the communicative actions, and the dialectical exchanges that give form to our intellectual lives. Logic, the study of inferences, is a central component of good argumentation. Students develop the conceptual vocabulary and critical skills to argue effectively and to evaluate arguments intelligently. These include interpretive techniques, like diagramming and fallacy identification, as well as the formal, analytic tools of symbolic logic.

section: PL 231-A - History of Ancient Greek Philosophy
subject: PL
title: History of Ancient Greek Philosophy
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomore Class Standing or Above
Description: A survey of ancient Greek thought through the ideas of the pre-Socratics, the Sophists, Plato, Aristotle, the Epicureans, and the Stoics. Primary, though not exclusive, attention will be to metaphysical and epistemological issues.

subject: PL
title: Philosophy and Art
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomore Class Standing or Above
Description: This course will provide a historical and theoretical introduction to the philosophy of art. We will ask questions such as, What is art? What is beauty? Does art need to be beautiful? Why do humans create art in the first place? Is the aesthetic experience primarily cognitive or emotive? Should art merely entertain us or ennoble and improve us?  Students will engage with these questions by reading and writing philosophical work.

subject: PL
title: Chinese Philosophy
Description: An introduction to major thoughts, texts, and thinkers in the "classical" period of Chinese philosophy, which covers roughly the sixth through the third centuries BCE (known as the Warring States period). We will cover Confucius, Mozi, Mencius, Zhuangzi, Laozi, Sunzi, Xunzi, Han Feizi, the Yijing or Book of Changes, and other important texts. Provides an overview of the philosophical questions that motivated thinkers in early China and aims to provide an appreciation for how various answers to these questions have shaped East Asian civilizations generally.

subject: PL
title: Reuman Reading Group
Description: Faculty and students jointly select, read, discuss, and argue about a philosophical text in regular, intellectually rigorous, but freewheeling and informal sessions that provide an opportunity to indulge our passion for philosophy. Nongraded.

subject: PL
title: Philosophy of Language
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Philosophy took a linguistic turn in the 20th century: philosophers have come to suppose that reflection on the nature of language and the linguistic representation can help solve longstanding philosophical problems. The development of the philosophy of language and its success, with special attention to the role of metaphor.

subject: PL
title: Phenomenology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomore class standing and above and one PL course (other than PL 151)
Description: The purpose of this course is to provide students with a historical, theoretical, and practical introduction to phenomenology. We will study major figures and texts in the tradition (such as Husserl and Merleau-Ponty) and recent developments (e.g., critical phenomenology), as well as practicing phenomenology ourselves. Students will gain an understanding of central phenomenological terms and concepts, such as intentionality, intuition, the lifeworld, and the reduction. Themes to be discussed include embodiment, empathy, freedom, gender, imagination, race, time, and transcendence.

subject: PL
title: Philosophical Encounters:
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Five Philosophy courses, including PL 151 and at least one 300-level, Junior or Senior class standing
Description: With topics and readings that change each semester, this seminar-style course features engagement with the work of contemporary philosophers through face-to-face encounters (via video conferencing and in-person visits). In addition to standard seminar-level work, students will read and discuss current works in the field and work together in preparing for various “philosophical encounters” designed to augment the material studied and to facilitate practice in the habits and skills of philosophical engagement.

subject: PO
title: Introduction to Policy Analysis
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: EC 293, GO 281, PS 214, SC 212, or SO 271
Description: This course offers an introduction to major theories and approaches in the analysis of public policy, with a particular focus on policy effects. Topics to be covered include case selection, the logic of causal inference, randomized experiments, quasi-experimental designs, comparing quantitative and qualitative approaches, causal mechanisms, and costs and unintended consequences.

subject: PO
title: Introduction to Policy Analysis
Section Details: Lovejoy 102 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 2:30 PM - 3:45 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: EC 293, GO 281, PS 214, SC 212, or SO 271
Description: This course offers an introduction to major theories and approaches in the analysis of public policy, with a particular focus on policy effects. Topics to be covered include case selection, the logic of causal inference, randomized experiments, quasi-experimental designs, comparing quantitative and qualitative approaches, causal mechanisms, and costs and unintended consequences.

subject: PO
title: Policy Lab Practicum
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission and must have taken EC 293, GO 281, PS 214, SC 212, or SO 271
Description: For this practicum, students carry out an in-depth, real-world policy analysis or evaluation project in an area of their interest for a partner organization in the community. Students meet as a group once a week, as well as individually with the instructor, who provides close mentoring and support. The bulk of the work is done outside the classroom visiting field sites, consulting with stakeholders, gathering and analyzing data, and producing a professional final report. The practicum serves as a bridge between academic policy knowledge and practical application. This course may be repeated for additional credit.

subject: PS
title: Introduction to Psychology
Description: An examination of classical and contemporary topics in psychology, including neuroscience, learning, memory, cognition, language, development, personality, psychopathology, and social psychology. Students will begin developing skills that will enhance understanding of the discipline of psychology, including explaining behavior from multiple theoretical perspectives, applying research to real-world contexts and thinking about implications of research.

section: PS 214-A - Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology I
subject: PS
title: Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology I
Section Details: Miller 008 (Active Learning Classroom) | MW | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: PS 111, and another 200-level PS course (may be taken concurrently); and Sophomore or Junior Class Standing
Description: Along with Psychology 215, provides students with knowledge of research design and statistical tools for working with data, which will allow them to engage in original empirical research. Topics include descriptive and inferential statistics, literature review, hypothesis formulation, and issues of control and ethics in research. Students practice a variety of statistical tests, work with SPSS, powerful statistical software, and prepare a written proposal for an experiment following the stylistic conventions of the American Psychological Association.  Lecture and laboratory.

subject: PS
title: Social Identities
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (Psych, Psych- NeuroSci, Psyc- Comp, Bio- NeuroSci or Ed Majors, or Rising Sophomores who are undeclared) who have taken PS 111
Description: Social identities are fundamental to how people understand themselves and how they relate to others. Examples of social identities include (but are not limited to) gender, social class, race, and religion. In this class, we will examine the psychology behind how social identities are developed, how they shape people's judgments of themselves and others, and what they mean to different people. Students will engage with published research, media (op-eds, videos), and fellow classmates to understand this diverse world.

subject: PS
title: Biological Basis of Behavior
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (PS, PSNS, PSIC, BINS, ED, STS Majors, or Rising Sophomores who are undeclared) and PS 111
Description: Broad survey of behavioral neuroscience will include instruction on neural anatomy and function; modulation of these systems by hormones, drugs, and disease; and the neural basis of psychopathology, as well as the neural mechanisms underlying other behaviors of interest to psychologists, including sex, sleep, and hunger. Students will gain a comprehensive working knowledge of the mammalian central nervous system in the context of psychology to use as they learn the historical and modern framework of specific questions by reading and discussing research articles and completing assignments.

subject: PS
title: Cognitive Neuroscience
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (PS, PSNS, PSIC, BINS, ED Majors, or Rising Sophomores who are undeclared) and PS 111
Description: Cognitive neuroscientists attempt to further our understanding of cognition by studying the brain. You will gain an understanding of the methodological toolkit of cognitive neuroscientists, including behavioral techniques, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), studies of patient populations, and computational modeling. You will learn how the field has advanced our understanding of high-level cognitive functions, such as memory, spatial navigation, semantic cognition, and language. In addition to reading the textbook and primary journal articles, you will analyze data and explore simulations of the brain.

subject: PS
title: Industrial and Organizational Psychology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ((PS, PSNS, PSIC, BINS, ED Majors, or Rising Sophomores who are undeclared) and PS 111) or First-year students with a score of 4 or 5 on the AP Psychology exam
Description: Industrial and organizational psychology is psychology applied to the world of work. This course will explore topics related to personnel selection, job performance, and training and development. This course will also look at how to improve employee motivation, job satisfaction, leadership, and organizational effectiveness. Previously offered as Psychology 298 (Spring 2020).

subject: PS
title: Lifespan Development
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ((PS, PSNS, PSIC, BINS Majors, or Rising Sophomores who are undeclared) and PS 111) or First-Year students with a score of 4 or 5 on the AP Psychology exam
Description: A study of human development across the lifespan with emphasis on the general characteristics of development from birth to death. Various theories will be explored to explain developmental processes. Topics include perceptual, cognitive, social, and identity development; the role of families, communities, and culture in development; and death and dying. Students have the option to participate in civic engagement activities in the local community. This applied work helps students explore how to apply the findings of research or tenets of theory to real-world contexts. Students with prior credit for Psychology 120 cannot receive credit for 259.

subject: PS
title: Sensation and Perception
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (Psych, Psych- NeuroSci, Psyc- Comp, Bio- NeuroSci, STS Majors, or Rising Sophomores who are undeclared) and who have taken PS 111
Description: A key part of psychology is understanding how we perceive and interact with our world. In this course we will discuss the functions of some of our sensory systems, how they work alone and in concert with each other to provide us with information. Through the course of the class we will review historic as well as our current understanding of the field with demonstrations as well as reading. By the end of the course, students will be able to identify the human sensory machinery and explain the perceptual process in varying situations, explain and evaluate the differing theoretical perspectives in the science of perception, as well as critically think about the science of psychology.

section: PS 336-A - Seminar in Experimental Social Psychology
subject: PS
title: Seminar in Experimental Social Psychology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Psych, Psych- NeuroSci, or Psych Comp Majors who have taken PS 215 with a C- or higher, (PS 219, PS 253, PS 251 or PS 223), and have Junior Class Standing or above
Description: Trains students to critically examine, write about, and discuss primary empirical sources/contemporary research in social psychology. Topics may include self-esteem, belief in free will, and perceptions of authenticity and meaning in life.

section: PS 337-A - Collaborative Research in Social Psychology
subject: PS
title: Collaborative Research in Social Psychology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Psych, Psych- NeuroSci, or Psych Comp Majors who have taken PS 215 with a C- or higher, (PS 219, PS 253, PS 251 or PS 223), and have Junior Class Standing or above
Description: Collaborative empirical research projects on topics discussed in Psychology 336. Students will design, conduct, and present an original research project that contributes to the knowledge of contemporary issues within social psychology. Collaborative and individual oral and written assignments, following the conventions of the American Psychological Association, will be used to evaluate students' research and communication competencies.

subject: PS
title: Seminar in Behavioral Neuroscience
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Psych, Psych- NeuroSci, or Psych Comp Majors who have taken PS 215 and (PS 233 or 242) and Junior Class Standing or above
Description: Key topics in behavioral neuroscience will be explored, with an emphasis on rat models of motivated behaviors, emotion, and cognition. Discussions will cover techniques to assess neuronal function and their behavioral relevance, including assays of neurotransmitter function and protein expression. There will be a major focus on using rat models to understand the efficacy of novel treatments for substance use disorders. Behaviors of interest may include assays of drug reward, withdrawal, and/or anxiety. Reading and discussion of empirical and review papers will develop skills to critically evaluate and integrate published and generated data.

section: PS 350-A - Collaborative Research in Behavioral Neuroscience
subject: PS
title: Collaborative Research in Behavioral Neuroscience
Description: Collaborative empirical research projects on topics discussed in Psychology 349. Empirical work addressing an original research question on a topic pertaining to a feature of neuronal function and a corresponding behavioral construct will be conducted. Collaborative and individual oral and written assignments, following the conventions of the field, will be used to evaluate students’ research and communication competencies.

subject: PS
title: Cognitive Aging Seminar
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (Psych, Psych- NeuroSci, or Psych-Comp majors) who have taken (PS 232, PS 244, or PS 259), and Sophomore Class Standing or above
Description: As the world's population is graying, understanding the aging process is critical for social and policy decisions. Examines how psychological processes change as we age, with an emphasis on the cognitive aspects critical for maintaining independence and health. Key areas include attention, memory, and language processes, with an examination of how changes in these domains influence psychological well-being. Students will develop an understanding of issues related to aging, theoretical approaches to explaining age-related changes, differences between healthy and disordered aging, and what factors can reduce risks of cognitive decline and dementia. Presentations, discussions, and critical analysis of original papers will support learning goals.

subject: PS
title: Seminar: Developmental Psychology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Psych, Psych- NeuroSci, or Psych- Comp Majors who have taken PS 120*, PS 259, PS 223, or PS 230 and have Sophomore Class Standing or above
Description: Psychological principles as they relate to developmental psychology. Topics including theoretical perspectives on how development proceeds will be addressed in the first half; specific topics related to development in the second. Topics are selected by students and have included dating violence, bullying, sexuality, domestic violence, links between systems of discrimination (sexism/racism/homophobia/classism), resiliency, parenting, attachment, friendships, mentoring, death, and dying. Students are expected to participate in applied work to reflect on how to bridge the gap between research/theory and using research/theory in the real world.

subject: PS
title: Seminar in Environmental Psychology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (Psych, Psych- NeuroSci, Psych-Comp, or Bio-NeuroSci Majors) who have taken (PS 219, PS 232, PS 233, PS 244, PS 253, or PS 272), and Sophomore Class Standing or above. ES majors and STS majors may enroll with instructor permission.
Description: Environmental psychology is a multidisciplinary field that investigates the bidirectional relationship between animals, such as humans, and their environment. We will focus on the intersection of psychology and neuroscience (e.g., social psychology, cognitive neuroscience) to study topics like climate change, the influence of the natural and built environment on mental and physical health, spatial navigation and memory, environmental perception/ethics, decision-making in individuals and groups, emotion, and nonhuman animal behavior. We will practice scientific communication, and you will develop a multimedia portfolio on your chosen topic.

subject: PS
title: Seminar in Political Psychology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Psych, Psych- NeuroSci, or Psych Comp Majors who have taken PS 215 with a C- or higher, (PS 219, PS 223, or PS 253), and have Junior Class Standing or above
Description: Why are reasonable people so divided by politics? Political polarization is on the rise, and political conflicts in the United States can feel intractable, pointless, and even dangerous. In this course, we will investigate the bidirectional ways that our identities shape our political beliefs, and how our political beliefs shape our identities. Discussion topics may include motivated reasoning, politics and morality, politics in the brain, polarization on social media, and polarized perception and misperception.

section: PS 365-A - Collaborative Research in Political Psychology
subject: PS
title: Collaborative Research in Political Psychology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Psych, Psych- NeuroSci, or Psych Comp Majors who have taken PS 215 with a C- or higher, have taken PS 219, PS 223, or PS 253, and have Junior Class Standing or above
Description: Students will design and conduct original empirical work on topics discussed in Psychology 364, testing how political identities influence perceptions and behaviors. Students competence in research and communication will be assessed, following the guidelines of the American Psychological Association, through individual and collaborative written assignments and presentations.

section: PS 366-A - Seminar in Foundations of Childhood Mental Health
subject: PS
title: Seminar in Foundations of Childhood Mental Health
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Psych, Psych- NeuroSci, or Psych Comp Majors who have taken PS 215 with a C- or higher, have taken PS 230, PS 254, PS 259, or 120* and have Junior Class Standing or above
Description: Explores the foundations of mental health focusing on early childhood (3-to-6-year-old children) using a developmental psychopathology framework that understands mental health disorders as normal development gone awry. Discussion topics may include core competencies that support positive mental health, the role of parenting and broader systemic and contextual influences on mental health, school readiness, risk and resilience in the development of psychopathology, and the prevention of and early intervention for childhood mental health disorders. Students will read, critically evaluate, discuss, and synthesize current empirical research.

section: PS 367-A - Collaborative Research in Foundations of Childhood Mental Health
subject: PS
title: Collaborative Research in Foundations of Childhood Mental Health
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Psych, Psych- NeuroSci, or Psych Comp Majors who have taken PS 215 with a C- or higher, have taken PS 230, PS 254, PS 259, or 120* and have Junior Class Standing or above
Description: Collaborative empirical research projects on topics discussed in PS366 (Seminar in Foundations of Childhood Mental Health). Students will design, conduct, and present original research related to early childhood mental health foundations, prevention, and/or early intervention following American Psychological Association conventions. In addition to weekly research-team meetings, this course also includes a weekly 3-hour commitment to volunteer in a community-based program (e.g., school, local early-childhood program, group-based social skills intervention, and/or other community setting), scheduled separately.

subject: PS
title: Senior Integrative Seminar
Section Details: Olin 019B (Active Learning Classroom) | W | 1:00 PM - 3:30 PM | 09/09/2026 - 12/21/2026
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (Psych, Psych- NeuroSci, or Psych- Comp Majors) with Senior Class Standing
Description: A culminating experience for students majoring in psychology, organized around the department's research colloquium series. Students will critically engage with a variety of current psychological research and will integrate theories, methodologies, and findings across areas of psychology. Specifically, students will attend research presentations by invited guest speakers, read companion papers selected by the speakers, meet in a seminar session to discuss each speaker's presentation, and write a final paper that integrates the theories, methodologies, or research findings of at least two colloquium speakers.

subject: PS
title: Senior Integrative Seminar
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Psych, Psych- NeuroSci, or Psych- Comp Majors with Senior Class Standing
Description: A culminating experience for students majoring in psychology, organized around the department's research colloquium series. Students will critically engage with a variety of current psychological research and will integrate theories, methodologies, and findings across areas of psychology. Specifically, students will attend research presentations by invited guest speakers, read companion papers selected by the speakers, meet in a seminar session to discuss each speaker's presentation, and write a final paper that integrates the theories, methodologies, or research findings of at least two colloquium speakers.

section: RE 117-A - A Passage to India: India and the Western Imagination
subject: RE
title: A Passage to India: India and the Western Imagination
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - RE :: RE: Eastern Religious Traditions
Program of Study Requirement - RE :: RE: Identity
Program of Study Requirement - RE :: RE: Interpretation
Description: Beginning with Walt Whitman's romantic journey toward the "soul" of the universe, Western attitudes towards India and India's encounter with Western culture will be studied. Literature and film include A Passage to India, The Razor's Edge, The English Patient, Siddhartha, The Namesake, Gitanjali, Blinded by the Light,  and Four Quartets. Historical, political, religious, and visual context of the texts will be provided. A close reading of the texts for their aesthetic value, their existential disclosures, and as narratives on colonialism, racism, and orientalism.

section: RE 128-A - Introduction to the Study of Religion
subject: RE
title: Introduction to the Study of Religion
Section Details: Olin 019B (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - RE :: RE: Interpretation
Description: This course is an introduction to the study of religion. Students will survey the methodologies and modes of inquiry scholars have used to examine religions, explore how these approaches have been employed in analyses and discussions of religion (in scholarly communities and beyond), and develop the theoretical skills and vocabulary to contribute their own analyses. This is the core gateway course for the study of religion at Colby, geared toward (but not limited to) students interested in majoring and minoring in religious studies. Previously offered as Religious Studies 228 (Spring 2023).

section: RE 143-A - Introduction to the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament
subject: RE
title: Introduction to the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - RE :: RE: Identity
Program of Study Requirement - RE :: RE: Interpretation
Program of Study Requirement - RE :: RE: Western Religious Traditions

subject: RE
title: Cults in America
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - RE :: RE: Identity
Description: America has a weird love-hate thing with cults. Some people dismiss them as weird or ridiculous, while others call them violent or downright evil. And yet there is an almost endless stream of documentary series, podcasts, news articles, and fictional series about cults of sorts-sex cults ("The Vow"), murder cults (American Horror Stories), diet cults (The Weigh Down), sports cults (CrossFit), political cults (QAnon). The list could go on because we can't seem to get enough of cult content. What's with our obsession with cults? What even is a cult-is Colby one? A sports team?  Are cults as weird or as bad as the media makes them out to be? "Cults in America" explores these questions and more, delving into both media coverage of cults and some of their beliefs and practices in order to understand them on their own terms.

section: RE 251-A - The Bible in American Cinema
subject: RE
title: The Bible in American Cinema
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - RE :: RE: Identity
Program of Study Requirement - RE :: RE: Interpretation
Description: This course explores the convergence of the Bible, film, and culture in the United States, investigating how cinematic depictions interpret biblical literature and respond to the shifting social and political circumstances of the past century. We will begin each week by reading portions of the biblical text that have received a great deal of attention from interpreters, both ancient and modern. We will then examine two types of films: films that retell biblical stories and films that use biblical allusions, figures, and/or the Bible itself to explore a range of themes, such as martyrdom, messianism, and apocalypse.

subject: RE
title: Senior Capstone
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Religious Studies Majors with Senior Class Standing
Description: The Senior Capstone is a new required two-semester course (2 credits/semester, 4 credits/semester for honors) for Religious Studies majors. In this course, students will discuss recent debates concerning theories and methods in the academic study of religion and will complete a major work of independent research.

subject: RU
title: Reel Russia
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: What role does Russia's "most important art" play in shaping the nation's present and future?  How does it legitimate or subvert the official notions of usable and unusable past?  What has caused the shift from the rigorous interrogation of the Communist past in the 1990s to the revival and reintegration of Soviet-era policies, practices, and values in the 21st century?  Students will combine intellectual inquiry into changing representations of social structures, ethnic relations, and gender roles in Russia with the development of visual literacy, analytical skills, and vocabulary necessary to think and write critically about film.

section: RU 120A-A - Vampires and Werewolves: Slavic Myth in Contemporary Culture (in English)
subject: RU
title: Vampires and Werewolves: Slavic Myth in Contemporary Culture (in English)
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: We will explore the representation of vampires and werewolves in the world of Slavic folklore. Over the course of the semester, we will read a number of texts--historical accounts, testimonies, folktales, fairytales, stories, novels, a play--that offer portraits of these two enigmatic figures. We will watch films from different time periods that present vampires and werewolves and determine what these portrayals say about Slavic and world culture. In our discussions, presentations, and writing assignments, we will discuss what the fascination with vampires and werewolves says about primal fears, superstitions, ignorance, identity, social conflict, sexuality, and the nature of good and evil.

subject: RU
title: Elementary Russian I
Description: Introductory course enables students to acquire a high degree of competence in elementary Russian through communicative learning and interaction. Acquisition of functions, grammar and vocabulary through substantial engagement in creative communication and role playing, reinforced by listening, readings, writing, and speaking assignments outside of the classroom. Cultural practices of Russians are studied through language. Concurrent Requirement: RU135 Tutorial.

subject: RU
title: Intermediate Russian I
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: RU 126
Description: The second-year language sequence in Russian builds on the communicative abilities mastered in elementary Russian by active classroom engagement in conversation and vocabulary building. Study of Russian culture through brief biographies of writers, watching film and Internet clips, and reading short fiction and poetry. The final stages of Russian grammar are introduced, practiced, and tested. Essay assignments increase writing skills, and oral tests allow students to develop fluency in speaking. Concurrent Requirement: RU235 Tutorial.

subject: RU
title: Beginning Russian Tutorial
Description: An informal, weekly, small-group meeting for first-year students concurrently enrolled in Elementary Russian I (RU 125) or Elementary Russian II (RU 126). This weekly session is mandatory for students enrolled in Elementary Russian I and II and counts towards the attendance and participation grades in RU 125 and RU 126. Topics for discussion include autobiography, education, leisure-time activities, travel, stores, and films. Conducted entirely in Russian. May be repeated for credit. Nongraded.

section: RU 197-A - Explore Russian: Language and Culture
subject: RU
title: Explore Russian: Language and Culture
Section Details: Lovejoy 102 (Active Learning Classroom) | W | 7:00 PM - 8:00 PM | 09/09/2026 - 12/21/2026
Description: Ever looked at a Russian sign and thought it looked like a secret code? Or wondered why everyone in Russian novels has three different names? Explore Russian is a low-stakes, high-reward entry into the language and culture of the world’s largest country. Students will master the Cyrillic alphabet, becoming proficient in reading and handwriting, and learn the grammar and vocabulary basics needed to describe objects, introduce themselves, and talk about family, and friends. Students will engage with authentic Russian culture and complete a discovery project by researching and presenting on a topic of their choice. For deeper immersion consider RU125.

subject: RU
title: Intermediate Russian Tutorial
Description: An informal, weekly, small-group meeting for second-year students concurrently enrolled in Intermediate Russian I (RU 127) or Intermediate Russian II (RU 128). This weekly session is mandatory for students enrolled in Intermediate Russian I and II and counts towards the attendance and participation grades in RU 127 and RU 128. Topics for discussion include autobiography, education, leisure-time activities, travel, stores, and films. Conducted entirely in Russian. May be repeated for credit. Nongraded.

section: RU 325-A - Advanced Russian I: Literature and Identity
subject: RU
title: Advanced Russian I: Literature and Identity
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: RU 128
Description: We will work to expand our ability to discuss complex topics, such as ecology, politics, and culture, while reviewing essential grammar and continuing to practice oral and written expression. As a semester-long project, students will create their own imaginary countries and give regular reports on their geography, folklore, education and political systems. Conducted in Russian.

subject: RU
title: Advanced Russian Tutorial
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: RU 128 or higher
Description: An informal, weekly, small-group meeting for advanced students concurrently enrolled in Advanced Russian I (RU 325/RU 425), Conversation and Composition (RU 326), or Seminar in Russian Culture and Literature (RU 428); other students require Instructor's permission. Topics accommodate student interests. Conducted in Russian. May be repeated for credit. Nongraded.

section: RU 425-A - Advanced Russian I: Literature and Identity
subject: RU
title: Advanced Russian I: Literature and Identity
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: RU 325 or RU 326
Description: We will work to expand our ability to discuss complex topics, such as literary analysis, visual arts, politics, and culture, while reviewing essential grammar and continuing to practice oral and written expression. Topic for fall 2026: Personal Identity in Russian and Russophone literature and culture of the long twentieth century. Conducted in Russian.

subject: SC
title: Introduction to Public Health
Description: This course provides a broad overview of the field of public health. Students will be exposed to core public health domains including epidemiology, social and behavioral health, health policy, and environmental health. Through case studies of various public health programs aimed at preventing infectious disease, improving maternal and child health, and addressing the health impacts of climate change, students will learn how to use existing data and evidence to assess public health problems and identify effective interventions. Students will also discuss a number of timely issues in public health such as preparedness for the next pandemic and the role of national and international bodies in promoting public health.

subject: SC
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
Section Details: Miller 008 (Active Learning Classroom) | MWF | 10:00 AM - 10:50 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Must not have taken SC 306 previously
Description: This course introduces the principles and methods of epidemiology as applied to public health practice. Students examine the historical development of epidemiology; the role of epidemiology in disease prevention; and differences between infectious and chronic disease epidemiology. Topics include sources of epidemiologic data; basic statistical concepts; measures of disease frequency and association; study designs; bias, confounding, and causal inference; and descriptive analysis of morbidity and mortality patterns.

section: SC 212-A - Introduction to Statistics and Data Science
subject: SC
title: Introduction to Statistics and Data Science
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomore Class Standing or Above
Description: An exploration of statistical methods relevant to a broad array of scientific disciplines. Students will learn to properly collect data through sound experimental design and to present and interpret data in a meaningful way, making use of statistical computing packages. Topics include descriptive statistics, design of experiments, randomization, contingency tables, measures of association for categorical variables, confidence intervals, one- and two-sample tests of hypotheses for means and proportions, analysis of variance, correlation/regression, and nonparametrics.

subject: SC
title: Statistical Modeling
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SC: SC 212, EC 293, or PS 214
Description: Students will expand on their inferential statistical background and explore methods of modeling data through linear and nonlinear regression analysis. Through the use of statistical software, they will learn how to identify possible models based on data visualization techniques, to validate assumptions required by such models, and to describe their limitations. Topics include multiple linear regression, multicollinearity, logistic regression, models for analyzing temporal data, model-building strategies, transformations, model validation.

subject: SC
title: Statistical Modeling
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SC: SC 212, EC 293, or PS 214

Through the use of statistical software, they will learn how to identify possible models based on data visualization techniques, to validate assumptions required by such models, and to describe their limitations. Topics include multiple linear regression, multicollinearity, logistic regression, models for analyzing temporal data, model-building strategies, transformations, model validation.

subject: SC
title: Statistical Machine Learning
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: (SC 212, EC 225 (293), or PS 215), and must have taken, or be in the process of taking, MA 253
Description: Statistical methods used in data science allow computers to make inferences and predictions about target variables. This course will provide students exposure to the common statistical methods and models used in this setting. Although the emphasis is on applications, the statistical and mathematical foundations for these data science techniques will also be covered. Topics will include linear modeling and classification techniques, cross validation, bootstrapping, non-linear modeling, tree-based methods, and data reduction strategies. Unsupervised learning techniques will also be covered as time allows.

section: SC 326-A - Statistical Graphics and Principles of Visualization
subject: SC
title: Statistical Graphics and Principles of Visualization
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SC: SC 212, EC 225 (formerly 293), or PS 215
Description: An effective statistical graphic is a powerful tool for analyzing data and communicating insights. From tabular to geospatial and network datasets, students will learn to create and interpret visualizations that show the raw data, statistical models of that data, and the statistical precision of those summaries. Students will also apply principles of human visual processing and data science workflows to ensure their statistical graphics are effective and reproducible. With the help of the tidyverse, ggplot2, rmarkdown, and shiny R packages, students will create static and interactive graphics, culminating in an interactive data dashboard. Previously offered as Statistics 398 (Spring 2021).

subject: SC
title: Probability
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomores and above who have taken MA 160 or 165
Description: A mathematical introduction to probability theory, the foundation for commonly used inferential statistical techniques (covered in Statistics 482). Students will learn the basic theorems of probability and computational techniques for finding probabilities associated with stochastic processes. Topics include axiomatic foundations, combinatorics, random variables, discrete and continuous probability distributions, special probability distributions, independence, conditional and marginal probability distributions, properties of expectations, moment generating functions, sampling distributions, weak and strong laws of large numbers, and the central limit theorem.

subject: SO
title: Introduction to Sociology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: Sociologists study processes by which people create, maintain, and change their social and cultural worlds. They investigate contemporary social issues and strive to explain relationships between what happens in peoples' lives and the societies in which they live. Sociology's research methods and theories apply to the full range of human behavior, from individual acts to global environmental, political, and economic change. An introduction to how and why sociologists study social and cultural phenomena such as inequality, race and ethnicity, gender, power, politics, the family, religion, social and cultural change, crime, and globalization.

subject: SO
title: Introduction to Sociology

section: SO 212-A - Introduction to GIS and Spatial Analysis
subject: SO
title: Introduction to GIS and Spatial Analysis
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Sophomores and above who have not earned credit for ES 212 or ES 214J
Description: An introduction to geographic information systems' (GIS) data management and visualization capabilities as well as the theory and application of spatial analysis techniques. Topics covered include spatial data representation in a GIS, effective map making, coordinate systems and projections, exploratory spatial data analysis (ESDA), and spatial statistical analysis.

subject: SO
title: Schools and Society
Section Details: Diamond 123 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: The complex relationships between schools and society will be examined by reviewing a variety of theoretical perspectives and empirical studies. Topics include social mobility and stratification; social reproduction; the dynamics of race, class, and gender in education; various forms of capital; teaching as a profession; and school choice. Particular attention will be given to the ways that small interactions within educational settings have much larger implications within society.

subject: SO
title: Classical Sociological Theory
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SO 131
Description: The history of sociology, and a critical survey of the systems of thought about society, centered on major schools of sociological theory and their representatives. The place of theory in social research as presented in works of foundational social theorists, including, but not limited to, Comte, Spencer, Durkheim, Weber, Marx, Du Bois, Simmel, and Mead.

subject: SO
title: Organizations
Description: Organizations frame our lives. From private-sector businesses to non-profits to government agencies, organizations coordinate how we accomplish common goals and deliver goods and services that we rely on. They drive economic and social change. Sometimes they foster spectacular innovations and at other times catastrophic disasters. In this course, we will explore why organizations exist, how organizations are structured, how people manage organizations, and whether popular organizational practices are effective. Through analyzing case studies and contemporary research, students will gain critical insights on managing and leading organizations.

subject: SO
title: Sociology of Immigration
Description: This course offers an introduction to the sociology of immigration, using the United States as its central case study. We will examine sociological theories explaining why people migrate, the history of U.S. efforts to control population movements, and patterns of immigrant incorporation. Special attention will be paid to the convergence of the immigration and criminal justice systems (often called crimmigration), the complexities of citizenship and legal status, and American public opinion on immigration.

subject: SO
title: Introduction to Policy Analysis
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: EC 293, GO 281, PS 214, SC 212, or SO 271
Description: This course offers an introduction to major theories and approaches in the analysis of public policy, with a particular focus on policy effects. Topics to be covered include case selection, the logic of causal inference, randomized experiments, quasi-experimental designs, comparing quantitative and qualitative approaches, causal mechanisms, and costs and unintended consequences.

subject: SO
title: Introduction to Policy Analysis
Section Details: Lovejoy 102 (Active Learning Classroom) | TR | 2:30 PM - 3:45 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: EC 293, GO 281, PS 214, SC 212, or SO 271
Description: This course offers an introduction to major theories and approaches in the analysis of public policy, with a particular focus on policy effects. Topics to be covered include case selection, the logic of causal inference, randomized experiments, quasi-experimental designs, comparing quantitative and qualitative approaches, causal mechanisms, and costs and unintended consequences.

section: SO 271-A - Introduction to Sociological Research Methods
subject: SO
title: Introduction to Sociological Research Methods
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SO 131
Description: Provides sociology majors with basic intellectual tools for understanding, evaluating, and conducting social science research. Specific objectives include (1) developing rudimentary statistical skills, (2) linking theoretical problems to hypothesis testing and statistical inference, (3) exploring major types of empirical research and their implications for problem solving (e.g., experiments, surveys, participant observation), (4) applying and refining knowledge of sociological methods through diverse readings in both the sociological literature (e.g., American Sociological Review, American Journal of Sociology, Social Forces, Sociological Methodology) and in non-academic publications (e.g., the Economist, the Atlantic, the New York Times).

subject: SO
title: Social Determinants of Health
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SO: Any Sociology course, and Sophomore Class Standing or above
Description: How do social factors like gender, race, and class “get under the skin” to stratify health outcomes? How do political and economic institutions mitigate or exacerbate health disparities? This course provides an overview of historical and contemporary patterns of health inequality in the United States and how social scientists have studied them, contextualizing the US case through comparisons to other societies.

subject: SO
title: Current Topics in Sociology
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SO 271, GO 281, EC 293, or PS 214; and Sophomore Class Standing or above
Description: An advanced reading and discussion class focused on analysis, critique, and application of works published in sociology in the past 18 months. Course is integrated with the department colloquium series; majors and minors who complete two semesters may count the course toward one elective requirement.

title: Qualitative Research Methods
