subject: SO
title: Policy Lab Practicum
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission and must have taken EC 293, GO 281, PS 214, SC 212, or SO 271
Description: For this practicum, students carry out an in-depth, real-world policy analysis or evaluation project in an area of their interest for a partner organization in the community. Students meet as a group once a week, as well as individually with the instructor, who provides close mentoring and support. The bulk of the work is done outside the classroom visiting field sites, consulting with stakeholders, gathering and analyzing data, and producing a professional final report. The practicum serves as a bridge between academic policy knowledge and practical application. This course may be repeated for additional credit.

title: Elementary Spanish I

Through an interactive approach to language learning, students gain communicative proficiency through fast-paced, task- and content-based exercises designed to integrate listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills. Videos, audio, and web materials introduce students to cultural differences within the Spanish speaking world.

section: SP 127H-A - Spanish Language for Heritage Learners
subject: SP
title: Spanish Language for Heritage Learners
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Colby Spanish Placement, 615
Description: Designed for students who come from a variety of Spanish speaking family backgrounds and have some knowledge of Spanish. The purpose of this course is to revitalize and gain confidence in the Spanish you have acquired; to master the language for formal and professional purposes; to improve strategic speaking, reading, and writing skills; to examine and recognize regional, social, and contextual variations; and to enhance your understanding and appreciation of Hispanic and Latinx cultures and sociopolitical realities.  Prerequisite: Permission of the instructor.

subject: SP
title: Conversation, Composition, and Culture
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SP 127 or equivalent
Description: Designed specifically to develop oral skills and critical thinking in Spanish, with additional practice in writing and continued work in vocabulary building and grammar review. This course fosters communication skills through conversation, composition, and analysis of cultural production from the Hispanic and Latinx worlds. Working with a variety of fiction and non-fiction texts and cultural products, students will acquire the skills to critique and interpret while engaging in active thinking.

title: Spanish Composition for Heritage Learners
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SP 127H or Colby Placement score (Spanish), 665
Description: Designed specifically to develop biliteracy skills in heritage learners of Spanish. Students will work in vocabulary building and academic writing literacy through the analysis of different cultural production. This course fosters understand of bilingualism and bilingual contact phenomena, examines and recognizes regional, social, and contextual variations, empower students by reflecting on their own language experiences and practices and builds community by making connections with students of similar backgrounds and life experiences.

section: SP 135I-A - Introduction to Critical Analysis: Indigeneities in Contemporary Popular Culture in the Americas
subject: SP
title: Introduction to Critical Analysis: Indigeneities in Contemporary Popular Culture in the Americas
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SP 128 or equivalent (and must not have taken SP 135* previously)
Description: This interdisciplinary course explores the construction of contemporary urban indigenous identities through an analysis of a wide range of cultural mediums (popular music, audiovisual arts, graphic memory, performance, comics, video games, aesthetics, among others) to analyze emerging patterns of cultural variegations, affective energies, and decolonized daily practices. Geographically, students will examine artistic productions from urban indigenous peoples in the Americas, focusing on indigenous and mestizo Latin America (Abya Yala) and Native American and Indigenous cultures in the United States (Turtle Island). Critical Race course.

section: SP 135M-A - Introduction to Critical Analysis: Hispanic Echo(logies)
subject: SP
title: Introduction to Critical Analysis: Hispanic Echo(logies)
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SP 128 or equivalent (and must not have taken SP 135* previously)
Description: This course explores how the sounds of the Spanish-speaking world reflect history, culture, and society. Moving beyond the written word, students will study soundscapes through the analysis of novels, films, and art. The course provides students with analytical tools to interpret and compare different works (from 16th-century classics to contemporary cinema) to examine how sound and silence reveal deep-seated social dynamics like race, gender, and social class. Through the investigation of these sonic environments, students will examine the relationship between human societies and the natural world, and develop strong skills in critical thinking and argumentation.

subject: SP
title: Advanced Spanish
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SP 128 or equivalent
Description: An in-depth analysis of Spanish grammar, focusing on the more complex and subtle linguistic and cultural dimensions of a variety of syntactical and lexical concepts. Students will achieve an advanced mastery of Spanish grammar and vocabulary.

section: SP 234-A - Diversity and Racism in Contemporary Spain
subject: SP
title: Diversity and Racism in Contemporary Spain
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - SP :: SP: Culture and Identity
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SP 135*
Description: Focuses on the cultures and communities that make up contemporary Spain, with particular emphasis on the modern waves of immigration that have radically changed the country. Covering the latter years of the dictatorship and into the democracy (from 1970 forward), we examine how regionalism, multiculturalism, and diversity have been represented across a range of media and literature in Spain. Topics may include Latin American, African and Asian migration and diasporas, sex and sexuality, racial politics, and linguistic and cultural difference in Spain.

section: SP 239-A - Latin America at the Movies
subject: SP
title: Latin America at the Movies
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SP 135*
Description: An introduction to the cinematography of Latin America covering a broad set of topics, countries and time periods. Students will explore how diverse themes-revolution, modernity, gender, race, labor, and neoliberalism-inform national history, particularly in Mexico, Argentina, Brazil and Cuba, nations that developed an energetic cinematography at various points in the 20th century. Students will gain experience in film analysis and how to articulate the relationship between content and artistic form. Fulfills Spanish G/S requirement.

title: Writing for Gaia: Creative Non-Fiction in Spanish
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - SP :: SP: Health and Environment
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SP 2XX
Description: This course combines reading and analyzing creative non-fiction as a literary genre with a workshop in which students compose their own pieces of writing. We will focus on how sensory experiences with natural environments are adapted into works of non-fiction. Students explore the question of how to allow space for “voices” from non-human beings in a world dominated by anthropocentrism. Students will be able to recognize the main features of creative non-fiction and produce their own examples. Also, students will be able to evaluate key Environmental Humanities ideas in non-fiction nature writing from Spanish and Latin American authors.

section: SP 340-A - Art and Activism in Contemporary Cuba
subject: SP
title: Art and Activism in Contemporary Cuba
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - SP :: SP: Gender and Sex
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: SP 2XX or above
Description: This course will examine how Cuban artists resist state control of the state’s cultural enterprise through artistic practice. The artists studied in this course reject the state’s strategies of isolationism and exceptionalism and bring visibility to art in Cuba and its diaspora, especially by underrepresented artists. Themes will include masculinities and sport; ruins and architecture; infrastructure and energy; sexuality and identity; and censorship and colonialism through artistic practice that prioritizes embodiment while considering Cuban art’s precarity. Students will also develop a facility with queer, postcolonial, and critical race theories that enable critiques of aspects of Cuba’s utopian socialist project.

subject: ST
title: Science, Technology, and Society
Description: What is science, who makes science, and how is scientific authority constructed? What does it mean to understand science and technology as social and cultural practices that produce and regulate truth, knowledge, and bodies? Who benefits from scientific and technological changes, and who loses? In this introduction to the field of science and technology studies, we approach such questions from an interdisciplinary perspective attuned to difference, power relations, social struggles, and the hope of creating a more just and equitable world.

section: ST 120F-A - Writing the Future: Technoscience and Power
subject: ST
title: Writing the Future: Technoscience and Power
Course Tags: Integrated Studies Clusters :: IS: 360 Degrees of A.I.
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year Class Standing
Description: This course introduces first-year students to critical reading and writing about contemporary science and technology. Students learn to analyze, interpret, debate, conduct library research, and write about the power structures that shape technoscientific landscapes. They tackle big questions concerning artificial intelligence, surveillance, reproductive justice, global pandemics, and more, with the aim of using writing to create a more just and equitable world.

section: ST 134-A - Science of Consciousness, Biological and Artificial
subject: ST
title: Science of Consciousness, Biological and Artificial
Course Tags: Integrated Studies Clusters :: IS: 360 Degrees of A.I.
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year Class Standing
Description: Introduces consciousness studies grounded in a scientific approach, beginning with the "hard problem" of consciousness, how phenomenal experience arises from biological systems. Discussions of potential biomolecular and quantum mechanical underpinnings of conscious experience will lead to the debate around what constitutes artificial sentience (AS) with inherent ethical implications. What does identity or consent mean in relationship to an AS? What rights does an AS have? Can humans terminate an AS? In addition to lectures and weekly readings, students will create an AI driven avatar to create a multimedia artifact exploring these questions.

subject: ST
title: Digital Infrastructure and Development
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: AY 112
Description: Infrastructures are complex networks involving movement of people, ideas, and technology. This anthropological class will consider topics of digital technology, "development", time, labor, space, and identity in a global context. In doing so, we will unpack how these structures are, at times, concepts and programs which can exclude and ostracize marginalized members of society. Students will follow classic and new debates in anthropology and informatics literature which will broaden their understanding of infrastructure constructions on a global level.

subject: ST
title: Ecological Restoration and Management
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ES 118, ES 120*, or ST 112
Description: Conservation in the twenty-first century often means intervening to restore degraded lands, manage species, and adapt to climate change. Human societies have shaped landscapes for millennia, using diverse systems of knowledge and management. Industrial development profoundly altered many of those relationships. This course explores the modern science of ecological restoration alongside the complex history of human relationships with the environment and practices of stewardship and land transformation. Through lecture, discussion, and a hands-on restoration lab in the Colby Woods, students learn the practice of ecological restoration while engaging ethical and practical questions about managing ecosystems in a changing world.

subject: ST
title: Food: Biochemistry to Biopolitics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ST 112, or BI 163, or permission of instructor. Students should enter a Prerequisite Override Request (through the Academics dashboard) for instructor approval.
Description: This course examines the socio-technical systems of food through a specific theme (e.g., pomology, dairy, grains). Moving beyond basic nutrition, students analyze the biochemistry of food production and transformation alongside political, environmental, and ethical frameworks. Through inquiry-based labs and research, the course investigates how scientific knowledge and technology shape—and are shaped by—cultural identity, policy, and climate change. Students who wish to have their prerequisites overridden should enter a Prerequisite Override Request (the link to the request can be found on Student Academic Dashboards in Workday.

section: ST 230 L-A - Lab: Food: Biochemistry to Biopolitics
subject: ST
title: Lab: Food: Biochemistry to Biopolitics
Description: Lab for ST 230/ BI 230- Food: Biochemistry to Biopolitics

section: ST 310-A - Creating Future Worlds: Computing, Ethics, and Society
subject: ST
title: Creating Future Worlds: Computing, Ethics, and Society
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: CS 231, C-  or greater
Description: Explores ethical and moral narratives associated with advances in computing/AI technologies. Students will investigate issues in computing ethics highlighting the responsibility of computing professionals to examine the impact of their work on individuals and society. Topics will include: AI bias, digital disparities, autonomous systems, intellectual property law, cybercrime, information privacy and security, tech corporate culture, and professional conduct in a diverse workplace. Students will critically evaluate and apply literature on responsible technology development and professional codes of ethics with evolving technologies.

subject: ST
title: Art, Medicine, and Race
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor Permission: ST 112, AA/AM 171, AA/AM 125, AR 101, or AA/AM/AR 157 - Copy
Description: This humanities lab explores the relations among art, medicine, and ideas about race from the eighteenth century to the present. Focusing on the Atlantic world and the African diaspora, we consider how chattel slavery, colonialism, and racial inequality have shaped constructions of medical knowledge, while medicine has informed conceptions of race as it intersects with gender, sexuality, and class. Students conduct independent research, deliver oral presentations, complete several writing assignments, and engage with contemporary artists and scholars.

section: ST 485-A - Senior Research Seminar in STS
subject: ST
title: Senior Research Seminar in STS
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: ST 112, Senior Class Standing as a STS major or minor, and must have completed a W1 course
Description: This seminar explores the latest scholarship across a wide range of topics in the social study of science and technology. Throughout the semester, students execute an original research project, developed through the synthesis of advanced readings, seminar discussions, thorough literature search and review, and final written work and presentation. Students develop confidence in their voice as a contributing scholar to the field of STS and culminate their interdisciplinary, liberal arts training with advanced inquiry founded in STS methods and frameworks.

section: ST 485-B - Senior Research Seminar in STS
subject: ST
title: Senior Research Seminar in STS

subject: TD
title: Intermediate Dance: Ballet Technique
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: TD 220
Description: After taking TD220, students may choose to repeat the Monday Ballet Technique class as many semesters as they wish. As students progress to 320 with instructor permission, adding 020 is a great way to continue to build strength in conjunction with the advanced contemporary dance technique course. Consistent and frequent physical practice helps students prevent injury and develop increased sophistication and skill. Ballet class moves through traditional progression from barre to center work to petite and grand allegro with an attention to efficient and clear anatomical placement, individuality, and artistry. Prerequisite: TD 220

section: TD 064-A - A performance in Break Burn Build
subject: TD
title: A performance in Break Burn Build
Description: Students participating in the Performance, Theater, and Dance Department production Break Burn Build as performers, designers, stage managers, theater technicians, and other production positions will be registered for credit. Students participating in faculty-directed work register for 264; students performing in a student-directed project register for 164; students who have met their maximum threshold for credit hours, register for 064. In all three cases, this represents an academic commitment, with required attendance. Casting by audition, sign-up, or other selection process. May be taken up to eight times for credit. Nongraded.

section: TD 110-A - Intro to Dance: Physical Practice and Contextual Analysis
subject: TD
title: Intro to Dance: Physical Practice and Contextual Analysis
Description: Introduces students to dance praxis broadly. Students explore multiple models of physical practice (or “techniques”); learn about dance performance historical and cultural contexts; practice watching, describing; understanding and interpreting dance, and engage in choreographic thinking and creative process. Class is active and requires movement exploration and creative collaboration.

section: TD 120-A - First-Year Writing: Performing Spaces/Writing the City
subject: TD
title: First-Year Writing: Performing Spaces/Writing the City
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: Explores how we understand the places, cities, and towns we inhabit. In what ways are our routes through these spaces a kind of performance, and how can writing help us closely observe, describe, analyze, and critique our environments? We'll discuss the embodied and spatial effects of Covid-19 and recent uprisings against anti-black violence and study topics like settler colonialism, resource extraction, redlining, and urban protests, amongst others. Concurrently, we'll try out performance strategies on campus that demonstrate its importance in understanding space. Throughout the semester, we will ask: how does space write the body and how does the body rewrite space?

subject: TD
title: Performance, Politics, and Practice
Description: Introduces students to the study of performance by exploring its power and questioning how it frames our world. We examine how performance helps us make sense of and challenge economic, gendered, sexual, racialized, political, and social structures. Through lectures, critical readings, discussion, field trips, and embodied practice, students will study performance as a creative act, a means of understanding power, a methodology for passing on memory and identity, and a way of comprehending the world. Topics include: theater, dance, performance art, everyday life, protest, and the gendered, sexed, and racialized performance of bodies.

section: TD 125-A - Island Humanities: Exploring the Humanities theme
subject: TD
title: Island Humanities: Exploring the Humanities theme
Description: Offered by the Center for the Arts and Humanities, this one-credit seminar series engages with experts from a variety of fields who explore the humanities theme of “Islands” in all its forms. In this course, you will participate in discussions with scholars, writers, and artists from a wide array of areas, giving you a comprehensive understanding of the theme. Through conversation, debate, and hands-on workshops, you will develop your own ideas and opinions on the theme while participating in humanities-centered modes of inquiry. Nongraded.

subject: TD
title: Stagecraft I
Section Details: Gordon 190 (Active Learning Classroom) | M | 1:00 PM - 4:00 PM
Description: Introduces students to scenic construction, theatrical rigging, lighting production, and prop-making concepts, techniques, equipment, and materials, emphasizing problem solving through research, experimentation, and collaborative learning while considering the environment, economic choices, and safety. Students will learn to appreciate the performative aspects of stagecraft by participating in a behind-the-scenes role during the construction period, technical rehearsals, and performances of a faculty-directed, department production. Previous experience is not necessary.

subject: TD
title: Applied Performance/Production
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Submit a prerequisite override request (on Academic Dashboard) to seek approval.
Description: Students participating in Theater and Dance Department productions as performers, designers, stage managers, theater technicians, and other production positions may register for credit. May be taken up to eight times for credit. Nongraded.

subject: TD
title: Acting I
Section Details: Gordon 280 (Active Learning Classroom) | MW | 2:30 PM - 4:00 PM | 09/09/2026 - 12/21/2026
Description: Explores the use of the body, voice, emotion, and intellect to create a theatrical character. Through close study of several acting systems, students prepare monologues and scenes to articulate possible interpretations of a play script or performance clearly and effectively. In-class performances further an awareness of individual and ensemble physicality in order to communicate emotion, thought, aesthetic intention, and mind-body awareness. Emphasis on analysis and concentration. Final performances stress the benefits and consequences of creative and aesthetic risk. No prior experience necessary.

title: Acting I

In-class performances further an awareness of individual and ensemble physicality in order to communicate emotion, thought, aesthetic intention, and mind-body awareness. section: TD 220-A - Intermediate Dance: Techniques in Context
subject: TD
title: Intermediate Dance: Techniques in Context
Description: This course focuses on ballet and contemporary dance. Progressive  warm-ups focus on increasing efficiency of movement articulation  at the joints, followed by locomotor patterns and phrase material  that explore more complex coordination challenges. This course  addresses movement traditions with an understanding of their contexts, histories, value systems, and contemporary applications through introductions to histories of ballet and contemporary dance with  viewings, reflection, and experiential anatomy exercises.

section: TD 229-A - Restaging the Real: 20th Century Theater and Performance
subject: TD
title: Restaging the Real: 20th Century Theater and Performance
Description: Throughout the 20th century, theatre and performance engage with crises of representation, by turns rejecting and reworking the concept of the “real” toward new forms and purposes. Through readings (plays, manifestos, performance history texts, performance theory), screenings (recorded performance, films), lecture, and discussion, this course will explore ways in which these experimental evolutions respond to surrounding sociopolitical contexts and craft interconnected histories. Students will trace major developments across key movements (e.g. symbolism, theatre of the absurd, postdramatic theatre, etc), and investigate how each rethinks/disrupts “the real” amid the echoes of early realism.

subject: TD
title: Stagecraft II
Section Details: Gordon 190 (Active Learning Classroom) | F | 1:00 PM - 4:00 PM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: TD 139
Description: Further exploration of scenic construction, theatrical rigging, lighting production, and prop-making concepts, techniques, equipment, and materials, emphasizing problem solving through research, experimentation, and collaborative learning while considering the environment, economic choices, and safety. An expansion of the course of study from Stagecraft I in which students will examine scene painting, computer-aided drafting (CAD), and CNC computer-assisted woodworking. Independent out-of-class work is essential.

section: TD 243-A - Leadership Behind the Scenes: Stage Management
subject: TD
title: Leadership Behind the Scenes: Stage Management
Description: It takes a coordinated effort by many people to put on a professional performance; stage managers are the conductors behind the scenes of those shows. In this course, students take a peek backstage and learn the complex systems by which productions are fully realized. Class explores techniques for successful collaborative work and helps students identify personal and productive leadership styles.

section: TD 264A-A - Colby Theater Company- Fall Play
subject: TD
title: Colby Theater Company- Fall Play
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Submit a prerequisite override request (on Academic Dashboard) to seek approval.
Description: Colby Theater Company Fall 2026 will help develop and perform a new play, Persistence, by Environmental Studies Professor Gail Carlson, about PFAS or “forever chemicals” and their impacts on farms and farmers. Students will rehearse 2-3 times per week and collaborate with faculty and professional guest designers to create a fully-supported production running for three performances November 13-14. Enrollment by audition only. Variable credit (1-3) depending on level of participation. This production-outcome class is designated as an Environmental Humanities course.

section: TD 264B-A - Colby Dance Company: Fall Repertory Projects
subject: TD
title: Colby Dance Company: Fall Repertory Projects
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Submit a prerequisite override request (on Academic Dashboard) to seek approval.

subject: TD
title: Advanced Dance: Contemporary Technique
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: TD: Student has completed, is in-progress, or is enrolled in: TD 220 and 221 or with Instructor Permission
Description: With the guiding principles of exploration, risk-taking, innovation, and individuality, students take an advanced approach to dance technique as embodied inquiry and as a profound way of knowing and learning. Each class presents an opportunity to engage in a process of discovery through physical experiences both familiar and new. These studio classes are meant to support a student’s work in departmental creative praxis courses or performance companies, deepening one’s sense of agency, specificity, and nuance in increasingly complex movement patterns.

subject: TD
title: Applied Choreography
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: TD 285 and CO-REQ: TD 110, 020, 220 or 320 or with Instructor Permission
Description: Students with previous experience in contemporary choreography at the college level will create original works for formal performance through a rigorous creative process that includes feedback from faculty and peers, presentation of design concepts, and collaboration with student lighting designers. Course will address contemporary issues in dance including viewings of work by active, acclaimed, and emerging professional choreographers. Co-requisite: TD 110, 020, 220 or 320.

subject: TD
title: Seminar: Ways of Seeing
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: PTD Majors/Minors with Junior Class Standing or above and must be registered for TD 124 or have completed it previously (or with Instructor permission)
Description: Students deepen their understanding of cultures, histories, aesthetics of performance and to further develop critical and analytical skills. Seminar-style discussions based on readings and viewings. Students will assume discussion leadership roles. Professional preparation workshops, and peer-to-peer tutorial sessions in which the reading/viewing material and the discussion are led by the students. Student majors will develop their Pathway rationale documents, portfolios, and senior capstone project plans within this course.

section: TL 101-A - Teaching and Learning Essentials for Peer Learning Assistants
subject: TL
title: Teaching and Learning Essentials for Peer Learning Assistants
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Submit a prerequisite override request (on Academic Dashboard) to seek approval.
Description: This course is the first course offered by the Center for Academic Success and Transformative Learning. TL courses (Transformative Learning) will provide essential content knowledge about teaching and learning along with application skills (facilitating student support sessions) for Peer Learning Support roles, such as the Learning Assistants who support active and inclusive learning in courses working with the Center for Teaching and Learning.

subject: WD
title: Writers' Workshop
Description: An individualized, weekly tutorial session with a trained peer writing tutor from the Farnham Writers' Center. Meets weekly for 1 hour during the time of your choice for a total of (at least) 10 hours per semester. Open to students from first-years to seniors. Students usually take WP112 with a W1 (first-year writing) , senior thesis, or other writing-intensive courses. Meetings may focus on writing assignments, reading assignments, grammar, professors' feedback or anything else related to writing or research for any courses. May be repeated for credit. Nongraded.

section: WD 115B-A - First-Year Writing: Genealogy: Research and Storytelling
subject: WD
title: First-Year Writing: Genealogy: Research and Storytelling
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: In this writing-intensive course, students investigate personal histories that matter to them while developing skills in research, writing, and oral communication. Bringing together genealogical and academic research practices, students will work with primary and secondary sources to explore larger questions of history, place, and identity. Students may define “family” broadly and will have flexibility in choosing the people, communities, or stories they wish to explore. Throughout the semester, students will communicate their ideas across multiple forms–writing, speaking, and interviewing, among others–as they adapt their work for different audiences and purposes. Students will complete three essays, deliver two presentations, and design a culminating visual project.

section: WD 115C-A - First-Year Writing: Reimagining the Essay
subject: WD
title: First-Year Writing: Reimagining the Essay
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: Reconsiders the essay's potential for self-expression and analytical argumentation. Students read powerful essays of the past 70 years, write five essays, and reimagine their relationship to the genre. Of particular emphasis are clarity of expression, development of ideas, logical organization, and effective and correct use of research to support claims--both to prepare for future writing assignments and to appreciate the form as a means to express ideas complexly, gracefully, and persuasively.

section: WD 115D-A - First-Year Writing: Food for Thought
subject: WD
title: First-Year Writing: Food for Thought
Section Details: Miller Library 205 (Active Learning Classroom) | MWF | 9:00 AM - 9:50 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: The food we interact with is an expression of our humanity, our many cultures, our selves. This peer-review and process-oriented course combines reading across genres with the development of writing skills that can be applied in all disciplines. Students will practice personal narrative, argument, synthesis, and research-based writing and read work by both new and established authors.

section: WD 115D-B - First-Year Writing: Food for Thought
subject: WD
title: First-Year Writing: Food for Thought
Section Details: Miller Library 205 (Active Learning Classroom) | MWF | 10:00 AM - 10:50 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: The food we interact with is an expression of our humanity, our many cultures, our selves. This peer-review and process-oriented course combines reading across genres with the development of writing skills that can be applied in all disciplines. Students will practice personal narrative, argument, synthesis, and research-based writing and read work by both new and established authors.

section: WD 115F-A - First-Year Writing: Writing about Writing
subject: WD
title: First-Year Writing: Writing about Writing
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: This writing-intensive course explores how public writing—graffiti, street art, and propaganda from World War II to today—reflects and challenges systems of power. How are visual and textual messages used to resist or reinforce dominant narratives? What stories do walls, posters, and murals tell—and erase? Through critical reading, rhetorical analysis, and multimodal composition, students examine rhetorical strategies employed by artists, activists, and institutions to explore themes such as racial justice, surveillance, public memory, and the politics of visibility. Assignments include multimodal compositions that focus on rhetorical analysis, personal narratives, and original artwork, understanding that all writing is social engagement. Students engage with feedback and revision as part of a collaborative community.

section: WD 115S-A - First-Year Writing: Writing about STEM Writing
subject: WD
title: First-Year Writing: Writing about STEM Writing
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: In this course, you will examine how writers in STEM fields present evidence, create arguments, and communicate with different audiences. You will analyze a range of STEM genres, including popular science journalism and academic research articles, to understand the rhetorical choices writers use to explain complex ideas. You will write three analytical essays and a final project in which you write a researched argument about a STEM issue of your choice and translate that argument for a public audience. This class includes weekly writing, peer workshops, and revision to support your understanding of making arguments, organizing, and synthesizing sources. You will also learn appropriate citation practices and the ethics of academic writing in STEM fields.

section: WD 115T-A - First-year Writing: Monster Theory Across Genres
subject: WD
title: First-year Writing: Monster Theory Across Genres
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: This first-year writing course explores representations of monstrosity from classical mythology to film representations of werewolves, vampires, and the monsters of the modern age. The central question of the course springs from the etymology of the word “monster,” which derives from the Latin words “to show” and “to warn.” What, then, are monsters showing us, and what exactly are they warning us about? As we examine what monsters from film and story reveal about culture, identity, and power, students will complete four major, revised writing projects designed to develop the critical reading, analytical thinking, and persuasive writing skills essential for college-level work. This course fulfills Colby's W1 first-year writing requirement.

section: WD 115T-B - First-year Writing: Monster Theory Across Genres
subject: WD
title: First-year Writing: Monster Theory Across Genres
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously

section: WD 116-A - The Stories We Tell Ourselves about Ourselves: Intro to Folklore
subject: WD
title: The Stories We Tell Ourselves about Ourselves: Intro to Folklore
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: Folklore examines how human beings create, modify, and circulate “the stories we tell ourselves about ourselves.” This broad overview of folklore considers its histories, methodologies, and globally diverse examples from genres such as rumors, crafts, folk medicine, ghost stories, memes, children’s rhymes, rituals, and folk dance. We will also consider how folklore both challenges and reinforces oppressive social norms.

section: WD 116B-A - The Country and the City
subject: WD
title: The Country and the City
Section Details: Miller Library 253 (Seminar Classroom) | TR | 9:30 AM - 10:45 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: This course examines representations of country and city life in literature, from antiquity to the present. Through in-class discussion and written work, students will practice techniques of literary analysis, employ critical thinking in analyzing and discussing literature, and will gain a foundation in all aspects of college-level writing. Topics for class discussion include: economic, racial, and historical factors that contribute to literary imaginings of country and city life; how and why country or city life is romanticized or demonized in literature; how aesthetic representations of country and city have changed over time.

section: WD 120A-A - Language, Thought, and Writing: Literary Conversations
subject: WD
title: Language, Thought, and Writing: Literary Conversations
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: First-Year class standing or has not taken a W1 previously
Description: Individual works of literature take part in a larger literary conversation that transcends time and space. Writers join the conversation by replicating existing literary forms and conventions. They also respond to perennial themes that have sparked writers' imaginations. Literary scholars also engage in ongoing conversations about the purpose and meaning of literary texts. We will enter these conversations by reading, writing about, and discussing literary texts. We will have regular opportunities to respond creatively and analytically, in speech and writing, to some amazing poems, plays, and novels.

section: WG 101-A - Introduction to Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies
subject: WG
title: Introduction to Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: An introduction to the interdisciplinary field of women's, gender, and sexuality studies, using classical and contemporary texts. An examination of the variety of feminist, anti-racist, and queer theoretical approaches to understanding raced, gendered and sexual lives in historical contexts. Previously listed as WG201.

section: WG 117-A - A Passage to India: India and the Western Imagination
subject: WG
title: A Passage to India: India and the Western Imagination
Course Tags: Program of Study Requirement - RE :: RE: Eastern Religious Traditions
Program of Study Requirement - RE :: RE: Identity
Program of Study Requirement - RE :: RE: Interpretation
Description: Beginning with Walt Whitman's romantic journey toward the "soul" of the universe, Western attitudes towards India and India's encounter with Western culture will be studied. Literature and film include A Passage to India, The Razor's Edge, The English Patient, Siddhartha, The Namesake, Gitanjali, Blinded by the Light,  and Four Quartets. Historical, political, religious, and visual context of the texts will be provided. A close reading of the texts for their aesthetic value, their existential disclosures, and as narratives on colonialism, racism, and orientalism.

section: WG 120B-A - Critical Inquiries in Medical Ethics
subject: WG
title: Critical Inquiries in Medical Ethics
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: Instructor permission required. Please contact Course Instructor directly for approval.
Description: We will engage with perspectives from feminist bioethics, disability studies, and critical race studies as a basis for analyzing, then developing, ideas and arguments about key topics in the field of medical ethics such as vaccination mandates, racialized health disparities, and biomedical research exploitation. Through frequent exercises and essay assignments, students will cultivate a sophisticated writing process that fosters intellectual growth as well as precision of analysis, persuasive argumentation, coherent organization, selection and incorporation of scholarly sources including scrupulous citation practices, and clarity of style.

subject: WG
title: Feminist Theories and Methodologies
Section Details: Miller Library 241 (Seminar Classroom) | TR | 9:30 AM - 10:45 AM
Student Eligibility Rule: PREREQ: WGSS Majors and Minors
Description: Takes an interdisciplinary, intersectional, and progressively transnational approach to feminist theory of the past three decades. Particular focus is given to feminist epistemology as we examine the similarities, differences, and conversations between postcolonial and postmodern feminist theory.Students will additionally engage with contemporary subfields in Women’s Studies including affect theory (emotions, sensations, and the body), feminist disability studies, transnational feminist theory, and new materialisms.

subject: WG
title: Surveillance Culture
Section Details: Miller Library 253 (Seminar Classroom) | TR | 11:00 AM - 12:15 PM
Description: Investigates the history and contemporary manifestations of surveillance culture in the United States. Asks about the roles played by surveillance in American culture, and the ways it shape our bodies, behaviors, relationships, communities, and political possibilities. We look at how surveillance unevenly affects marginalized communities, and consider how artists and activists have responded to surveillance culture through tools of resistance. Students will learn to use multiple disciplinary and theoretical frameworks and conduct original research into the techniques and effects of surveillance technologies.
